2a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna names the four primary categories of damage: ox, pit, maveh, and fire.
Each primary category is distinct; halakhot of one cannot be inferred from another, based on living-spirit differences.
Ox, maveh and fire share a mobile nature causing harm, unlike the pit, which stays in place.
Common feature of all four: their typical harm, and the owner must guard against it and pay restitution.
Gemara infers from the mishna's term primary categories that subcategories must also exist.
Asks whether subcategories are governed by the same halakhot as their primary categories.
Cites the Shabbat mishna listing forty-less-one primary categories of labor.
Repeats the inference from the term primary categories to the existence of subcategories, now for Shabbat.
For Shabbat labors, subcategories match primaries in sin-offering and stoning liability alike.
Asks what practical difference exists between a primary category and a subcategory.
Difference: two unwitting primary labors, or two subcategories of different primaries, each incur their own sin-offering.
A primary plus its own subcategory in one lapse incurs only a single sin-offering.
Raises Rabbi Eliezer's view that one is liable for a subcategory alongside a primary.
Asks why one labor is called primary and the other subcategory, given that liability is the same.
Labels follow significance in the Tabernacle: labors significant there are primary, others subcategories.
Cites the impurity mishna listing primary categories, bringing a parallel example from ritual impurity.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna's impurity example: subcategories of corpse-impurity are not alike their primary category.
Primary impurity from a corpse defiles persons and vessels, while its subcategory defiles only food and drink.
Asks what Rav Pappa held about this point.
Rav Pappa: among damage primaries, some subcategories match their primary and some do not.
Baraita lists three primary damage categories from the ox: horn, tooth, and foot.
Asks from where the primary category of horn-goring is derived.
Derives goring-with-horn from Exodus 21:28, citing Kings' iron horns as proof that goring uses horns.
Adds Deuteronomy 33:17, the firstborn bull with horns of a wild ox, as further support.
Asks what the second verse introduced by 'and it says' is meant to establish.
Objects that legal derivations cannot rest on Prophets, since they are not Torah text.
Answers with Deuteronomy's firstborn-bull verse, which is from the Torah itself.
Upholds the citation: the verse merely discloses that goring is done with a horn, not a legal derivation.
Concludes that goring is performed with the horn, and the verse is simply a disclosure.
Raises a concern: the distinction between innocuous and forewarned ox might apply only to detached horns.
Cites the Deuteronomy verse on the firstborn bull to show attached horns also count as goring.
Asks what the subcategories of goring are.
Subcategories of goring: pushing, biting, crouching, and kicking, done with the body to cause damage.
Asks why goring is a primary category while pushing, which is also written in the Torah, is not.
Notes that the verse on pushing is also written, so pushing should also be a primary category.
Replies that the verse's pushing is in fact goring, since the same act is described with both terms.
Baraita opens with pushing and closes with goring, showing the two terms describe one action.
Asks what distinguishes an ox goring a person from the wording used for goring a person.
Asks what distinguishes the wording used for an ox goring an animal.
A person can defend himself, so the Torah uses the stronger term for goring a person.
An animal cannot defend itself and is easily hurt, so the Torah uses the lesser-force term for it.
Incidentally, a forewarned ox for persons is forewarned for animals, but not the reverse.
Asks whether biting is a subcategory of eating, since the animal both bites and eats with its teeth.
No: eating gives the animal pleasure, whereas biting is done purely to cause damage.
Asks whether crouching and kicking are subcategories of trampling with the feet.
No: trampling damage is commonplace while the animal rarely crouches or kicks on utensils.
Rather, subcategories are dissimilar to their primary, as Rav Pappa said.
Asks which primary category Rav Pappa had in mind, and what makes goring distinct.
Goring is distinct because the ox aims to cause damage and its owner must guard it.
Objects that the subcategories share the same features, aiming to cause damage and requiring owner's guarding.
Subcategories of goring are like goring; Rav Pappa's dissimilarity refers to tooth and foot.
Asks where tooth and foot are written in the Torah to make them primary categories.
Baraita cites Exodus 22:4, the verse on an animal consuming a field, as the source.
Sending forth refers to trampling by feet, supported by Isaiah 32:20 on the ox and donkey.
Consumed refers to eating by teeth, supported by the Kings verse on consuming as with fire.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Completes the quoted verse from Kings on consuming until all is gone.
Baraita cites 'and he sends forth' as trampling, supported by Isaiah's verse on the feet of ox and donkey.
Asks how the phrase would be interpreted if that verse did not exist.
Goring and eating are each written elsewhere, so the phrase must refer to trampling.
The verse is needed to rule out that both phrases refer to eating, one with total and one with partial destruction.
Asks how we derive liability for eating-type damage where the object is not fully destroyed.
Eating is juxtaposed with trampling, so liability applies whether or not the object is fully destroyed.
Baraita cites 'and it consumed' as eating, supported by Kings' verse on consuming with the tooth.
Repeats the Kings phrase on consuming until all is gone as the reason for the eating interpretation.
Asks how the phrase would be interpreted if the other verse did not exist.
Goring and trampling are written elsewhere, so the phrase must refer to eating.
The verse is needed to rule out both phrases referring to trampling, one for self-caused and one for sent animals.
Asks how we derive liability for trampling where the animal caused damage on its own.
Trampling is juxtaposed with eating, so owner liability applies whether he sent the animal or not.
Suggests the Merciful One could write only 'and he sends forth', which would already cover both categories.
Shows 'sends forth' connotes trampling, citing Isaiah 32:20 on the feet of ox and donkey.
Shows 'sends forth' connotes eating, citing Deuteronomy 32:24 on the teeth of animals.
Without the extra phrase, the verse could mean either trampling or eating, so it is needed to fix the eating case.
Asks why both categories would not be derived equally, leaving the phrase unnecessary.
The phrase teaches that the owner is liable even when the animal damaged on its own.
Asks what a subcategory of eating is.
Rubbing against a wall or soiling produce with rolling, done for the animal's own pleasure.
Asks what distinguishes eating as a primary category from its subcategories.
Subcategories of eating also involve the animal's pleasure and the owner's duty to guard, so they are not dissimilar.
Subcategories of eating are like eating, so Rav Pappa's dissimilarity must refer to trampling's subcategories.
Asks what a subcategory of trampling is.
Damage by the body, entangled hair, a rope, a bit, or a neck bell while walking.
Asks what distinguishes trampling as a primary category, given its commonplace damage.
Its subcategories also involve commonplace damage and the owner's duty to guard, so they are not dissimilar.
Subcategories of trampling are like trampling, so Rav Pappa's dissimilarity must refer to pit subcategories.
Asks what a subcategory of pit is.
If the primary pit is ten handbreadths and the subcategory nine, neither depth is written in the Torah.
Not difficult: the Torah's pit with a dead animal is ten handbreadths, which is primary.
Cites Exodus 21:34 on the carcass being for the owner, which the Merciful One stated.
Tradition: a ten-handbreadth pit kills, a nine-handbreadth pit only injures, so each is a primary for its own kind of damage.
Rav Pappa's dissimilar subcategories refer to pit obstacles: stone, knife or load left in the public domain.
Asks under what circumstances the owner is liable for these obstacles, given Rav and Shmuel's views.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the obstacles were not declared ownerless, the earlier identification as pit or ox conflicts with each Sage's view.
Asks what distinguishes the pit as a unique category, given its ownerless obstacles' similar features.
Pit's creation is done in a damage-causing manner, and obstacles in the public domain share this, so they are alike.
Subcategories of pit are like pit; Rav Pappa's dissimilarity must refer to the subcategory of maveh.
Asks what the primary category of maveh is.
Per Shmuel, maveh is eating, and its subcategories were already shown to be like eating.
Per Rav, maveh is the category of a person causing damage, not property or animals.
Asks what primary and subcategories would exist under Rav's reading of maveh.
Proposes awake versus asleep as the distinction, but a mishna holds a person liable whether awake or asleep.
Cites the mishna that a person is always liable for damage, whether awake or asleep.
Asks what the case of phlegm and spittle would look like as a possible subcategory.
Damage in flight is direct action, while damage after landing is an ownerless obstacle, a subcategory of pit.
Subcategories of maveh are like maveh, so Rav Pappa's dissimilarity must refer to subcategories of fire.
Asks what a subcategory of fire is, using an object dropped from a roof by wind.
If the object caused damage while moving through the air, that is a case of fire.
Asks what distinguishes fire as a unique category, since wind also contributes.
Wind likewise contributes to the roof-object damage, so its subcategories are like fire.
Subcategories of fire are like fire, so Rav Pappa's dissimilarity must refer to trampling.
Objects: subcategories of trampling were already established as like trampling.
Pebbles propelled by a walking animal are liable by tradition for half damages, a rule not written explicitly.
Asks why this unique rule is still classed as a subcategory of trampling, given its different payment.
Rava raised a dilemma on whether such half damages are paid from the animal's body or superior property.
Though Rava doubted it, Rav Pappa considered payment from superior property obvious, hence the classification.
Asks why Rava classes this as trampling, given its differences, rather than as a distinct category.
Cites the mishna listing the categories of maveh and fire.
Asks what the term maveh means.
Rav reads maveh as a person causing damage; Shmuel reads it as eating.
Rav cites Isaiah 21:12, where the terms for inquire refer to a person who inquires.
Shmuel cites Obadiah 1:6, where nivu relates to revealed teeth, hence eating.
Asks from where it follows that nivu connotes eating.
Rav Yosef's Aramaic rendering of nivu as revealed shows maveh refers to teeth shown when eating.
Asks why Rav did not read maveh as eating, as Shmuel does.
Rav could object that the mishna's form is maveh, not the passive niveh.
Asks why Shmuel did not read maveh as a person's action, as Rav does.
Shmuel could object that the mishna's form is bo'eh, not maveh, for actions one causes another to take.
Verses are not precise for either Sage, so their dispute must rest on another issue.
Asks why Rav did not read maveh as eating, given the mishna's ox category.
Rav holds the tanna's ox category covers goring, eating, and trampling, leaving maveh for a person.
Rav Yehuda: the tanna teaches ox for horn and maveh for tooth, so maveh is eating.
Goring has no pleasure for the animal, while eating does, so the two categories are contrasted.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Eating, lacking intent to harm, is not like goring, whose animal intends to cause damage.
Asks whether goring could be derived from eating a fortiori, since goring is the stricter case.
The Torah had to state goring, lest one think the owner is exempt as with a slave's or maidservant's damage.
Rav Ashi: slave cases are exempt only to prevent a slave from exploiting liability to avenge on his master.
The mishna rules out deriving ox from maveh by contrasting intent and pleasure in each category.
Asks why trampling is absent from the mishna's list of ox categories.
The general closing principle in the mishna covers trampling as well.
Asks why the Torah would not state trampling explicitly if the tanna intended it.
Rava: the tanna teaches ox for foot and maveh for tooth, contrasting commonplace damage and pleasure in each.
Asks why goring is missing from the mishna's list of ox categories, given Shmuel's reading.
The closing general principle of the mishna covers goring as well.
Asks why goring is not explicitly taught if the tanna intended it.
The mishna speaks of categories where the animal is forewarned from the outset; goring is not like that.
Asks why Shmuel did not read maveh as Man, as Rav does.
If maveh were man, the mishna's latter clause would not need to mention damage by a person.
Asks why the tanna did not list man in the first clause among primary categories.
The first clause treats damage caused by property; damage caused by one's body is not treated there.
Asks the same about Rav: the latter clause mentions man's damage.
Rav: that mention adds human damage among the cases where the owner is forewarned.
Asks what the mishna's contrast between ox and maveh means under Rav's reading.
Ox's ransom and man's four types of indemnity are the points of contrast the mishna makes.
Cites the mishna's common denominator that these categories typically cause damage.
Asks whether an ox typically causes damage by goring.
Once a forewarned ox has gored repeatedly, goring becomes its typical manner of causing damage.
Asks whether damage by a man while sleeping is typical for him.
A sleeper contracts and extends his limbs, so damaging nearby objects is his typical manner.
If maveh is man, the safeguarding phrase fits poorly, and Karna's baraita has the same difficulty.
Rabbi Abbahu corrected the baraita to state that a person is responsible for safeguarding his own body.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara restates the mishna's point that a person is responsible for safeguarding his own body.
Rav Mari proposes that maveh refers to water, citing Isaiah's verse on fire boiling water.
The verse says water boils from fire, with fire as subject, so it does not prove maveh means water.
Rav Zevid proposes that maveh is fire, since the verse's tiveh is written with fire.
If maveh were fire, the mishna would list only three categories, not four.
Suggests the tanna taught ox with two categories, but that reading contradicts the mishna's wording.
The living-spirit contrast in the mishna cannot fit fire, so maveh cannot be fire.
Rabbi Oshaya's baraita lists thirteen primary categories: four bailees, five indemnities, and the mishna's four.
Asks why the mishna teaches only four categories when Rabbi Oshaya lists nine more.
For Shmuel, the mishna covers property damage only, so bodily categories are not taught.
Asks why, for Rav, the mishna does not teach these nine categories.
For Rav, the mishna's primary category of man covers all human-caused damage, including Oshaya's additions.
Asks whether Rabbi Oshaya, too, would already be covered by the mishna's category of man.
Rabbi Oshaya distinguishes two kinds of human damage: injuring a person, and damaging an ox or property.
Asks why the ox category is not likewise split into two cases: ox injuring ox, and ox injuring a person.
Human damage to property pays only for the loss, while injuring a person adds indemnities; ox cases need no such split.
Bailees and borrowers also damage property, so Oshaya's separate listing of them appears inconsistent.
Oshaya lists man for direct damage, and the bailees for damage that occurs on its own.
Rabbi Ḥiyya lists twenty-four categories, including thefts, indemnities, conspiring witnesses, and teruma offenses.
Asks why Rabbi Oshaya omitted the eleven fine-based categories.
Oshaya teaches only cases of monetary restitution, not cases where a fine is paid.
Asks why Oshaya did not list the thief and robber, which are monetary restitution cases.
He does include them: the unpaid bailee who falsely swears the deposit was stolen pays like a thief.
Asks why Rabbi Ḥiyya lists the unpaid bailee and borrower separately if they are already covered.
Ḥiyya distinguishes theft of property obtained legitimately from theft of property obtained illegitimately.

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why Rabbi Oshaya omits conspiring witnesses from his list, given that they pay a fine rather than restitution.
Presses that if Rabbi Oshaya follows Rabbi Akiva he should list separate categories for ox damaging property and ox injuring a person.
Cites a mishna where Rabbi Akiva makes the liability for an innocuous ox injuring a person differ from liability for property damage.
Explains that Rabbi Akiva softened his position, so the innocuous ox injuring a person is not a primary category.
Quotes a baraita where Rabbi Akiva limits payment for injury to a person to the ox's body, derived from a verse.
Asks why the rapist, seducer and defamer, all paying restitution, are not listed as categories.
Argues each payment named is either already covered as damage or is a fine, which Rabbi Oshaya does not address.
Asks why those who render teruma impure, mix teruma, or pour wine for idolatry are not listed as categories.
Argues that whether invisible damage counts as damage or as a fine, the cases are either already included or outside the list.
Suggests Rabbi Hiyya holds invisible damage is not damage, since otherwise he would have listed it as restitution.
Rejects the suggestion: Rabbi Hiyya treats visible and invisible damage as distinct types within his list.
Asks what purpose the total of twenty-four categories in Rabbi Hiyya's list serves, given the other totals.
Explains the count excludes an informer and a priest who renders an offering piggul.
Asks why Rabbi Hiyya did not list the informer case, given he listed the piggul case or omitted it for consecrated items.
Explains the informer differs because its damage is done through speech, and Rabbi Hiyya does not cover speech damage.
Objects that the defamer's damage is through speech, yet Rabbi Hiyya lists it.
Explains the defamer case is speech tied to an action, namely intercourse with the wife.
Objects that conspiring witnesses are speech without action, yet Rabbi Hiyya lists them.
Explains the Torah treats the witnesses' speech as an action, citing the verse that they must do as they conspired.
Asks what the subcategories are, since the terms primary categories imply subcategories for each rabbi's list.
Rabbi Abbahu says calling them primary categories means each one is paid from the best property, not that subcategories exist.
Asks what the source is for paying from one's best property in all these categories.
Derives it by verbal analogy from the terms in place of, give, pay and money found in the four verses.
Quotes the mishna: the defining feature of the Ox category is not like that of the Pit-Maveh category.
Asks what the mishna means by stating that the categories are not alike.
Rava's teaching: the Torah should write one category and derive the rest, but one category cannot be derived from another.
The mishna continues: the features of Ox and Maveh, which have a living spirit, are not like the Fire category.
Asks what the tanna means by this continuation.
Rav Mesharshiyya, citing Rava, explains the tanna is teaching the same point about the Fire category as the previous clause.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Teaching that the Torah should write only two primary categories, since no category can be derived from two others.
Rava teaches that all categories except Goring can be derived from Pit, since they are forewarned from the outset.
On the opposing view, Goring is the superior category, so it too can be derived from a common factor.
Asks why the Torah writes all primary categories explicitly if they can be derived.
Goring is written explicitly to distinguish the halakhot of an innocuous ox from those of a forewarned ox.
Eating and Trampling are written to exempt owners whose animals act in these ways in a public domain.
Pit exempts vessels falling in a pit; for Rabbi Yehuda it also exempts a pit's owner for a person's death.
Man is written to make the offender liable for four additional types of indemnity for injuring a person.
Fire is written to exempt liability for a concealed object consumed by fire.
Asks what halakha Fire teaches explicitly, given that Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable even for concealed objects.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the added cases: fire scorching a plowed field or singeing stones, where the object survives intact yet liability still applies.
The mishna's common denominator is that the components typically cause damage; it is stated to add further cases.
Asks in order to add what halakha the mishna's common denominator is cited.
Abaye: it adds liability for stones, knives or loads placed on a roof that fall in a wind and cause damage.
Asks under what circumstances liability arises, noting a case of moving objects would be a subcategory of Fire.
If so, what distinguishes Fire as a category, since the wind-borne objects also involve another force and remain the owner's property?
Proposes the case of objects resting on the ground as an obstacle, asks when liable, and says a declared-ownerless case is Pit.
What distinguishes Pit as a category, given the roof objects also have an initial formation causing risk and remain the owner's property?
Proposes liability even without a declaration of ownerlessness, and asks what the common denominator then teaches, per Shmuel.
The mishna teaches liability only for declared-ownerless objects, which differ from Pit because another force, the wind, causes the damage.
Fire proves that another force involved in causing damage does not exempt one from liability, so the derivation from Pit stands.
What distinguishes Fire is that its typical manner is to spread and cause damage, unlike objects blown into the public domain.
Pit proves that an atypical manner of causing damage does not exempt the owner, so liability is derived from Pit and Fire together.
Rava: the common denominator adds liability for a pit-like obstacle rolled by passersby' feet or animal hooves to cause damage elsewhere.
Asks what circumstances apply to that case, and says a declared-ownerless case is a subcategory of Pit.
What distinguishes Pit as a category, given the rolled obstacle also has an initial formation and remains the owner's property?
Proposes liability even without ownerlessness, and asks what the common denominator then teaches, per Shmuel.
The mishna covers declared-ownerless objects, which differ from Pit because Pit's damage comes from the owner's own digging action, not passersby.
Ox proves that the owner's action not causing the damage does not exempt him from restitution, so the derivation from Pit stands.
What distinguishes Ox is that its typical manner is to proceed and cause damage, unlike an obstacle kicked by passersby.
Pit proves that a non-typical manner of causing damage does not exempt the owner, so the derivation from Pit still applies.
Pit and Ox each show the other's defining feature is not decisive, so liability is derived from their common denominator as the mishna states.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: the common denominator adds liability for damage from sewage and water that people are permitted to pour into the street.
A baraita permits draining sewage into the street in the rainy season and holds the person liable if the drainage causes damage.
Asks what circumstances apply if the sewage damages while moving, since that would be direct action like any other damage.
Proposes the case where sewage came to rest and a passerby slipped on it, and asks when liable, with a declared-ownerless case being Pit.
What distinguishes Pit as a category, given the sewage also has an initial formation causing risk and remains the owner's property?
Proposes liability even without ownerlessness, and asks what the common denominator then teaches, per Shmuel.
The mishna covers declared-ownerless sewage, which differs from Pit because Pit is dug without permission, while this sewage was channeled with permission.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ox proves that an animal entering the public domain with permission does not exempt its owner, so the derivation from Ox stands.
Ox is distinguished by its typical manner of moving and causing damage, which sewage lacks, so the derivation is challenged.
Pit proves the atypical manner of causing damage does not exempt the owner, so liability is derived from Pit and Ox together.
Ravina: the common denominator is stated to add liability for a fallen wall or tree that caused damage.
Cites a mishna: the owner of a wall or tree that fell and caused damage is exempt only within the time allotted for removal.
Asks under what circumstances liability arises, and says a declared-ownerless tree or wall is a subcategory of Pit.
Pit is distinguished by commonplace damage and the owner's responsibility for it, which the fallen tree or wall also share.
If not declared ownerless, per Shmuel, the case is still a subcategory of Pit.
The mishna covers declared-ownerless trees and walls, which differ from Pit because Pit's initial formation risks damage, while planting or building does not.
Ox proves that a non-damaging initial formation does not exempt the owner, so liability is derived from Ox.
Ox's typical manner of moving and causing damage is absent in the case of a tree or wall, so the derivation is challenged.
Pit proves a lack of typical manner does not exempt, so liability for trees and walls is derived from Pit and Ox together.
The mishna states that the one liable for damage must pay from best-quality land.
Asks why the tanna uses the unusual expression ḥav instead of the standard ḥayyav.
Rav: the tanna is a Jerusalemite who uses a concise formulation, since ḥav is shorter than ḥayyav.
The mishna continues: the one liable pays restitution from his superior-quality land.
A baraita cites the verse about best of field and vineyard, with Rabbi Yishmael holding payment matches the injured party's land.
Rabbi Akiva: the verse only allows collection from the liable party's superior land, and consecrated property follows a fortiori.
Asks, on Yishmael's view, whether an animal that ate from a poor garden bed should pay the value of a rich one.
Rav Idi bar Avin: when the animal ate from one of several beds and it is unknown which, the owner pays the value of a rich bed.
Rava objects that without knowing which bed it ate from, paying rich-bed value is unreasonable, since the claimant bears the burden of proof.
Rav Aha bar Ya'akov: the dispute concerns a case where the liable party lacks money and the court collects from his land.
The tanna'im dispute whether land is appraised from the injured party's side (Yishmael) or the liable party's side (Akiva).
Yishmael's reason: the word field appears both above and below in the verse, so the lower field refers to the injured party's land.
Rabbi Akiva holds the verse means the best of the one paying, meaning the liable party's best fields.
Yishmael replies that the verbal analogy and the verse's plain meaning both hold, each teaching a distinct halakha.
When the liable party has both lands, he pays from his best land, since his inferior land cannot be measured against the injured party's superior land.
Restates the baraita's Akiva view and the a fortiori inference that consecrated property collects from superior-quality land.
Asks what the a fortiori inference from ordinary damage to consecrated property refers to.
If an ox of a Jew gored consecrated property, the verse excludes damage to consecrated animals, so the proposed case fails.
Rather, the inference concerns a vow to donate to Temple maintenance, collected from the vower's superior land if he lacks money.
The Temple treasurer should not be treated better than an ordinary creditor, so he should not take from superior land.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The halakha is that a creditor collects only from intermediate-quality land, not from his superior land.
Supposes Rabbi Akiva holds that even a creditor collects from superior land, which would still leave the a fortiori inference open.
The a fortiori inference fails: a creditor's power to collect damages was enhanced, while the Temple's was weakened, so the comparison does not hold.
The case is an ox goring consecrated property, and Rabbi Akiva follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, rejecting the objection about another's ox.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya: consecrated oxen are exempt when gored by a common ox, but the common owner pays in full when his ox gores consecrated property.
If so, how do we know Akiva and Yishmael dispute the appraisal of land, rather than everyone agreeing and the dispute lying elsewhere?
Akiva follows Ben Menasya and Yishmael follows the Rabbis, so the dispute concerns the Temple treasury rather than the appraisal of land.
If so, why does the verse come only to allow collection from superior land, which suggests Akiva disagrees about how the verse is read?
If Akiva follows Ben Menasya, damage to consecrated property is stricter, so no a fortiori inference could be drawn for the Temple treasury.
Rav Ashi's baraita states that the verse's appraisal is of the injured party's best land for Yishmael and the liable party's best land for Akiva.
Abaye raises a contradiction to Rava: the verse says pay from best land, which implies he may not pay from any other property.
A baraita: the phrase he shall recompense is superfluous, so it includes any item of value, even bran, as valid payment.
Rava resolves it: he shall recompense applies to voluntary payment, while best land applies when payment is forced after a lawsuit.
Ulla bar Ilai: the verse's wording he shall pay also indicates forced payment against his will, supporting Rava's resolution.
Abaye objects: the verse does not say he shall be paid in the passive, and he shall pay can also mean voluntary payment.
Abaye offers an alternative resolution, following a method his teacher Rabba used on a different difficulty.
A baraita: a wealthy person who cannot sell his property may receive poor man's tithe up to half the value of his assets.
Asks why the owner could not sell his land, given that land values fell generally, so he should be given more than half.
Rather, others' land appreciated while his was known to be in need of cash, so buyers offered less and his land depreciated.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks: if so, the man should not get even a slight amount of poor man's tithe, since his assets have high value.
Rabba: the half-value limit applies where a man cannot sell due to seasonal price swings, since land is cheap in Tishrei and dear in Nisan.
A man in need sells in Tishrei at low prices, so he may take tithe only up to the depreciation, which is at most half the land's value.
Abaye applies the same distinction to damages: the injured party collecting in Tishrei takes a relatively large amount of superior land.
If the injured party accepts intermediate land instead, the liable party can value it at the appreciated Nisan price, so the payment is smaller.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov objects that this weakens injured parties' rights, since the Torah intends to enhance them, not lower their payment.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov proposes comparing the case to a creditor collecting a loan in Tishrei, with the same seasonal valuation.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika objects that this would deter lenders, since a creditor who lent money would be penalized by the seasonal valuation.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika proposes comparing the case to a woman's marriage contract collected in Tishrei, with the same seasonal valuation.
The Gemara returns to Abaye's contradiction and notes the original difficulty still stands.
Rava: whatever he pays must be of the best of its kind, so the phrase best of his field applies to any form of payment.
Asks: but the verse says best of his field, which seems to require land as the payment.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna: all movables count as best quality, but land must be best land because it is harder to sell.

The Gemara asks whether the first clause follows Rabbi Tarfon and the last clause follows the Rabbis.

Ravina, citing Rava, reads the whole baraita as Rabbi Tarfon's: produce use is one party's, while oxen use is shared.
For eating the courtyard is the injured party's, while for goring it is like a public domain, so half payment applies.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita then lists only three principles, not four.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak makes a further statement, which the view cuts off.

ranges.en: There are three principles, listed as four cases because they apply in four different places.
Mishna: damages are assessed in money and paid before a court on testimony from free Jewish men; women and both parties are included.
The Gemara asks what the phrase assessed in money means.
Rav Yehuda: the assessment is made only in terms of the monetary value of the damage.
Baraita on a cow and a cloak: offsetting is not presumed, so each side's damage is appraised separately in money.
Baraita: payment is made with items worth money, meaning only land serves as collateral, unless the injured party seized movables.
The Gemara restates the baraita: the phrase items worth money refers to land as the guarantee property.
The Gemara asks from where this inference is drawn.
Rabba bar Ulla: items worth money are those not subject to price fraud, as with land.
Objection: slaves and documents are also not subject to price fraud, yet they are not included.
Rabba bar Ulla revised: items acquired with money, as with land but not with movables.
Objection: slaves and documents are also acquired with money.
Rav Ashi: these items are worth money without being money, since they have its defining traits.
Rav Yehuda bar Ḥinnana raises a contradiction to the view of Rav Huna.
Baraita: only land serves as guarantee for payment of damages.
Second baraita: the superfluous He shall recompense includes movables, even bran, so payment may be made with movables.
The first baraita concerns damages collected from orphans, whose liability attaches only to the inherited land.
The Gemara asks why the court collects from the father's seized movables if the case concerns orphans.
As Rava cites Rav Naḥman: seizure while the debtor was alive is valid, so here too the damager was alive.
The Gemara asks what the phrase before a court means.
It qualifies the land rule: only land still held by the liable party at hearing time may be collected from.
Objection: a borrower who sold land before court would then escape the loan, which is certainly incorrect.
Rather, before a court excludes non-ordained judges from adjudicating damages, which count as fines.
Mishna: payment is made based upon the testimony of witnesses.
This excludes one who admits liability for a fine, who is exempt even if witnesses later testify against him.
The Gemara asks what this clause teaches if the view holds that witnesses later make the admitter liable.
The clause prefaces the next clause, that only certain witnesses are accepted in cases of damages.

ranges.en: Mishna: witnesses must be free men and members of the covenant, excluding Canaanite slaves and gentiles.
Both exceptions are needed: a slave lacks lineage and a gentile lacks connection to the mitzvot, so each must be taught.
Mishna: women are included in the halakhot of damages in the same way as men.
The Gemara asks from where the inclusion of women in the damage laws is derived.
A school of Rabbi Yishmael derives the equality of women from the false-oath verse, equating them in all punishments.
The school of Rabbi Elazar derives equality of women in civil laws from the verse about laws set before them.
Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derive equality from the verse on an ox that kills a man or a woman.
Each source is needed: the first alone might limit equality to punishments, not to civil laws.
The second source alone might limit equality to civil law, not to the obligation of atonement.
The first two alone might be limited to their cases, so the ox-killing source is needed for ransom liability.
The ransom source alone might suggest equality only where life is lost, so the first two are needed.
Mishna: both the injured party and the one liable for the damage are involved in the payment.
Amoraic dispute: Rav Pappa calls half-damages restitution, while Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua calls them a fine.
Rav Pappa: ordinary oxen are not presumed safeguarded, so the Torah lightened the full liability as restitution.
Rav Huna: ordinary oxen are presumed safeguarded, so the Torah penalized the owner with a fine given to the injured party.
Objection: if half-damages are a fine, it is inaccurate to say the injured party is involved in the payment.
The clause is needed because the injured party absorbs loss from carcass depreciation before court.
The Gemara asks how the mishna can refer to carcass depreciation when the first clause already implies it.
The principle is stated twice, once for an innocuous ox and once for a forewarned ox.
Both cases are needed, since each alone might wrongly suggest the Torah limits liability only there.
A mishna distinguishes innocuous and forewarned oxen: the former pays half from its body, the latter full from superior property.
If half-damages were a fine, the mishna would also say the innocuous ox owner does not pay on his own admission.
The tanna omitted certain distinctions, and a tanna would not omit just one case, so another halakha must be missing.
The omitted halakha: an innocuous ox owner pays no ransom at all, while a forewarned owner pays the full ransom.
The claim that the mishna omits this is flawed, since the mishna follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who has half ransom.
The Gemara suggests another proof from a mishna in Ketubot.

ranges.en: Mishna: if one admits that his ox killed a person or another's ox, he pays on his own admission.
The Gemara asks whether the mishna refers only to a forewarned ox or also to an innocuous one.
The mishna's halakha concerns a forewarned ox, so no proof about restitution arises.
The Gemara asks what the halakha would be for an innocuous ox, and why the mishna did not teach the distinction in its first clause.
Objection: the mishna would have noted that an innocuous ox admission is not payable, so half-damages are restitution.
The mishna speaks only of forewarned oxen, so the omission proves nothing.
The mishna's concluding principle: one who pays more than the damage does not pay on admission, implying the payment is not restitution.
Rejection: the inference is only that one pays on admission when liable for exactly the cost of the damage.
The Gemara asks what happens when liability is less than the damage, arguing the mishna would then state it, refuting the fine view.
The halakha is that half the cost of the damage is a fine.
The Gemara notes the inconsistency: a refutation of the fine view, yet the halakha follows that view.
Resolution: the refutation is not conclusive, since the tanna cannot state an absolute rule even under restitution.
Pebbles kicked by a walking animal pay half by tradition as restitution, which is why the mishna omits such cases.
On the fine view, dogs eating lambs or cats eating chickens are not collected in Babylonia, where ordination is unavailable.
This applies only to attacks on large animals; attacks on small ones are Eating and collected in Babylonia.
Even on the fine view, seized property is not reclaimed; the owner may be excommunicated until he removes the danger.
Rabbi Natan's baraita derives from Deuteronomy 22:8 that one may not keep a vicious dog or unstable ladder at home.
Mishna: five acts make an animal forewarned only after warnings, and five others make it forewarned immediately.
Mishna: an animal is not forewarned for goring, pushing, biting, crouching, or kicking, so only half is paid.
Mishna: forewarned acts include eating with the tooth, breaking with the foot, the three-time goring ox, and damage by a person.
Mishna lists wild animals as forewarned; Rabbi Elazar says domesticated ones are not, but the snake always is.
From the mishna's wording, the Gemara infers that the cases concern damage in the injured party's courtyard.
The Gemara asks who holds that goring in the injured party's courtyard pays only half, and answers that it is the Rabbis.
Reading the latter clause as Rabbi Tarfon's view: full payment for goring by an innocuous ox in the injured party's courtyard.
The Gemara asks whether the first part of the latter clause follows the Rabbis and the next part Rabbi Tarfon.
Yes, as Shmuel told Rav Yehuda to follow his interpretation, dividing the latter clause between the two opinions.
Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rav, presenting a different interpretation of the mishna.

ranges.en: The mishna's opening ruling is said to follow Rabbi Tarfon throughout.
Explains the first clause: a jointly used courtyard is private for eating damage but public for goring.
Rav Kahana reports that he taught this explanation before Rav Zevid in Neharde'a.
Rav Zevid challenges whether the whole mishna can really be read as following Rabbi Tarfon.
Rav Zevid cites the mishna's rule that eating damage counts only for food fitting the animal.
Rav Kahana's difficulty: on Tarfon's view, goring in the courtyard should be fully liable even for unfit food.
Rav Kahana resolves it by saying the mishna follows the Rabbis, with a missing clause supplied.
Ravina objects that the mishna's later case about the ox on the injured party's property would then be unexplained.
Ravina resolves this by saying the mishna is incomplete and supplying the missing five-act clause.
Ravina's reading of the mishna's second half, with its dispute and the list of other forewarned animals.
A baraita is brought in support, repeating the same reading of the mishna.
Some raise the mishna as a contradiction, since the list of forewarned animals seems incomplete.
Ravina's reply resolves the apparent contradiction by reading the mishna's list as incomplete.
The mishna says an animal is not forewarned for crouching; Rabbi Elazar limits this to large vessels.
The Gemara suggests a baraita supports Rabbi Elazar, since it lists crushing vessels as forewarned behavior.
The Gemara rejects the proof: the baraita may refer to pushing vessels against a wall.
A different version of Rabbi Elazar's position: even small vessels are atypical when crouched upon.
An objection from a baraita stating that crushing vessels is a forewarned act.
Rabbi Elazar replies that the baraita may refer only to pushing vessels against a wall.
A contradiction is raised between the mishna's exclusion of crouching and the baraita's inclusion of crushing.
Rabbi Elazar resolves it: the mishna concerns large vessels and the baraita concerns small ones.
The mishna lists the wolf, lion, bear, leopard, bardelas and snake as forewarned from the outset.
The Gemara asks what a bardelas is.
Rav Yehuda identifies the bardelas as a nafreza.
The Gemara asks what a nafreza is.
Rav Yosef identifies the nafreza as an appa.
A baraita adds the hyena and snake, which seems to conflict with identifying the hyena as a bardelas.
Rav Yosef explains that the hyena in the baraita is the appa.
The contradiction is resolved by distinguishing a male hyena in the baraita from a female hyena in the mishna.
A baraita describes how a male hyena changes into successive creatures over seven-year periods.
The Gemara restates Rabbi Meir's addition of the hyena as the basis for the next discussion.

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar says the snake is also forewarned, unlike the other animals he names.
The Gemara objects: the mishna says the snake is always forewarned, which conflicts with a different reading.
The baraita should be emended to read only that a snake is forewarned, not also.
Shmuel rules that a lion clawing and eating prey is exempt in the public domain, but tearing it apart is liable.
Explains Shmuel's ruling: clawing and eating is typical eating, while tearing apart is atypical goring.
Asks whether tearing apart prey is simply not the typical manner of a lion.
Cites the verse in Nahum about the lion tearing prey, then reads each phrase as food for its young.
A baraita is brought against Shmuel: a wild animal in the courtyard that tore and ate an animal pays full damages.
The baraita is about a lion that tore prey intending to store it and then reconsidered and ate it.
Questions how the lion's intention can be known, and whether this undermines Shmuel's own ruling.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak reads the baraita as two disjunctive cases, each typical, upholding Shmuel.
Ravina explains Shmuel's view as concerning a domesticated lion, following Rabbi Elazar's position.
Objects to Ravina: on his reading even clawing and eating should make the owner liable.
Ravina concedes that his explanation is not about Shmuel but about the baraita in the courtyard case.
If the lion's act is atypical, it should count as goring and pay only half the damages.
The baraita refers to a lion that was already forewarned.
If so, why does the baraita list this under eating rather than goring? Conceded as a difficulty.
The mishna contrasts an innocuous ox, paying half from its body, with a forewarned ox paying full from higher property.
Asks what the mishna means by higher property, the word aliyya.
Rabbi Elazar explains aliyya as the superior-quality items of one's property.
Supports this reading with verses about burial in the best of the sepulchers, read as the finest of the family.
Asks what the verse's spices and perfumes (zenim) are.
Rabbi Elazar explains zenim as many different types of perfumes.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani reads zenim as zenut: perfumes that lead the smeller to licentiousness.
Cites Jeremiah's verse about digging a pit and setting snares for his feet.
Rabbi Elazar: the pit refers to suspicion of intercourse with a zona.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: the pit refers to suspicion of intercourse with a married woman.
If zona is meant, pit is a metaphor for her; but on the married-woman reading, why use pit?
A married woman who commits adultery is also called a zona, so the term pit still fits.
On the married-woman reading, the verse about plans to kill fits; but what is meant by kill under the zona reading?
The kill refers to their casting him into a pit of mire.
Rava offers a homiletic interpretation of the verse.
Quotes Jeremiah's verse asking that they be made to stumble in the time of anger.
Rava explains that Jeremiah asked God to make them stumble even while they do charity, to deny them reward.
Cites the verse that the people made honor for Hezekiah at his death.
The verse teaches that a yeshiva was established at his grave.
Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis disagree: one says they studied there for three days.

ranges.en: Other opinions on the length of the mourning study: seven days, or thirty days.
A baraita explains the honor for Hezekiah: thirty-six thousand men went out in mourning, per Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Nehemya objects that this honor was also shown to the wicked Ahab, so it is not unique to Hezekiah.
The unique honor was placing a Torah scroll on his bier and declaring that he fulfilled what it says.
Objects that nowadays people do the same for great scholars, so the practice is not unique.
Offers an alternative: nowadays a scroll is laid on the bier, but the declaration is not made.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that the declaration was unique to Hezekiah.
Objects that Torah study is valued because it leads to mitzvot, so praising Hezekiah for studying seems odd.
Not a difficulty: the earlier statement concerns study for oneself, while the praise concerns teaching others.
Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai gives a homily on the verse about sowing by all waters.
Derives the reward of two tribes from verses on sowing, water, and the blessings of Joseph and Issachar.
Another reading of the same comparison, drawing on Moses' blessing of Joseph and the men of Issachar's understanding.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter on the four primary damagers.
Mishna: an animal is forewarned for trampling while walking, and for kicking or pebbles it pays half.
Mishna: if a broken shard breaks a second vessel, full damages for the first and half for the second.
Mishna: chickens are forewarned for trampling in their typical walk, but a leashed or hopping chicken pays half.

ranges.en: Ravina asks why the mishna repeats trampling with the foot and with the body as if they were the same halakha.
Rava explains that the tanna first teaches the primary category, then its subcategories.
Ravina challenges this: the Eating clause has no subcategories yet still repeats the forewarned phrase.
Rava gives a humorous reply: he resolved one mishna's difficulty, so Ravina should resolve the other.
Asks what the reason is for the apparent redundancy in the Eating clause.
Rav Ashi explains: domesticated and undomesticated animals are taught separately, with the latter included by derivation.
If so, the derived halakha should have come after the explicit one, not before.
Asks why the first clause does not likewise begin with what is derived by interpretation.
The two cases differ: in Eating both kinds are primary categories, while in Trampling the foot is primary.
Here with Trampling, would the tanna leave the primary category aside and teach a subcategory first?
Alternative: the tanna began with trampling because the previous mishna ended with trampling.
Baraita: an animal is forewarned for walking and breaking, including with its body, hair, saddle or bell, paying full damages.
Sumakhos says that pebbles propelled while walking, or a burrowing pig, make the owner pay full damages.
Asks what is novel in Sumakhos's view, since a pig's damage is obviously fully liable.
Rather, Sumakhos's novelty concerns pebbles propelled by the animal, which he holds are fully liable.
Asks who mentioned pebbles at all in the baraita.
The baraita is incomplete: the Rabbis pay half for pebbles, and Sumakhos pays full, with the pig case parallel.
Tosefta: chickens flying and breaking vessels with their wings are full liability, but wind from their wings is half.
Another baraita on chickens hopping on dough or produce, with Sumakhos again holding full liability.
Another baraita on wind from a flying chicken's wings: half liability, in line with the Rabbis.
Rava raises a difficulty: the Rabbis' half liability seems inconsistent with treating wind as the animal's own act.
Rava resolves it: the Rabbis hold full liability in principle, and half for pebbles is a received tradition.
Rava's principle: any act that makes a zav's contact impure yields full liability, and indirect pure contact yields half.
Asks whether Rava's principle merely restates the pebbles halakha, and so what he adds.
Rava adds the case of a calf pulling a cart, which counts as direct damage rather than indirect.
Baraita in accordance with Rava: the same list of forewarned walking damages, now including a calf pulling a cart.
Chickens pecking a bucket rope, so the bucket falls and breaks: full liability.
Rava's dilemma: if a trodden vessel rolls and breaks elsewhere, is the initial act or the final breaking decisive?
Proposes resolving the dilemma from Rabba's case of a vessel thrown from a roof and broken by a stick.
Rejects the proof: the case is clear for Rabba but remains a dilemma for Rava.
Brings a baraita: a chicken hopping is not forewarned, though some say it is forewarned.
Questions the baraita's wording: hopping is typical, so it must concern a vessel rolled by hopping and broken elsewhere.
The Tannaim disagree about which act is decisive, so the baraita is explained differently.

ranges.en: The baraita's tannaim dispute the Sumakhos question: full or half liability for pebbles propelled during walking.
Brings a baraita about chickens pecking a bucket rope, concluding that the initial act is decisive.
Rejects that conclusion: the baraita concerns the rope, with half liability for the bucket.
But a rope is atypical food for a chicken, so it should count as goring rather than eating.
The rope was greasy with kneaded dough, so pecking it is typical behavior for a chicken.
But the baraita says the bucket broke, so the dispute concerns the bucket, not the rope.
Rather, the baraita follows Sumakhos, who holds full liability for pebbles propelled by an animal.
If it follows Sumakhos, why not state the shard case, and does Sumakhos hold half liability for pebbles?
Proposed resolution: Sumakhos distinguishes a force from a force generated by a force, conceding half for the latter.
Asks Rav Ashi's dilemma: is secondary force treated like direct force under Sumakhos's view?
Infers that the baraita must not decide Rav Ashi's dilemma, so Sumakhos does not distinguish the forces, and the Rabbis follow the initial act.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye: the baraita is no proof, since the bucket was continually propelled, so the dilemma remains.
Rava's dilemma: is half liability for pebbles paid from the animal's body or from superior land?
Brings a baraita on hopping chickens: not forewarned, though some say forewarned, as the resolution of Rava's dilemma.
Questions the wording: hopping is typical, so the baraita must concern pebbles propelled while hopping.
The baraita's disagreement is about body versus superior-land payment, so Rava's dilemma is a tannaitic dispute.
Brings a mishna on a dog that carried a hot loaf to a grain stack: half liability for the grain, per the first tanna.
Asks why the first tanna holds half liability for the grain stack.
It is analogous to pebbles propelled from the loaf, and a baraita says half is paid from the animal's body.
Objects: on Rabbi Elazar's view, full liability is never paid solely from the animal's body, so this cannot be the reading.
Alternative: the dog acted atypically, making it goring, so Rabbi Elazar follows Rabbi Tarfon's view on innocuous goring.
Rejects that reading: the baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon only because of the difficulty about payment from the body.
Alternative: Rabbi Elazar follows Sumakhos and Rabbi Yehuda, so innocuousness remains in the body-payment half.
Rav Samma tells Ravina to assume Rabbi Yehuda's view on innocuous turned forewarned oxen, and distinguish trampling.

ranges.en: Challenges the prior reading: did you hear him distinguish parts of payment, given no innocuousness for pebbles?
Rather, Rabbi Elazar's full-payment ruling concerns a forewarned owner; the tanna and Rabbi Elazar dispute forewarning for pebbles.
Objects that if so, Rava's dilemma about forewarning for pebbles could be resolved from this dispute.
Rava meant only the Rabbis who disagree with Sumakhos; in this baraita both follow Sumakhos, since pebbles are atypical.
Rejects the parallel to Rabbi Tarfon: did you hear that restitution comes only from the animal's body?
Yes: Rabbi Tarfon derives full liability for an innocuous ox by a fortiori from public-domain goring, limiting payment to the body.
Objects: from that mishna, Rabbi Tarfon seems to reject the principle that a conclusion matches its source.
He rejects it only when rejection would refute the a fortiori inference; here it is applied in a limited way.
Rava's dilemma: is pebble damage liked to goring with forewarning, or a subcategory of trampling never changing status?
Brings a baraita: a chicken is not forewarned for hopping, though some say it is forewarned.
Questions the baraita's wording: hopping is typical, so it should concern pebbles propelled while hopping.
Proposes three repetitions and a tannaitic dispute, then rejects it: perhaps only one occurrence, and the dispute mirrors Sumakhos.
Brings an amoraic dispute: excrement dropped onto dough, with full versus half liability, as a resolution.
Proposes three repetitions, then rejects it as one occurrence; the animal was forced into a narrow space.
Objects that the behavior is atypical, so under the goring rule only half should be paid.
Asks why the amoraim did not simply state the halakha as following Sumakhos or the Rabbis.
Excrement is novel: one might think it is body-like, so stating the dispute teaches it is like propelled pebbles.
Brings a baraita: a rooster crowing into a glass vessel breaks it with sound waves, full liability.
Rav Yosef reports the school of Rav: a horse neighing or donkey braying breaks vessels with sound waves, half liability.
Proposes that the case is one where the animal did it three times, so the dispute is about forewarning.

ranges.en: The tannaim dispute forewarning for pebbles; the dispute parallels Sumakhos and the Rabbis on pebbles.
Objects that a rooster's atypical head-insertion should count as goring and so pay only half.
The rooster's act was typical because there were seeds in the vessel.
Rav Ashi's dilemma: does atypical pebble propulsion change the payment from one-quarter, or not?
Resolves it from Rava's dilemma about forewarning; then rejects that resolution, leaving the dilemma open.
Rav Ashi's second dilemma: under Sumakhos, is secondary force treated as direct force, or was it not learned as a tradition?
Mishna: kicking or pebbles from under the feet that break vessels pays half the cost of the damage.
Asks which case the mishna addresses: a direct kick, or pebbles from a kick, versus typical pebble propulsion.
If typical pebble propulsion pays full, then the mishna must follow Sumakhos.
Brings the latter clause of the mishna about shards breaking a second vessel as a resolution.
Objects that if the mishna follows Sumakhos, half for the shard case contradicts his view on pebbles.
Hypothetical resolution: the first and second vessels differ by one or two forces, which Sumakhos distinguishes.
Objects: if so, why is Rav Ashi's dilemma still open, since it could be resolved from here?
Rav Ashi holds the mishna follows the Rabbis, so pebbles from a kick yield a quarter of the damage.
Alternative: a kick's pebbles pay half with no change in status; this dilemma stands unresolved.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel's dilemma: a walker who must propel pebbles, and whether that is typical manner.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: pebbles kicked in the public domain, liken to goring or subcategory of trampling?
Rabbi Zeira answers that it is clearly a subcategory of trampling.
Yirmeya asks about pebbles propelled in the public domain that damage private property.
Zeira answers, using Shabbat terms: no lifting here, but there is placing, so the case is different.
Objects with a baraita on walking animals propelling pebbles in both domains, liable; reads it as public-to-public.
No: the baraita refers to pebbles propelled publicly that damage private property.
Yirmeya recalls Zeira's earlier rule: no lifting here but there is placing here.
Zeira retracts his earlier statement.
Yirmeya objects from the mishna on shards, with the first vessel in public domain exempt as trampling.
A baraita adds that in the public domain the first vessel is exempt and the last vessel liable.
Asks whether the baraita concerns pebbles propelled and damaging in the public domain.
No: the reference is to pebbles propelled publicly that damage private property.
Yirmeya again recalls Zeira's rule: no lifting here, but placing here.
Zeira retracts his statement.
Yirmeya asks whether the owner is exempt for pebbles propelled in the public domain.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects with Rabbi Yohanan's principle that half damages do not differ by domain: is that not stated even for public pebbles?
No: Rabbi Yohanan's principle concerns pebbles propelled publicly that damage private property.
Yirmeya recalls Zeira's earlier rule: no lifting here, but there is placing here.
Zeira retracts, or alternatively says Rabbi Yohanan's principle applies to goring, not to propelled pebbles.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia and Rabbi Oshaya meet; one asks whether an animal swinging its tail that causes damage is liable.
The other sage replies that since tail-swinging is typical, the owner need not grasp the tail to prevent it.
Objects: then goring too should require grasping the horn, yet goring is still liable.
Goring is not typical, so the owner must prevent it; tail-swinging is typical and so exempt.
Asks what the dilemma is, since typical behavior in public is obviously exempt; answers it concerns excessive swinging.
Rav Eina's dilemma: if an animal swings its penis and causes damage, is it like goring, with intent or not?
Mishna on forewarned chickens and strings; Rav Huna limits half liability to strings that became tied by themselves.
Asks who pays if the string tied itself: the string's owner if negligent, or none if he concealed it.
Rather, the mishna concerns a concealed string, so the chicken's owner is liable.
Asks why half liability would not also be exempt, since the verse about pits covers only a man opening a pit.
Cites the verse on a man opening a pit and not an ox, to show an ox-made pit is exempt.
Rather, the chicken moved the string itself, so half is paid as for pebbles; Rav Huna's distinction is general.
Asks what primary category makes the owner liable for the string.
Rav Huna bar Manoah: it is a subcategory of pit, a pit rolled at people's and animals' feet.
Mishna on eating: a domestic animal is forewarned for eating produce; full value only on the injured party's property.
Mishna: if the animal benefits from eating in the public domain, the owner pays for the benefit, depending on location.
Baraita: an animal's eating of fit food and drinking of fit drinks in the injured party's courtyard pays full damages.
Baraita continued: a cow eating barley, a donkey eating vetches, a dog licking oil, and a pig eating meat, all pay full.
Rav Pappa: unusual eating under duress is still eating, so a cat eating dates or a donkey eating fish pays full.
A donkey ate bread and broke the basket; Rav Yehuda ruled full for the bread and half for the basket.
Asks why the basket should not also be full, since eating bread and breaking baskets are both typical for a donkey.
The donkey ate the bread and then broke the basket, showing intent to cause damage, so it is goring.
Asks whether a donkey's eating of bread is typical behavior at all.
Raises a baraita: eating bread, meat or cooked food pays half, which seems to concern a domesticated animal.
Questions the rejection: an undomesticated animal eats meat, which is typical.
Clarifies: roasted meat is atypical for wild animals; or it concerns deer, or an animal eating at a table.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A goat ate a turnip from atop a clay barrel and broke the barrel; Rava holds the owner fully liable.
Why is the owner liable for the barrel, since breaking barrels is not typical goat behavior?
Eating a turnip is typical, so climbing to reach it is typical too, and the breakage falls under Eating.

ranges.en: The tanna's list: a zav's ziva, spittle, semen and urine, and menstrual blood impart impurity by touch and by carrying.

At the moment of throwing, the action lacked the capacity to break the vessel, since the cushions would have caught it.
Rabba says one who threw a child from a roof and another impaled him on a sword is subject to the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis.

The chapter-ending formula, introducing the next chapter on the mishna of the kad.

Rav Ḥisda asks Rav Naḥman the fine for humiliation by kneeing, kicking, and punching, and for hitting with a hoe's handle or top.

ranges.en: Dismisses the difficulty: Ben Bag Bag holds an individual view, and the Rabbis disagree with him.
Rabbi Yannai offers an alternative reading of breaking his teeth as suing him in court.

Brings a baraita about an ox pushed off another ox that dies, where the lower owner is exempt.
Asks whether that ruling really concerns a forewarned ox, where the lower owner suffers no loss.
Replies that the ruling concerns an innocuous ox, where the lower owner would suffer a loss.
Objects that the latter clause would make no sense for an innocuous ox, since the lower owner is liable.
He is liable because he should have removed his own ox instead of harming the other one.
Brings a baraita about a man who fills another's courtyard with jugs of wine and oil.
Explains the courtyard ruling as allowing breaking through only to go to court or fetch proof of ownership.
Brings a baraita on an eared slave injured while being evicted, and a verse showing no compensation is owed.
Asks what case the baraita is actually dealing with.
The case is a slave who is a thief, so the master suffers a loss if he stays.
Objects that until now the slave did not steal, so why would he begin only now?
The master's authority restrained the slave until now, but no longer does once he is freed.
Offers an alternative: the master gave him a Canaanite maidservant, now forbidden to him once he is free.
Brings a mishna where one who stumbles on a jug in the public domain is exempt, implying liability if he broke it deliberately.
Rav Zevid rejects the proof: the same holds even if he broke it, and the mishna mentions stumbling for another reason.
Brings a baraita on a woman who grabs a man's genitals, inferring she is punished even if she could not save him otherwise.
Replies that the verse refers to a case where she could save him by other means, otherwise she is exempt.
Objects that the baraita should have taught the exemption within the verse itself, rather than by excluding an emissary.
Explains the baraita does say this: if she cannot save him otherwise, her hand is like a court emissary's and she is exempt.

Rava explains that the owner may prevent taking from the unallocated side only in monetary terms; both count as pe'a.
Brings a baraita on a renounced vineyard: the owner must give the gifts to the poor but is exempt from tithes.
Mishna: if a jug breaks in the public domain and someone slips in the water, the owner is liable; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes intent.
Rav Yehuda, in Rav's name, limits that liability to cases where the slipper's clothes were soiled by the water.

ranges.en: If the person himself was hurt, the jug owner is exempt, since the ground rather than the jug or water caused the injury.

The first clause conflicts with Rav's view and the last clause conflicts with Shmuel's view.
Retort: by your reasoning the baraita itself contradicts you, since one clause exempts and the other makes liable.

Shmuel resolves it: the stone is like a pit, so following Rabbi Yehuda, the owner is liable for vessels damaged by a pit.

An alternative version of Rabbi Elazar's teaching holds the owner liable even if the pedestrian stumbled on the ground, in line with Rabbi Natan.

ranges.en: Mishna continued: the cross beam carrier who stops is liable, the barrel carrier who stops is exempt, and the same applies to lamp and flax.

Mishna: two people walking or running in the public domain who damage each other are both exempt; a baraita gives Isi ben Yehuda's view that runners are liable.
