Did Rabbi Yohanan really say that, given his principle that the halakha follows an anonymous mishna, which exempts runners?
The mishna refers to twilight on the eve of Shabbat, when running is permitted; on a weekday the runner is liable, and both running are exempt.
The Master said Isi concedes that running at Shabbat twilight is exempt because it is permitted; what is the reason running then is permitted?
It is like Rabbi Hanina, who would say at Shabbat twilight a certain statement that explains the permission.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yannai's practice at Shabbat twilight of welcoming the Sabbath bride, with an alternative formulation of the call.
Mishna: one who chops wood and sends a chip causing damage is liable in all cases, whether public or private domains are involved.
Gemara explains why each case must be taught separately, since each carries a distinct reason for or against liability.
Tosefta: a carpenter is exempt if the visitor entered without permission and died from a flying chip, but liable if permitted.
What does the baraita mean by liable for the carpenter?
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: for injury the carpenter pays four kinds of damages, but for death he is exempt from exile.
The carpenter's case differs from the forest case in the Torah, since the victim in the shop entered another's property.
Rava argues a fortiori that the carpenter should be exiled, since the forest case already treats entry with consent as liability.
Rava's own explanation: exemption from exile is because the death is nearly intentional, and exile cannot atone for that negligence.
Objection from a mishna about lashes with one extra stroke, where the court's agent is exiled though the death seems nearly intentional.
Rav Shimi of Neharde'a: the error was in counting, not in administering the lashes.
Rava slaps Rav Shimi and rejects this: a baraita shows the judge counts, and the lash-giver only strikes.
Rav Shimi revised: the judge himself miscounted, the striker did not notice, so the killing is wholly unintentional and exile applies.
Objection from a mishna on throwing a stone into the public domain: the killer is exiled, though it seems nearly intentional.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak: the case is demolishing a wall bordering the public domain, so it is not nearly intentional.
The Gemara questions this: he should still have checked whether anyone was present.
Resolution: the demolition happened at night.
Even at night he should have checked for people, so this does not resolve the difficulty.
Alternative: the wall was demolished by day, into a garbage heap.
What are the circumstances of this heap: if frequented it is intentional, and if not he is an accident victim and exempt from exile.
Rav Pappa: the heap is used only at night, so by day the killer is neither intentional nor fully an accident victim, so exile applies.
Rav Pappa in Rava's name: Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina's ruling refers to the first clause, where entry was without permission.
Explanation of which clause Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina's statement addresses, and why the last clause means liability for exile.
Does the victim with permission get exiled? A baraita on a welder's shop says the welder is exempt even when entry was permitted.
The baraita concerns the welder's apprentice, whom the master urged to leave but who stayed.
If the master urged him to leave, why would he stand to be killed, and why does the baraita specify an apprentice?

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Another person lacks awe of his mentor, so the welder must verify departure; the apprentice does not, so the welder is not liable for his death.
Rav Zevid in Rava's name: Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina's ruling concerns a case of someone who exposes himself to danger, citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Explains that the ruling about the stone-thrower applies to that baraita, while the carpenter baraita is covered a fortiori, and the stone case is fully exempt.
Tosefta: hired laborers who enter the employer's courtyard to collect wages and are killed by his ox or dog; the employer is exempt, others disagree.
What are the circumstances: if the employer is usually in town, or usually at home, why would each tanna hold as they do?
Only where the employer is sometimes in town; saying yes at the gate means come in for the others, but stand there and I will come out for the first tanna.
A baraita supports the reading that yes means stand in your place, since otherwise the employer with permission would be liable.
Mishna: when two innocuous oxen injure each other, each owner pays half the difference; forewarned oxes pay the full difference.
Mishna continues on mixed cases of forewarned and innocuous oxen and persons, and Rabbi Akiva's view that an innocuous ox gored a person pays in full.
Baraita derives from Exodus that an ox gored person is judged like an ox gored ox, with half damages for innocuous and full for forewarned.
Rabbi Akiva: the case follows the lower verse, a forewarned ox, but payment comes only from the ox's body, not superior property.
Why does the Rabbis' reading need the word this, since they also compare the cases?
From where does Rabbi Akiva derive that the four kinds of indemnity do not apply to oxen, and does the Torah's verse on maiming show it?
The Rabbis derive it from the phrase according to this judgment, which limits compensation to the damage itself and excludes medical costs and lost livelihood.
Mishna: an innocuous ox worth one hundred gores one worth two hundred; the owner of the goring ox must give it over to the injured owner.
Baraita: Rabbi Yishmael says the ox is appraised in court first, while Rabbi Akiva says it was already assigned, so the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yishmael sees the dead ox's owner as a creditor with money claims only, while Rabbi Akiva sees them as partners in ownership.
They dispute the verse on selling the live ox and dividing its value: the court's role for Rabbi Yishmael, the parties' sharing for Rabbi Akiva.
What is the practical difference between the two views?
If the injured party consecrates the ox, Rabbi Yishmael says he cannot until the court transfers it, while Rabbi Akiva allows it.
Rava asks Rav Nahman: if the liable party sold the ox, is that valid according to Rabbi Yishmael, who treats the claim as money only?

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since the ox is liened to the injured party, is the owner barred from selling it at all?
Rav Nahman replies that it is not sold.
Rava objects: a baraita says if the owner sold it, the sale stands, and the injured party collects from the buyer.
The sale stands for plowing: the buyer may use the ox until the injured party collects from him.
Does this mean a debtor's movables can be sold and the creditor collects from them, as the belligerent ox is only a lien for the injured party?
But Rava says a slave given as designated repayment can be collected from the buyer, while an ox so given cannot. Why the difference?
A slave given as security is publicly known and buyers are aware of the lien; a goring ox is also publicly known as such, so the buyer knows of the lien.
Rav Tahalifa of the West taught before Rabbi Abbahu: if the owner sold the ox it is not sold, but if he consecrated it, it is consecrated.
Who sold the ox, the injured or liable party? Which tanna's view does the baraita reflect in each clause?
If the injured party sold it, the sale fails by Rabbi Yishmael but the consecration works by Rabbi Akiva, so the baraita fits neither view. Is that right?
It refers to the liable party, and all agree the sale fails since the ox is liened to the injured party.
Consecration takes effect only by a rabbinic decree, so redemption is required by a minimal payment, so Temple property is not denigrated.
Baraita on an innocuous ox: a sale or consecration before trial takes effect, but after trial sale, consecration, and gift are void.
Creditors who seize an innocuous ox first achieve nothing, since compensation comes only from the ox's body.
Baraita on a forewarned ox: its sale, consecration, slaughter, and creditors' seizure all take effect, since compensation comes from superior property.
Gemara explains: a sale of an innocuous ox is valid only for plowing until the injured party collects.
Consecration does not really take effect, but requires redemption by minimal payment, per Rabbi Abbahu.
If the owner slaughtered the ox, how does that affect the injured party? Let him collect from the slaughtered ox's meat.
A baraita derives from the verse on selling the live ox that the injured party is paid even if the ox was slaughtered.
Rav Sheizevi: this applies only to the ox's diminished value after slaughter; the owner pays no more than its current value.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: one who damages another's liened property is exempt, as it does not belong to the lienholder.
Is this not obvious? The point is to exclude cases where spirit was taken rather than the body, so intangible damage is also exempt.
Rabba's principle makes this unnecessary: burning another's documents of debt is exempt too.
The documents case is only paper, while digging pits or caves on liened land is substantial damage and liable; the point is to exempt even substantial damage.
Here the slaughter is like digging pits and caves, and the tanna says that in this case what he did is done.
Baraita continued: creditors who seize an innocuous ox first achieve nothing, since compensation is paid only from the body of the ox.
If the injured party came first, the lien applies; but if the debt came first, why does the creditor not have precedence?

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does the baraita imply that a later creditor who collected before an earlier one has an invalid collection, given the debt preceded the damage?
No: if the creditor seized the belligerent ox, the injured party can claim it first, since he is paid from that very ox.
Baraita: an ox worth 200 injured another and lost 50 zuz, then the injured ox appreciated; the damage is assessed by the value at the time of injury.
Baraita continued: if the injured ox depreciated, damage is assessed at standing trial; the belligerent ox's share follows the same timing rules.
The first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael, who treats the injured party as a creditor, so whose view is the latter clause?
The latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva, who sees partnership, so how can the baraita combine Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva?
Both clauses follow Rabbi Akiva; the appreciation here stems from the owner fattening the ox, so the injured party has no share in the gain.
If the appreciation is due to fattening, why state the first clause at all, since the liable party clearly must still pay?
Rav Pappa: the first clause applies whether fattening or natural appreciation occurred, to teach payment at injury time; the latter clause applies only to fattening.
If the injured ox depreciated due to labor, the liable party could argue he should pay less; what caused the depreciation?
Rav Ashi: the depreciation came from the continuing effect of the wound, since the horn of the belligerent ox remains lodged in the injured ox.
Mishna: an innocuous ox worth 200 gores another worth 200 with a worthless carcass; Rabbi Meir cites the verse on selling the live ox and dividing its value.
Rabbi Yehuda objects: the verse's second clause, dividing the dead ox too, is ignored in that case; it must refer to a carcass worth fifty.
Baraita gives Rabbi Yehuda's view: with a carcass worth fifty, each side takes half the live ox and half the dead ox, as the Torah's belligerent ox case.
Rabbi Meir: the Torah case is a worthless carcass, and the words and the dead they shall divide mean the dead ox's loss is shared through the live ox.
Both views give each side 125 when the carcass is worth fifty, so what is the practical difference between them?
Rava: the difference is in the carcass's depreciation after death; Rabbi Meir has the injured party bear it, Rabbi Yehuda has the liable party bear half.
Abaye objects to Rava: then Rabbi Yehuda's view would be found to conflict with the mishna's own reasoning.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perhaps the innocuous ox is stricter than the forewarned one, as the mishna states: Rabbi Yehuda says an innocuous ox is liable and a forewarned one exempt.
Objection: perhaps Rabbi Yehuda held that only regarding safeguarding do the verses make innocuous stricter, not regarding compensation.
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda, with a carcass worth one sela, gives the injured party more than his ox was worth, so Rabbi Yehuda cannot hold the stricter view for compensation.
Rabbi Yehuda's logic: the forewarned case is singled out to be stricter, so the innocuous case, being more lenient, must also cap liability at the damage's value.
Rava's explanation of the Meir-Yehuda dispute should be rejected; Rabbi Yohanan says the dispute concerns appreciation of the carcass after death.
This is what troubled Rabbi Yehuda in another baraita: if the liable party shares the carcass's appreciation, the owner gains more than his ox was worth.
Rabbi Yehuda's reply: a liable party never gains from damage, and the verse says he shall pay, so he takes no more than the ox's value.
Why add the verse he shall pay, if a liable party never gains? Perhaps only where the injured party suffers loss, and not where he does not.
The added words counter that claim: the liable party pays and takes no more than the ox was worth at the time of damage.
Rav Aha bar Tahalifa objects to Rava: then Rabbi Yehuda's view makes the liable party pay more than half the damage, contrary to the verse on dividing the live ox.
Rava: Rabbi Yehuda holds only the diminished value of the dead ox is compensated by dividing the live ox, so the liable party never pays more than half.
From where does Rabbi Yehuda derive this? Not from the verse on the carcass, since he already derived from it that both parties split each half.
Had only that halakha been meant, the verse would omit also; the word also teaches two rules, the carcass is shared and liability is capped at half.
Mishna: one can be liable for his ox's act but exempt for his own act, and vice versa, with examples of humiliation, eye and tooth, parents, and Shabbat fire.
Rabbi Abbahu taught before Rabbi Yohanan a baraita that all destructive labor on Shabbat is exempt except injuring and kindling fire.
Rabbi Yohanan rejects this baraita as not for the study hall, and notes that if it were a mishna, injuring and kindling would be permitted only when purposeful.
The mishna's Shabbat fire case is compared with the ox's fire: the ox's fire is purposeless, so the owner's fire must be likewise purposeless.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: So too the mishna's lighting case is one where ashes are not needed, yet the mishna exempts him as liable to death, so Rabbi Yohanan's view is contradicted.
No, the comparison runs the other way: the ox's fire is like the man's, where the fire must serve a need for ashes.
How can one find a case where the ox set fire in order to obtain ashes?
Rav Avya: an intelligent ox bitten on its back burned the haystack so it could roll in the ashes and heal.
How do we know it burned the haystack for this reason?
Is there really such an ox?
Yes: an ox at Rav Pappa's house with a toothache broke a utensil lid, drank the liquor inside, and was cured.
The sages objected to Rav Pappa: the mishna exempts the ox's humiliation but liable for a person's, so an ox cannot intend humiliation.
The ox intended to injure; a person who intends to injure is liable for humiliation even without intent to humiliate.
Rava: the mishna concerns an unintentional lighting, which carries the death penalty if deliberate, so he is exempt from restitution.
This follows the school of Hizkiyya: killing an animal and killing a man are compared in Leviticus, so both apply regardless of intent.
The Hizkiyya baraita derives from the Leviticus verses that one who kills a man is exempt from monetary restitution in any event, as with one who kills an animal.
The sages ask Rava: can the mishna be read as unintentional, when it says he is exempt because he is sentenced to death, which needs intent?
Rava: the mishna refers to the deliberate act, which would be capital, so when done unintentionally he is still exempt from damages.
Mishna: an ox pursuing another ox is injured with no witnesses; the burden is on the claimant, and similarly for two pursuing oxen of different owners.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah case: two pursuing oxen of one owner, large and small or innocuous and forewarned; claimant bears the burden of proof.
Mishnah case of two injured and two belligerent oxen, large and small or innocuous and forewarned, same burden-of-proof ruling.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba explains the mishnah as rejecting Sumakhos's view that disputed property is divided between the parties.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks whether Sumakhos's division principle applies even when both parties claim with certainty.
Rabbi Hiyya confirms that Sumakhos holds the division principle even when both sides claim with certainty.
Asks how we know the mishnah concerns two certain claims, since the parties speak in definite assertions.
Rav Pappa objects that if the first clause concerns two certain claims, the latter clause must as well, by parallel reasoning.
Quotes the latter clause of the mishnah, which places the burden of proof on the claimant, to support the parallel reading.
Objection: if the claimant lacks proof and takes the defendant's version, this refutes Rabba bar Natan's full-exemption ruling.
Reply: the mishnah must describe a certain claim against an uncertain one, so it does not refute Rabba bar Natan.
Asks which party makes the certain claim and which the uncertain one, since either arrangement still seems to refute Rabba bar Natan.
The injured party makes an uncertain claim and the defendant a certain one, so his admission stands and he owes it.
Infers that the first clause must likewise describe an uncertain claim by the injured party and a certain one by the defendant.
Asks whether Sumakhos's division view would apply even here, where the claim is uncertain, making the mishnah's teaching unnecessary.
First clause describes a certain injured-party claim and uncertain defendant claim, the case where the Rabbis reject Sumakhos.
Objection: on this reading the first clause does not parallel the last, so it should concern two certain claims instead.
A certain-uncertain pair and an uncertain-certain pair are one matter, while two certain claims differ, so the clauses align.
Rabba bar Natan states that if the claimant asserted wheat and the defendant admitted barley, the defendant is fully exempt.
Asks what new point this teaches, since the same ruling already appears in a mishnah in Shevuot.
Cites the Shevuot mishnah: a wheat claim answered by a barley admission leaves the defendant exempt.
Without that mishnah one might exempt only the wheat value, so Rabba bar Natan teaches complete exemption including the barley.
Quotes the mishnah on two injured oxen of unequal size, where a claimant lacking proof takes the defendant's version.
Objects: under Rabba bar Natan's view, why is any compensation owed, since the wheat and barley cases fully exempt the defendant?
The mishnah says only that the injured party is fitting to take compensation, but in practice he receives none.
Asks: a baraita says the injured party is paid from the other ox, which shows he does receive compensation.
The baraita concerns an injured party who seized the ox, which the court leaves with him though it cannot compel payment.
Quotes the mishnah again on unequal oxen, where a claimant lacking proof takes compensation per the defendant's account.
Objects: why does the claimant receive compensation at all, given the wheat-and-barley parallel and Rabba bar Natan's full exemption?

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishnah does not say the injured party collects; it says he is fitting to take compensation but in practice gets none.
Challenge from a baraita: the injured party is paid for his small ox from the forewarned ox, so he does receive payment.
The baraita concerns an injured party who seized the ox, which the court leaves with him though payment cannot be compelled.
Quotes the mishnah: if the two pursuing oxen belong to one owner, both are liable.
Rava asks whether one may infer that the claimant can collect from either ox's proceeds, since both are liable.
Rav Ashi answers that the case is forewarned oxen, so the claimant collects from any of the owner's property.
Rava objects: if the case is forewarned oxen, the latter clause should be quoted, which places the burden of proof on the claimant.
Quotes the latter mishnah clause on unequal oxen, large and small, with the burden of proof on the claimant.
Objects: if forewarned, it makes no difference which ox caused the damage, since the liable party pays a full ox regardless.
Rav Ashi replies that the latter clause concerns innocuous oxen, while the first clause concerns forewarned oxen.
Rav Aha the Elder asks: if forewarned, why does the mishnah say they are liable in the plural, and what does both refer to?
Rather, the first clause concerns innocuous oxen, following Rabbi Akiva, who makes the injured party and owner partners in the ox.
Chapter-opening mishnah: an innocuous ox that gored several oxen in succession; the owner of the last one gained, per Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Shimon's case: an innocuous ox worth 200 kills an ox worth 200; each side takes 100 dinars from the sale.
Second goring under Rabbi Shimon: the last injured party takes 100, the earlier one 50, and the owner takes the remainder.
Third goring: the last injured party takes 100, the previous one 50, and the first two split the rest, a gold dinar each.
Asks whose opinion the mishnah reflects, since it seems to follow neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva.
Under Rabbi Yishmael, creditor priority would favor the earliest injured party; under Rabbi Akiva, partnership explains the surplus ruling.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the mishnah does not say the surplus returns to all prior injured parties, since they jointly own the belligerent ox.
Rava: the mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, where injured parties are creditors; a claimant who seized the ox becomes a paid bailee.
If so, the mishnah should say the surplus returns to the owner, since half the ox is his and he bears no later damage.
Ravina explains the surplus returns to the earlier injured party when the later party's loss was smaller than the earlier one's.
Ravin reports Rabbi Yohanan's teaching that the mishnah addresses a bailee's negligence, supporting this reading.
Asks whether the mishnah follows Rabbi Yishmael, given that its latter clause quotes Rabbi Shimon's ruling on the 200-dinar ox.
Quotes the further goring cases under Rabbi Shimon, with the first two injured parties each receiving a gold dinar.
Asks whether the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael and the latter Rabbi Akiva, since Rabbi Shimon's ruling reflects Akiva's partnership view.
Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda that the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael and the latter Rabbi Akiva, and to drop the single-opinion assumption.
Rabbi Yohanan's practical difference: whether an injured party can consecrate the ox, which parallels Yishmael versus Akiva.
Cites a mishnah: one who slaps another pays a sela, while Rabbi Yehuda, quoting Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, says one hundred dinars.
Rav Toviya asks whether the mishnah's sela is a Tyrian sela of four dinars or a provincial sela worth half a dinar.
Rav Yosef replies that a provincial sela could not divide the gold dinar into whole coins, so the mishnah uses Tyrian coinage.
Rav Toviya objects that this proves nothing, since the tanna need not list every case, like a peddler advertising all his wares.
Resolution: Rav Yehuda cites Rav that Torah coinage is Tyrian and Sages' coinage is provincial, so the slap fine is a provincial sela.
The slapped man declines the half-dinar fine as beneath him and asks that it go to the poor, then retracts and asks to keep it.
Rav Yosef replies that the poor already acquired the fine and the court stands in for them, as Shmuel's ruling on orphans shows.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Orphans need no prosbol because the court is legally their steward, so their debts transfer to the court automatically.
Rami bar Hama's teaching: orphans need no prosbol, since Rabban Gamliel's court acted as their fathers, a status courts keep.
Hanan slapped a man and was ordered to pay a half-dinar; unable to make change, he slapped him again and paid with a clipped dinar.
Mishnah: an ox forewarned for one species or person pays full damage only for that kind; for any other kind it pays half.
The Sages ask Rabbi Yehuda about an ox forewarned for Shabbatot but not for weekdays: what is the halakha?
Rabbi Yehuda rules full damage on Shabbat and half on weekdays; the ox reverts to innocuous after three Sabbaths without goring.
Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa offer different readings of the mishnah's opening clause, each based on a different wording.
Rav Zevid holds that an ordinary ox counts as forewarned for all species; Rav Pappa holds it does not.
Rav Zevid infers his reading from the mishnah's latter clause, while Rav Pappa infers his from the former clause.
Rav Zevid's inference from the latter clause: forewarning for small specimens implies forewarning for large ones, a broader ruling.
If the mishnah means an ox forewarned for its species is not forewarned for others, the latter clause seems problematic.
Rav Pappa replies that the latter clause is needed, since attacking one member does not make the ox forewarned for all its species.
Rav Pappa's inference from the former clause: forewarning for people does not make the ox forewarned for animals in ordinary cases.
If forewarning for one species extends to others, the next clause about people and animals seems unnecessary.
Rav Zevid replies the first clause concerns reversion: an ox reverting for animals counts as reverted even without reverting for people.
Objects with a baraita of Sumakhos: forewarned for people means forewarned for animals a fortiori, apparently contradicting Rav Zevid.
Rav Zevid replies Sumakhos concerns reversion: since the ox has not reverted toward people, it has not reverted toward animals either.
Rav Ashi cites the mishnah's Shabbat case as proof for Rav Zevid, since the Sages' question would otherwise be pointless.
Objects that the mishnah's reply would be pointless, since the Sages already stated the ox is not forewarned for weekdays.
Rav Yannai infers Rav Zevid's view from the mishnah's former clause on full versus half damage by kind of victim.
This clause clarifies the species case: full damage is owed only when the ox gores a kind it is forewarned about.
If the first clause already says an ox not forewarned for its species is not forewarned for others, the repeated payment rule seems superfluous.
Even on Rav Pappa's view, an ox that gores an ox, a donkey and a camel becomes forewarned for all three species.
Baraita: an ox that gores every other ox it sees becomes forewarned for alternate oxen, showing alternating forewarning.
Baraita: an ox alternating between goring and sparing different animals becomes forewarned for alternate animals of every species.
The Sages raise an unresolved dilemma about an ox that gored a particular kind, which the Gemara leaves open.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dilemmas: after an ox gores a donkey and camel, is a later goring counted with the earlier species, or only with oxen?
Dilemmas on Shabbat goring: whether a later Shabbat counts with the weekday goring or only as a Shabbat pattern.
The Gemara leaves these dilemmas unresolved.
A case: an ox gores on the 15th, 16th and 17th of successive months, paralleling Rav and Shmuel's dispute about a cycle.
Cites the parallel dispute about menstrual bleeding on shifting dates: Rav says a cycle is set, Shmuel requires three skips.
Rava: an ox that gores after hearing a shofar three times becomes forewarned with regard to the sound of shofarot.
Asks whether this is obvious; Rava teaches that the first blast was not a mere startle but a consistent impetus.
Mishnah: no liability when a Jew's ox and consecrated or gentile property clash, but full damages when a gentile's ox gores a Jew's.
Gemara: the mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, citing a baraita reading 'the ox of another' as excluding consecrated oxen.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya: a consecrated ox that gores a non-sacred one is exempt, but a non-sacred ox gored damage is owed in full.
The Sages ask what Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya holds, since the distinction between the two directions seems unclear.
Proposed answer: he reads 'another' precisely, and derives liability when a non-sacred ox gores consecrated property a fortiori.
Objects: an a fortiori ruling cannot be stricter than its source, so full damages for an innocuous ox contradicts the half-damages rule.
Reish Lakish: full damages are the default, and 'another' limits half damages to an innocuous ox's harm to another's ox.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that if an exemption were meant for forewarned oxen, the verse's wording would be needless, so it must address innocuous oxen.
Mishnah: a Jew's ox that gores a gentile's ox is exempt, while a gentile's ox that gores a Jew's ox pays full damages.
Dilemma: whether 'another' is read precisely or inclusively, the ruling appears difficult whichever way one reads it.
Rabbi Abbahu derives from Habakkuk 3:6 that God permitted gentile property to Israel, because the Noahides failed their seven mitzvot.
Rabbi Yohanan derives the same principle from Deuteronomy 33:2: gentile wealth was revealed to Israel when the Torah was given.
A baraita teaches the same ruling, citing Habakkuk 3:6 and Deuteronomy 33:2 to support it.
Asks why the baraita adds a second verse, if the first already seems sufficient.
The second verse supports the expositions of Rav Mattana and Rav Yosef, which derive the ruling from Habakkuk's wording.
Shows vayyatter means uprooting, citing the same root in Leviticus 11:21, where it denotes leaping on the earth.
Rav Yosef's exposition: God saw the seven Noahide mitzvot unfulfilled, so He permitted their prohibitions to Israel.
Asks whether gentiles profit from permitted prohibitions, and cites a baraita that even a gentile studying Torah has priestly status.
Rav Yosef means they receive no reward as one commanded and performing; Rabbi Hanina says the commanded performer is greater.
Story: Roman military officials studied the Torah with the Sages three times, then departed with a complaint.
The officials argue the ruling is inconsistent whichever way 'another' is read, exposing a flaw in the halakha.
Statement that this matter is not disclosed to the kingdom, closing the officials' story.
The daughter of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda dies; the Sages urge Ulla to console him, and Ulla objects that Babylonian consolation is heresy.
Ulla goes alone to console Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda and addresses him directly.
Cites Deuteronomy 2:9, God telling Moses not to contend with Moab, as the basis for discussing Moses's reasoning.
Explains that Moses reasoned a fortiori from the Midianites, who only aided Moab, that the Torah commanded war with them.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: is it not all the more clear that the Moabites themselves should be attacked?
God replies that He had two virtuous descendants to draw from Moab and Ammon, Ruth and Naamah, so they are spared.
Ulla's a fortiori argument: if God spared the nations for two righteous women, a righteous daughter would certainly have survived.
Rabbi Yohanan teaches that God never withholds reward, even for a pleasant euphemism in speech.
Setup: the elder daughter's naming of Moab, and what God told Moses about that nation.

The Rabbis: what then do they do with the lying in wait verse? The house of Rabbi Yannai says it excludes one who throws a stone inside.
What does this look like: if nine Canaanites and one Israelite are among them, the majority are Canaanites; or half and half, a doubt in life, to be lenient, so it is not needed?

It is needed where nine Israelites and one Canaanite; although most are Israelites, since one Canaanite is among them, it is fixed, and a fixed case is half and half, a doubt in life, resolved leniently.
Mishna: the ox of a woman, of orphans, of a steward, of the public domain, of the sanctuary, or of a convert that died without heirs, is liable to death.
Rabbi Yehuda says the ox of the public domain, of the sanctuary, or of a convert that died is exempt from death, because it has no owners.
Baraita: the ox of a woman, of orphans, of a steward, of the public domain, of the sanctuary, or of a convert, when it died without heirs, is liable.
Rabbi Yehuda says the ox of the public domain, of the sanctuary, or of a convert that died without heirs is exempt from death, because it has no owners.
Rav Huna exempts Rabbi Yehuda even where it gored and then was consecrated, or gored and then was declared ownerless.
From where do we know this?
From the mishna listing two items, the ox of the public domain and the ox of a convert that died without heirs, these are one: an ownerless ox.
But this teaches that even if it gored and then was consecrated, or gored and then was declared ownerless, it is exempt; and so is taught elsewhere.
Exodus 21:29: and its owner was warned, and it killed, so death and standing trial must be equal for both.
Is a final judgment not required? But the ox is stoned, which is a final judgment; rather, say death and trial must be equal.

Mishna: an ox going out to be stoned, if its owners consecrated it, is not consecrated; if slaughtered, its flesh is forbidden; if before judgment, it is consecrated; if slaughtered, its flesh is permitted.
Baraita: an ox that killed before its judgment was final, and its owner sold it.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: if an ox was consecrated and slaughtered, its meat is permitted; if returned to its owner after judgment, it is restored; if sold, it is not sold.
Rabbi Yaakov says that even after judgment is final, if the guard returns it to its owner, it is restored.
Shall we say they dispute this point?
The Rabbis hold that one does not say the benefit prohibition; here is yours, before you.
Rabbi Yaakov holds that one does say it; Rabbah says all agree that one says the benefit prohibition, here is yours before you.
Otherwise we would dispute the case of chametz on Passover; rather, the dispute is whether judgment on an ox may be completed in its absence.
The Rabbis hold judgment on an ox is completed only in its presence, since if it were returned, it would have fled to the marsh.
Rabbi Yaakov holds that judgment on an ox may be completed in its absence, since eventually they would complete the judgment.
What is the reason for the Rabbis?
Exodus 21:29: the ox shall be stoned and its owner put to death; as the owner's death is in their presence, so the ox's death is in its presence.
Rabbi Yaakov: granted, owners can make claims, but an ox is not capable of making claims.
Mishna: if it was given to a free guard or to a borrower.
Baraita: four enter in place of the owners: a free guard, a borrower, a paid guard and a renter; if killed, the killers are liable, and they pay the kofer.
Except a free guard: what is the case? If he guarded it, all of them would be exempt.
If he did not guard it, even a free guard would be liable?
Here we deal with minimal guarding by a free guard, whose guarding ended, unlike the others whose guarding did not end; this follows Rabbi Meir.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a renter is like a free guard, why not teach the renter alongside the free guard? Or if he is like a paid guard, why not teach it that way too?
Rav Huna bar Hiyya: this is the view of Rabbi Elazar, who says a guard has only a knife, and for a renter he follows Rabbi Yehuda, who says a renter is like a paid guard.
Abaye: really it follows Rabbi Meir, as Rabbah bar Avuh taught and as he switched the case.
The mishna teaches: how is a renter treated? Rabbi Meir says like a paid guard, and Rabbi Yehuda says like a free guard.
Rabbi Elazar: if one gave his ox to a free guard, the guard is liable if it caused damage, and exempt if it was harmed.
What case is this? If the guard accepted responsibility for its damage, even if it was harmed he would be liable; if not, even if it caused damage he would be exempt.
Rava: really he accepted responsibility, and here we deal with a case where he knew the ox was a gorer, and it was not his habit to let others cause damage on his account.

Mishna: if the owner tied the ox with a rope and locked it in his presence properly, and it went out and caused damage, the innocuous and forewarned are liable per Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yehuda says innocuous liable and forewarned exempt; Rabbi
What is the reason of Rabbi Meir?
Rabbi Meir holds that oxen in general are not in a state of guarding, and the verse says innocuous is liable, which requires minimal guarding, while not guarding it applies to forewarned.
For the forewarned, the verse requires superior guarding, and he derives goring for innocuous and goring for forewarned.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that oxen in general are in a state of guarding; the verse says innocuous is liable, so superior guarding is needed.
Rabbi Yehuda: the verse not guarding applies to the forewarned, requiring superior guarding; one addition after another, so the verse excludes minimal guarding.
But if you say goring for innocuous and goring for forewarned, the verse excluded this one and not another; but the verse should have said not guard it, so why write this?
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says innocuous and forewarned are exempt if the guard kept minimal guarding.
What is the reason?
He holds with Rabbi Yehuda, that a forewarned ox suffices with minimal guarding, and derives goring for innocuous and goring for forewarned.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: Rabbi Yehuda exempts only the side of forewarning, but the side of death remains standing.
Rav: a forewarned ox is forewarned for a right horn, not for a left horn.
Whose view is this: if Rabbi Meir, then innocuous and forewarned require superior guarding; if Rabbi Yehuda, why the left horn, when even the right horn has a side of death?
They say it is always Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Adda bar Ahava does not hold this; rather, in such a case one finds both a side of death and a side of forewarning.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A forewarned ox that is fully exempt from the death side is never found; Rabbi Elazar holds a guard has only a knife.
What is the reason for Rabbi Elazar's view?
Rabbah: the verse says he shall not guard it, so there is no guarding for this one.
Abaye objects: then likewise the verse says he shall not cover it, so there is no covering for this one either.
Abaye: but if you say so, the mishna teaches that if it was covered properly and an ox or donkey fell into it and died, the owner is exempt.
Abaye concludes: this is the reason of Rabbi Elazar, as taught in a baraita.
Rabbi Natan: how do we know one may not raise a vicious dog in his house or set a rotten ladder in his house? The verse says you shall not place blood in your house.
Closing formula of the chapter: the ox that gored four or five times.
Mishna: if an ox gored a cow and her fetus was found beside her, and it is unknown whether she was pregnant before being gored, the owner pays half damages for the cow and a quarter for the fetus.
Likewise if a cow gored an ox and its fetus was found beside it, the damages are half from the cow and a quarter from the fetus.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: this is the view of Sumchos, who says money in doubt is divided; the Sages say the great rule is the burden of proof is on the claimant.
Shmuel: why say this great rule? It is needed, since even if the damaged party claims certainty and the damager claims it is doubtful, the burden is on the claimant.
Or else: come and see what was said.
If one sold an ox that turned out to be a gorer: Rav says it is an erroneous sale; Shmuel says he may say I sold it to you for slaughter.
Why not check: is the buyer buying for ripeness, or for slaughter? The case is one where the buyer bought for both.
Let us check whether the ripeness is equal to ripeness, or slaughter to slaughter; is this not the case?
No: the case is where the buyer made the meat more costly, and stands at the price of the ripe ox.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara challenges: if the seller cannot repay, may the buyer keep the ox instead of money?
Case is needed where the seller can repay and the buyer still wants his money back.
Rav holds this is a mistaken sale, following the majority purpose of buying oxen for plowing.
Shmuel rejects majority reasoning in monetary matters; the claimant bears the burden of proof.
A baraita about the goring ox and cow supports Rav Yehuda that the mishna follows Sumakhos.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani asks the source for placing the burden of proof on the claimant.
Exodus 24:14 is cited, read as requiring the claimant to bring proof.
Rav Ashi objects that a verse is unnecessary, since the principle is evident by reasoning.
The verse is actually needed to show the claimant must be heard before the defendant.
The Neharde'ans hold that sometimes the court hears the defendant first.
Asks what the circumstances are for that exception.
The exception applies when the defendant's property is losing value due to the claim.
The mishna teaches that a cow gored an ox and its offspring is found at its side; half and a quarter.
Why does the mishna say half the damage, if only half is owed, and what is the point of the quarter?
Abaye explains half means a quarter, split between cow and newborn, with one-eighth from the newborn.
If cow and offspring have one owner, why split payment; the claimant could demand the full half from the cow.
The ruling is needed when the cow and offspring have different owners.
If the claimant sues the cow owner first, the cow owner can demand proof of partnership.
The case is where the claimant first sued the calf's owner, revealing a partner.
Some say the cow owner may dismiss a claim by noting he knows the calf is his partner.
Rava objects that Abaye's reading would make the mishna teach a quarter and an eighth, not half and a quarter.
Rava explains the mishna concerns a cow and its offspring with one owner; half is paid from the cow.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the cow is absent, only a quarter of the damage is collected from the offspring.
Explains the reason: when the calf's presence in the womb is uncertain, only a quarter is paid from it.
Rava holds that a pregnant cow's damage is collected from its offspring, as the fetus is part of it.
A hen's egg is only a secretion, not part of the hen's body, so the damage cannot be collected from it.
Rava rules the calf is appraised together with its mother, otherwise the damager is wrongly weakened.
Parallel cases of a severed slave's hand and damage to part of a field support Rava's appraisal principle.
Rav Aha son of Rava objects that weakening the damager by money loss would otherwise be the correct halakha.
Rav Ashi replies the damager can claim he assessed the pregnant cow's value for the injured party.
Asks who receives compensation for the cow's increased bulk from pregnancy when the owners differ.
Rav Pappa says the owner of the cow takes it, Rav Aha son of Rav Ika says they divide; the halakha is division.
Mishna: damage from goods placed in another's courtyard without permission falls on the owner of the goods, with or without permission.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a homeowner is exempt for damage from goods or animals that entered his courtyard without permission, and liable with permission.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the homeowner is liable in none of these cases unless he explicitly accepts responsibility for safekeeping.
Explains the potter's liability: without permission he is liable, and permission does not imply he took on safekeeping.
Asks whose opinion the mishna's first clause follows.
Identifies Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds that unspecified permission does not transfer responsibility for safekeeping.
The mishna's last clause follows the Rabbis, who hold that permission implies the owner accepts safekeeping.
Points out that the mishna mixes Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view at the start and end with the Rabbis in the middle.
Rabbi Zeira says the mishna is disjointed; Rava says the opening follows the Rabbis, with liability even for wind breakage.
Mishna continues on produce: if the animal slipped on it, the owner is liable, but if it ate it, Rav exempts.
Asks what the reason is for exempting the owner when the animal ate the produce.
The reason is that the animal should not have eaten it, so the owner is not responsible.
Rav Sheshet says Rav spoke while dozing and the halakha is not precise as stated.
A baraita on poison placed before an animal: exempt by human law, liable by Heaven.
From the baraita, edible produce would make the placer liable by human law, unlike poison.
Asks why the placer of produce should be liable, if the animal should not have eaten it.
Sages reply that even produce exempts by human law, and the baraita teaches poison is liable by Heaven; or afrazta is meant.
A baraita on a woman who grinds wheat in a house without permission challenges Rav's reasoning about eating.
Sages reply that the baraita may concern slipping on the wheat, not eating it, as the mishna does.
Asks what exactly the earlier questioner was asking.
The mishna says damage from slipping, while the baraita does not specify, so it may concern slipping too.
A second baraita on an ox that ate wheat and died challenges the view that the animal should not have eaten.
Rava replies the case with permission differs, since the owner accepted responsibility for safekeeping even against self-strangulation.
Dilemma: when the courtyard owner takes on safekeeping, does he cover only his own damage or all outside damage?
A baraita from Rav Yehuda bar Simon, on produce eaten by an ox from elsewhere, is brought as a solution.
Asks who the exempt and liable parties are, and whether the courtyard owner is meant in both.
Rejects that reading: the exempt party is the owner of the damaging ox, and the liable party is the owner of the ox.
Asks: but if it refers to the owner of the ox, what then?

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the difference is between damage with permission and without permission.
Damage with permission is Eating in the injured party's domain, liable; without permission it is in the public domain, exempt.
A baraita on an ox entering a courtyard and being gored, with or without permission, is brought as a proof.
Asks who is exempt and who liable, and whether the courtyard owner is meant in both cases.
No: the exempt party is the owner of the goring ox, and the liable party is also the owner of that ox.
If so, why does the baraita specify permission and non-permission for an ox that gores?
The baraita follows Rabbi Tarfon, who holds goring in the injured party's courtyard is paid in full, and in public only half.
A woman baked in a house, a goat ate her dough and died; Rava holds her liable for the goat.
Objection: Rava would then disagree with Rav, who exempts the owner when the animal should not have eaten the produce.
The cases differ: without permission she took on no safekeeping, while with permission she accepted responsibility for the dough.
Asks how this differs from the baraita on a woman who grinds wheat without permission, exempt by eating.
Grinding needs no privacy so owners stay and are responsible; baking needs privacy so the woman takes on safekeeping.
Mishna: if one brings an ox in without permission and the homeowner's ox gores it, the homeowner is exempt.
Rava holds an ox that digs pits in a courtyard without permission makes its owner liable for the damage.
Objection: the verse on digging a pit refers to a man, not an ox that digs, so the courtyard owner would be exempt.
Reply: the courtyard owner should have filled the pit, so he is treated as if he dug it himself.
Rava adds: if an ox crouches and causes damage to the homeowner, the ox's owner is exempt.
Asks whether the owner is exempt because the crouching caused the damage.
Rav Pappa explains that crouching means dropping dung, which is a pit, and pits do not cause liability for utensils.
If any obstruction is a pit by Shmuel's view, what does Rav say, since property is a pit only once renounced?
Owners usually renounce ordinary dung, so it counts as a pit even according to Rav.
Rava: whoever enters a courtyard without permission is liable for damage he causes or suffers, but the owner is exempt for injuring him.
Rav Pappa limits this: if the owner knew of the intruder, the owner is liable for injuring him.
Reason: you had permission to eject him, but no permission to injure him.
The Gemara notes that Rava and Rav Pappa each hold their positions consistently, in the attribution given.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: when both parties are on the premises with or without permission, each who injures the other is liable; mutual stumbling exempts.
Explains the reason: liability requires both to be in the same permitted or unpermitted status, so mixed status changes the outcome.
Mishna: an ox that fell into a pit and fouled its water makes its owner liable.
Rava limits this to fouling at the moment of falling, since the carcass afterward is like utensils in a pit, not covered.
Asks, on Shmuel's view that any obstruction is a pit, what Rav can say about the carcass.
Rava's correct version: only a carcass fouling water is liable; stench alone is indirect damage, so the owner is exempt.
Mishna: if the homeowner's father or son died in the pit, the ox's owner pays the ransom.
Asks why a ransom is owed, since an innocuous ox should owe none.
Rav: the ox is forewarned about falling into pits, so it is liable for ransom.
Asks: if so, the ox would be put to death, since forewarning implies intent.
Rav Yosef: the ox meant to eat grass at the pit's edge and fell, so no intent, but ransom still applies.
Shmuel: the ox is innocuous and the mishna follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, so only half a ransom is owed.
Ulla: the mishna follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili on ransom, yet also Rabbi Tarfon, so a full ransom is owed.
Asks why the mishna names a father or son if Shmuel's reading covers any person and any place.
The mishna gives the typical case, where the victim is usually a relative of the pit's owner.
Mishna: if he brought the ox into the courtyard with permission, the courtyard owner is liable for damage.
Rav holds the halakha follows the first tanna, while Shmuel holds it follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A baraita on an owner who is told to safeguard or who promises to safeguard the ox, with liability assigned accordingly.
Difficulty: the first clause seems to contradict itself about who is liable when told to safeguard.
The reason: an explicit safeguard instruction shifts liability, while without it the courtyard owner accepts safekeeping by default.
The latter clause of the baraita: the courtyard owner promises to safeguard, so he is liable for injury.
The reason: his explicit promise makes him liable; without it he does not accept safekeeping, so the ox owner is liable.
Concludes: the first clause follows the Rabbis and the latter clause follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabbi Elazar says the baraita is disjointed; Rava says it all follows the Rabbis, with the wording of safeguarding being symmetry.
Rav Pappa says it all follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and the first clause follows Rabbi Tarfon, so the owner pays full damage.
Without the safeguard instruction, granting entry creates a partnership courtyard, so only half the damage is owed.
Mishna: an ox aimed at another ox that struck a pregnant woman, causing miscarriage, is exempt from payment for the fetus, unlike a person.
Explains the assessment: the value of the woman before and after giving birth is compared, and the difference is paid.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel begins a dissenting view on the payment for miscarried offspring.

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the court appraises the offspring and pays the husband, or his heirs, not the woman; a freed or converted wife is exempt.
The mishna's wording implies that an ox intending to gore a woman makes its owner liable for miscarried offspring.
Objection: this would refute Rav Adda bar Ahava, who holds oxen intending to gore a woman are exempt.
Rav Adda could reply that intent toward the woman also exempts; the mishna's wording mirrors the verse on a person striking a pregnant woman.
Rav Pappa: an ox that gored a Canaanite maidservant and caused miscarriage makes its owner pay for the offspring.
The reason is that a Canaanite is like property, citing Genesis 22:5 where the word for donkey is linked to Canaanites.
Asks whether the mishna should say the increase in value rather than the compensation for the offspring.
The mishna states both: the compensation for miscarried offspring and the increase in the woman's value from the pregnancy.
Mishna: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that if so, the result is absurd, since a woman's value rises after birth.
Asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means by his objection.
Rabba explains: a woman's value is higher after birth, so the court appraises the fetuses and pays the husband.
A baraita repeats Rabba's explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, supporting it.
Rava explains: the increase belongs to the husband, while the wife gets none; the court pays the fetuses and they divide the increase.
A baraita repeats Rava's explanation, with damage and pain assessed separately and the husband and wife dividing the increase.
The first baraita's view that a woman's value falls in pregnancy conflicts with the second baraita's view that it rises.
No conflict: the cases differ, one a woman bearing her first child, the other a woman who is not.
Asks the reason for the Rabbis' view that the increase in value also goes to the husband.
A redundancy in Exodus 21:22 is read as teaching that the pregnancy increase goes to the husband.
Asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel derives from the extra word pregnant.
He derives that a blow must reach the womb area, as taught by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and clarified by Rav Pappa.
Mishna: a maidservant or convert who was freed or converted, and the owner is exempt.
Rabba explains: if the injury occurred during the convert's lifetime, the assailant acquires the money once the convert dies without heirs.
Rav Hisda objects that the money is not a bundle of coins; a baraita says the wife collects if the husband is dead.
Rabba's reading can be upheld: the baraita is like the mishna, read as injury during the convert's life or after his death.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes correcting the baraita wording so that the woman, not the assailant, is the one who acquires.
Asks whether the Rabba and Rav Hisda dispute reflects a dispute between tannaim on a convert's wife's miscarriage payment.
No difficulty: one baraita follows the Rabbis, the other Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
If Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds it, why specify after the husband's death, when she has a share even while he lives?
Both baraitot follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel but address different payments: increase in value versus miscarriage compensation.
The Sages challenge this: why distinguish the two cases, since the woman inherits the increase and Shimon's view might extend.
The first assumption fails: the woman has a share in the increase from the start, but not in miscarriage compensation.
Rav Yeiva the Elder asks Rav Nahman whether taking a convert's documents after his death acquires the document or only the land.
Rav Nahman's rebuttal: the document is useful as paper, and Rav Yeiva replies that covering a flask is a mundane purpose he intends.
Rabba: a Jew's collateral held by a convert, returned to its owner when the convert dies without heirs, since the lien is abrogated.
If a convert's collateral is held by a Jewish lender who dies, the lender takes his share and the other claimant takes the rest.
Asks why the lender does not acquire all of it through his courtyard, given that a courtyard effects acquisition without knowledge.
The courtyard effects acquisition only if the creditor could have taken it himself; otherwise the courtyard does not acquire, as ruled.
Mishna: digging a pit that opens onto another domain makes the digger liable for resulting damage.
A baraita: Rabbi Yishmael holds the Torah's pit is one opened into the public domain; Rabbi Akiva holds it is one where ownership of the pit remains.
Rabba explains the dispute: all agree that opening or digging into the public domain creates liability, and the verse covers both acts.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva holds that a pit on one's own property also creates liability, since the verse refers to a pit with an owner.
Rabbi Yishmael holds the owner of the hazard is liable even when he renounced ownership of a pit dug in the public domain.
Asks what Rabbi Akiva means by the Torah pit, if one is liable for every pit under Rabba's reading.
The Torah pit is the one the verse introduces first, for compensation, and then covers pits on one's own property.
Rav Yosef: all agree a pit on one's own property creates liability, since the verse refers to a pit with an owner.
Rabbi Yishmael holds a pit dug in the public domain is also liable, since the verse covers both opening and digging.
Rabbi Akiva's reading of the verse wording: separate phrases are needed for opening and digging, so each needs its own covering rule.
Under Rav Yosef's reading, asks what Rabbi Yishmael means by the Torah pit for public-domain digging.
The Torah pit is the one the verse introduces first for damages, as Rabbi Yishmael explained.
Objection from a baraita: a pit dug in the public domain and opened onto private property is exempt, since no hollow may be made under the public domain.
Asks whose opinion the baraita follows, since neither Rabbi Yishmael nor Rabbi Akiva fits Rav Yosef's reading of the first clause.
Rav Yosef replies that everyone agrees with the whole passage; the first clause concerns a pit where no ownership was renounced.
Rav Ashi: since Rav Yosef reads the baraita as agreeing with all, Rabba need not read it as a dispute between tannaim.
Objection from a baraita: a pit dug on one's own property opened into the public domain is liable, but adjacent private property is exempt.
The objection continues: Rabba's reading makes the whole passage Rabbi Yishmael's, but Rav Yosef's leaves the last clause unexplained.
Rav Yosef replies that the last clause concerns one digging for foundations, on which all agree.
A baraita on Nehunya who dug pits and transferred them to the public, exempt, and the Sages' praise, plus his daughter's rescue.
Asks the daughter who brought her up out of the well.
She says a ram came to her, led by an old man who pulled her out.
Asks Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa whether he is a prophet, since he knew she had ascended.
He replies he is no prophet nor prophet's son; he reasoned that Nehunya's offspring should not stumble where the righteous man suffered.
Rabbi Aha: despite Nehunya's care for others, his son died of thirst.
Psalms 50:3 and 89:8 show God is exacting with those near Him, even over a hairsbreadth.
Rabbi Hanina: whoever says God is forgiving of transgressions will have his life relinquished.
Deuteronomy 32:4 is cited: God's ways are justice, so He does not waive heavenly judgment.
Rabbi Hana, or Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, introduces the next question about a verse.
Asks: what is the meaning of that which is written?

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The plural erekh appayim shows God is patient with both the righteous and the wicked, not only with anger.
A baraita: one may not throw stones from his property into the public domain; a pious man's rebuke is later vindicated when the thrower loses his field.
Mishna: one who digs a pit in the public domain is liable if an ox or donkey falls in; excavations under ten handbreadths are exempt if it dies.
Rav holds the pit is liable for suffocating fumes only, while Shmuel holds the Torah covers both fumes and impact, even woolen sponges.
Asks what practical difference lies between the views of Rav and Shmuel.
The difference: a raised mound in the public domain, where Rav exempts for lacking fumes and Shmuel holds liable for the impact.
Asks what Rav's source is for exempting the mound case.
Rav reads the verse's falling as the normal fall into a pit; Shmuel reads any falling as covered.
Objection to Rav from the mishna's extra phrasing, which for Rav would have no function beyond the pit.
For Rav the extra phrase covers trenches and water channels, which the mishna first states and then explains from the Torah.
Asks why the mishna needs to list each of these separate excavation types.
Each type is needed, since a pit, ditch, cave, trench or channel might otherwise be exempt at ten handbreadths for lacking fumes.
Challenge from the mishna: an excavation under ten handbreadths killing an animal exempts, yet injury makes the digger liable.
Asks whether the exemption for death is only because there is not enough impact.
Exempt because there are no lethal fumes, yet injury is covered since the fumes suffice to cause damage.
Ox story: Rav Nahman deems a tereifa an ox that fell into a shallow channel and was slaughtered, implying impact below ten handbreadths.
Rava objects to Rav Nahman from the mishna: if impact cannot kill below ten handbreadths, why is the animal a tereifa?

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Nahman: no liability for lack of lethal fumes, but impact can kill, which is why a channel animal is suspected tereifa.
Rava objects from the stoning structure of two-person height: if impact below ten handbreadths killed, why need such height.
Rav Nahman: the stoning height is set for a quick, compassionate death, citing Leviticus 19:18 as the basis.
If so, why not raise the structure higher to make death even less painful?
Rava objects again from the roof parapet law of Deuteronomy 22:8: if impact below ten handbreadths killed, why require ten for the roof.
Rav Nahman: a structure under ten handbreadths is not a house, so only a house needs a parapet.
Rava: then count the house height from outside, minus ceiling and plaster, and it falls short of ten.
Rav Nahman: the owner hollowed extra space inside the floor to reach ten handbreadths.
Rava: then a house under ten outside but ten inside would also be exempt, so the reasoning fails.
Rav Nahman's reasoning: the ox lands on its stomach, four plus six handbreadths make ten, so impact comes from ten.
Why not say a six-handbreadth pit also suffices, given the mishna's ten-handbreadth standard?
The mishna refers to an animal that rolled into the pit, so the full ten handbreadths is required.
Mishna: a pit owned by two partners, uncovered by both in turn, makes the second partner liable for damage.
How can a pit owned by two partners arise, under Rabbi Akiva's view and under the view that renounced ownership exempts?
If both appoint an agent to dig, neither is liable; if each digs five handbreadths, only the second's digging counts.
Asks how such a jointly owned pit can arise for the Rabbis on both death and damage, under Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: both partners remove a chunk of earth simultaneously, completing the pit to ten handbreadths together.
Asks what the opinions of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis are on this case.
A baraita: a digger of nine handbreadths and a second who finishes to ten; the second alone is liable for death, both for damage.
Reason for the Rabbis: the verse's repeated phrase is read as covering a second digger who makes the pit and bears responsibility.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replies that both verse clauses are needed, and the Rabbis hold the same for their interpretations.
The Rabbis' reason: the verse says a man digs a pit, one person, not two, so the second digger alone is responsible.
How does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi read the phrase if a man shall dig a pit?
He uses it to exclude an ox digging a pit; the Rabbis derive one person and not two from the repeated phrase.
What does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derive from the repetition, and why assume the verse makes the first digger liable?
The verse says the carcass shall be his, marking the one who completed the death-causing pit, the second digger.
Asks what the second clause of the verse teaches, if not the carcass-for-him point, given Rava's ruling on consecrated oxen.
Rava's case of a consecrated ox that falls into a pit is exempt, since the carcass goes to its owner; the case concerns a human digger.
A baraita: a digger of ten, followed by a second to twenty and a third to thirty, are all liable.
Objection: a baraita holds that only the last digger is liable when a second person finishes ten handbreadths by scraping.

51b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the two baraitot reflect Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view and the Rabbis' view respectively.
Rav Zevid: both follow the Rabbis; the last digger is liable only if the first dug less than ten handbreadths.
Asks: in the cistern baraita the first digger reached ten, yet the last is liable; how does that square with the Rabbis?
There the pit was too wide to have lethal fumes until the second narrowed it with plaster, adding the fumes.
Others say Rav Zevid meant both baraitot follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, with the second case lacking fumes for death or damage.
Rava: one who places a stone at a pit's mouth and raises the ground to reach ten brings us to the dispute on liability.
Asks: is this not obvious, since it is exactly the case under dispute?
It is needed lest one think the lethal fumes come from the bottom only, so that additions at the top would not create liability.
Rava's dilemma: if one closes the extra handbreadth or removes stones, does the original digger regain sole responsibility? Unresolved.
Shmuel bar Marta: a pit of eight handbreadths with two of water is liable, since each water handbreadth counts as two dry.
Further dilemmas on pits with water: nine with one handbreadth of water, seven with three; and Rav Sheizevi's widening question. Unresolved or raised.
Rabba: widening reduces the fumes so no liability; Rav Ashi suggests liability depends on whether the animal died of fumes or impact, and which side it fell.
Rabba and Rav Yosef transmit a dispute on a pit as deep as wide: whether fumes need depth exceeding width or the reverse.
Asks from what point the first partner is exempt for a pit he left uncovered.
Two versions of Rabba bar bar Hana's ruling: exemption from when he stops using it, or only once he hands over his bucket.
A baraita on drawing water from a cistern shows a tannaitic dispute on when the first drawer is exempt.
Asks on what principle these tannaim disagree.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds designation applies retroactively, while the Rabbis hold there is no such designation.
Ravina: the same dispute appears in the Nedarim mishna about partners and their courtyard, so both follow their reasoning.
Mishna in Nedarim: partners who vowed no benefit may not enter their courtyard, though Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits entering one's own part.
Asks on what principle these tannaim disagree in the courtyard case.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds retroactive designation so each enters his own part; the Rabbis hold the courtyard remains jointly owned.
Rabbi Elazar: when a seller hands the buyer his bucket for drawing water, the buyer acquires the cistern.
Asks how the bucket effects acquisition: if by payment, why not pay money; if by taking possession, why not possession by use.
The sale was by taking possession, and handing the bucket amounts to telling him to take possession and acquire it.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: whoever sells a house to another (the ruling continues).

52a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Once the seller hands the buyer the key, the buyer acquires the cistern.
Asks the circumstances: if by money, why need the key; if by taking possession, why not acquire by taking possession.
The sale was by taking possession, and handing over the key is like telling him to take possession and acquire it.
Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai: a seller who hands over the mashkukhit of a flock transfers the flock to the buyer.
Asks the circumstances of the flock sale: by pulling or by conveying.
It was a sale by pulling, and conveying the mashkukhit is like telling him to pull and acquire it.
Asks what the mashkukhit actually is.
Babylonian rendering: a bell the shepherd rings; Rabbi Yaakov: the lead goat; an anecdote on a blinded leader as divine anger.
Mishna on pits: a second passer who fails to cover an uncovered pit is liable; ox and donkey cases, digging-sound cases, and who is exempt.
Asks until when the first digger is exempt once the pit is found uncovered.
Rav: until he is aware; Shmuel: until others inform him; Rabbi Yohanan: until he can hire workers and cut cedars to cover it.
Mishna: if he covered the pit properly and an ox or donkey fell in and died, he is exempt.
Asks how an animal could fall into a pit that was properly covered.
Rabbi Yitzhak bar bar Hana: the cover rotted from within, so he could not have known it was damaged.
Dilemma: a cover able to bear oxen but not camels, weakened by camels, then broken by oxen; is the digger negligent?
Circumstances matter: if camels are common he is negligent; if they come occasionally, the question is whether he must anticipate them.
Objection from the mishna: properly covered pit with a fall exempts, so the cover must have been suitable only for oxen, not camels.

52b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If camels are common, why is he exempt; if not, the case of occasional camels suggests exemption now that camels are absent?
No: he covered it for both oxen and camels, and the fall is explained by the cover rotting from within, per Rabbi Yitzhak.
Objection from the mishna: an improperly covered pit where an ox or donkey dies makes him liable; the case must be one of partial suitability.
Asks the circumstances: if camels are common or occasional, is he negligent, and does the mishna then teach a novelty?
It may be that he covered for oxen but not camels, camels being common, and the latter clause is cited to complete the pair.
Some say the dilemma was never raised, since occasional camels make him negligent in any case.
Restates the dilemma: is negligence about camels also negligence about the rotting from within, or not?
Objection from the mishna on a cover that rotted from within: the case suggests negligence about camels does not extend to rot.
Rejects the objection: the cover suited both animals and rotted from within; the mishna teaches he need not knock to test it.
A further objection: where the cover is unsuitable for camels, and camels are common, the mishna's liability implies negligence transfers to rot.
The first clause covered for oxen but not camels; the latter clause is cited as well, so the answer stands.
Objection from a baraita: a blind, deaf or night-walking ox makes the owner liable, so negligence in one matter might carry over to another.
Rav: forward means literally in front of the pit, backward means literally behind it, on the mishna's wording.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Both cases concern falling into the pit itself, though falling backward still exempts the digger.
Rav: the Torah makes the digger liable only for lethal fumes, not impact, so a backward fall exempts.
Shmuel: liable whether the animal falls forward or backward, since fumes and impact both count.
Shmuel's reasoning: if fumes alone are covered, impact is covered a fortiori.
Asks what the mishna's backward-fall exemption means on Shmuel's view.
Example: the ox stumbled on the pit and fell behind it, outside the pit, and was injured there.
Objection from a baraita: liable whether the animal falls forward or backward, which refutes Rav.
Rav Hisda, Rabba and Rav Yosef each reconcile the baraita with Rav: by the owner's dual liability, a tumbling fall, or contaminated water.
Rav Hananya cites a baraita in support of Rav: the usual manner of falling is required, with forward and backward treated differently.
Asks why the digging-noise forward fall is liable, since the noise may be the cause rather than the pit.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi: this follows Rabbi Natan, who holds the pit owner causes the damage and pays when the digger cannot.
A baraita: an ox pushing another into a pit makes the first owner liable, with Rabbi Natan dividing half and half.
Objection: another baraita has Rabbi Natan assign three-quarters to the pit owner and one-quarter to the pusher.
Resolved: one baraita concerns an innocuous ox and the other a forewarned one, which changes the shares.
If both are fully responsible or each made half, Rabbi Natan's three-quarter division seems unexplained.
Rava: Rabbi Natan is a judge; the pusher's partnership claim lowers his share, and the owner of the killed ox recovers the rest from the pit owner.
Rava: a stone at a pit's mouth makes an ox stumble and fall in, a case of the dispute between Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis.
Asks whether this is obvious, since it makes no difference whether another ox or a stone caused the fall.
The ruling is needed: the stone-owner's claim fails, since without the stone the ox would not have fallen into the pit.
Introduces a further ruling, which the continuation of the daf states.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sets up the case: an innocuous ox and a disqualified consecrated firstborn gore together.
Abaye says the owner pays half the damage; Ravina says one-quarter.
Explains the dispute: both can follow the Rabbis (half each) or Rabbi Natan (full each), with innocuous or forewarned oxen.
Another version: Abaye says half and Ravina says full, each on a different reading of Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis.
Alternatively both follow Rabbi Natan, with Ravina on a forewarned ox and Abaye on an innocuous one.
Rava: pushing a person or animal into a pit makes each party liable for different compensation categories.
Asks what the reason is for the exemption of the pit owner regarding the disqualified consecrated ox.
The verse on the carcass being his limits liability to whoever owns the carcass, excluding a consecrated ox.
Asks whether this was obvious to Rava, since he had raised a dilemma about the carcass of a consecrated ox.
Rava was initially in doubt but resolved that liability is limited to whoever owns the carcass.
From where does the owner attend to the carcass, and why derive from one verse rather than reversing it?
The exemption fits the Pit verse, since Pit exempts vessels too, so Pit is more lenient than Ox.
Mishna: an ox and its vessels fall into a pit and break, and the pit owner is exempt for the vessels.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda makes the pit owner liable for vessels, so the mishna does not follow him.
The Rabbis derive from the verse that only an ox, not a person or vessels, creates pit liability; Rabbi Yehuda reads or to include vessels.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The word or separates ox and donkey, so either falling alone creates liability; Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis read the singular verb differently.
Challenges: a general term followed by a detail includes only what the detail contains, so only ox and donkey count.
Sages reply: the verse is general, detail, general, so only items like the detail, which are animals, are included.
Challenge: if animals are included by their carcass causing impurity, birds should be included too, which the Torah excludes.
Had the Torah written only ox or only donkey, each would limit liability differently, so both are written to exclude birds.
Rather, the verse the carcass shall be his covers anything subject to death, and it applies to both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks: vessels are not subject to death, so why is a separate source needed to derive their status?
Vessels are subject to death in the sense that their breaking is tantamount to their death.
On Rav's view that the pit's liability is for fumes only, asks whether vessels can be broken by fumes, requiring exclusion.
There is such a case for new vessels, which crack from the fumes.
Asks whether the carcass verse is needed for Rava's ruling on a disqualified consecrated ox, so it cannot ground a second halakha.
Objection to deriving liability from the money-to-owners verse: it would then include vessels and people as well.
The verse says ox, not person, and donkey, not vessels; but for Rabbi Yehuda, what does the donkey exclude?
Rava: the donkey in the Pit verse and the sheep in the lost-property verse are puzzling; the mishna lists ḥeresh, shoteh and katan oxen as liable.
Asks what the mishna's ḥeresh, shoteh or katan ox means: an ox owned by such a person, or an ox impaired by such a condition.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: it means an ox that is itself deaf, an imbecile, or very young, not one owned by such a person.

Resh Lakish says one who mates two kinds of animals is flogged

Ulla's principle: each kind belongs to its own domain, land or sea, so mating them is forbidden
Asks the law for one who leads a goat and a sheep together, which belong to different domains
Ravina objects that the same logic would make one who joins wheat and barley liable in two places
The distinction holds because liability applies in the land but not outside it, so both cases are liable
Chapter-closing formula announcing the end of this chapter and the opening words of the next

ranges.en: A flock properly locked into its pen causes damage after escaping, so the owner is exempt

If bandits themselves drove the flock out, the bandits are liable for the damage
