If the owner entrusted the flock to a shepherd, the shepherd takes the owner's place in liability

Explains that the court appraises a field of one seah of seed and the garden's loss in value within it

A baraita defines locking the door properly as one that withstands a typical wind

Rabbi Eliezer holds that a forewarned ox has no safeguarding except slaughter with a knife
Teeth and legs differ, since the Torah limited their required safeguarding, so Rabbi Meir can still hold this
Rabbi Elazar teaches a baraita listing four matters where the Torah limited the required safeguarding
The verse about the pit shows the owner is exempt if he covered it
The verse about the fire shows liability only for acts similar to actively kindling the fire

Rabba says the mishna's wording about sheep is precise and intentional

A baraita lists four acts that are exempt in human law but liable in heavenly law
Asks what case the wording of breaking a fence before another's animal refers to, and why liability is not also in human law

ranges.en: Explains that the baraita concerns an unstable wall that would have fallen anyway
Asks what the circumstances are of bending another's grain before a fire
Objects that if the fire reached in a typical wind he would be liable under human law too
Rather, the fire reaches the grain only in an atypical wind, so he is exempt under human law
Rav Ashi explains the case as one of a concealed item that was bent over to hide it
Asks what the circumstances are of one who hires false witnesses
Objects that if he hired them for himself he would be liable under human law too
Rather, he hired the witnesses for another's benefit, so the injured party cannot sue either
Asks what case the baraita on withholding testimony is dealing with
Objects that with two witnesses the duty is obvious from Torah law, so the baraita would be superfluous
Rather, the case is a single witness, whose testimony alone cannot render another liable
Raises a further case, the mnemonic of cases involving poison, agents and purification water, to show others exist
Raises another case: placing poison before another's animal, which exempts under human law
Raises another case: sending fire by the hand of a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor
Raises another case: frightening another person so that he is injured
Raises the cases of a broken jug or fallen camel left in the public domain, with Rabbi Meir's view
Rabbi Yehoshua needed to state these cases lest one think they are not liable even under heavenly law
Breaching a fence that was about to collapse anyway is stated so one does not think it is exempt in heaven
Bending grain is stated because one might argue no one knew an atypical wind would come, so heaven liability is taught
On Rav Ashi's view, the concealer might claim he protected the item, so heaven liability is stated
Hiring false witnesses is stated because the witnesses are the ones who sinned by listening to the hirer
Withholding testimony is stated because one might argue that the other party would have lied, so heaven liability is taught
Introduces the mishna case of a pit wall breached at night or by bandits, where the owner is exempt
Rabbah says the case applies when the wall was dug through, not when it was merely breached
Asks why he is liable if the wall was sound and not dug through, and what else he should have done
Explains that in an unstable wall, the start was negligence and the end was unavoidable, so the owner is exempt
On the other view, the start was negligence and the end was unavoidable, but the owner is liable
Asks what else can be said to resolve the disagreement
Rather, the mishna concerns a sound wall, and the owner is liable even if he did not dig through
Asks whether Rabbah's statement was said about the final clause of the mishna
Quotes the final clause: left in the sun or given to an incapable person, the owner is liable
Rabbah rules that even if the animal dug through, the owner is liable, since the whole matter is negligence
Explains the point of Rabbah's ruling: it teaches that the whole matter is negligence, not a split case
Rabbah's reasoning: once left in the sun, the animal used every trick available and went out
Quotes the mishna's last rule: bandits who drove the animal out are liable

ranges.en: Questions the need for the ruling, since once the animal is removed it is in their possession
Answers that the ruling is needed when they only urged the animal on without leading it, as in Rav's case
Abaye applies Rav Yosef's explanation to the mishna: bandits who struck the animal are liable
Asks in place of whom the shepherd enters when the owner entrusts the animal to him
Objects that if he replaces the owner, the mishna's ruling would be redundant given the earlier one
Rather, the shepherd replaces the bailee to whom the owner gave the animal
Objects that the mishna would then fully exempt the first bailee, refuting Rava's ruling
Rava answers that the shepherd typically passes the animal to his assistant, so the mishna is not a refutation
Suggests the mishna's wording supports Rava, since it teaches only the shepherd's usual practice
The Sages reject that inference, since the same ruling would hold if the shepherd gave it to someone else
States the dispute: Rabba holds a lost-item safekeeper is an unpaid bailee, Rav Yosef a paid bailee
Explains that Rabba sees no benefit, while Rav Yosef sees the benefit of not feeding the poor
Another explanation: Rav Yosef holds the Torah imposes a high standard because the duty is compelled
A mnemonic listing the halakhot and difficulties to be discussed next
Rav Yosef raises an objection to Rabba's view from a baraita

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A finder who returns a lost item where the owner will see it need not tend it, but is liable if it is stolen or lost

Rabba replies that it refers to loss from the place where the finder returned the item
Rav Yosef objects that the baraita says he need not tend it, showing no negligence
Rabba answers that the final clause concerns returning at midday, when the owner is not present
Restates the first halakha: a morning return where the owner regularly passes exempts the finder
Restates the second halakha: a midday return where the owner will not see it leaves the finder liable
Rav Yosef objects with the continuation: the finder is liable even if it was stolen from his own house
Rabba concedes for lost animals, which tend to wander and so need extra safeguarding like a paid bailee
Rabba objects that the verse return them adds that returning to any place of the owner's discharges the duty
Asks what the phrase to his garden or to his ruin means
Objects that if the places were secured the phrase would be redundant, so they must be unsecured
Concludes that the finder is like an unpaid bailee in his liability

Rabbi Elazar holds that returning a lost item needs no owner's knowledge, since the Torah grants many ways
Abaye objects that a finder is then a paid bailee, since one who falsely claims theft pays double
Rav Yosef answers the case is a false claim of an armed bandit, which exempts even a paid bailee

Abaye raises an objection from a baraita

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that if an armed bandit is like a thief, a paid bailee would pay double when claiming bandits took it

Abaye objects with a baraita and an a fortiori argument that a borrower is liable for theft and loss

Rabbi Zeira says the case is an armed bandit claim later revealed to be an unarmed bandit

Asks whether Rav applies his standard principle here, citing his view on produce left in another's courtyard
Objects that the cases cannot be compared, since Rav's claim concerned an animal that was itself injured

Asks how the animal fell and in which case the ruling applies

Rabba: the owner's despair also causes acquisition, but it is unclear whether this is Torah law or rabbinic law.

Objects: a lost item is found permissibly unlike a stolen one, so the analogy fails and the rule must be rabbinic.
Rabbinic institution: thieves are encouraged to repent by letting them keep the item and reimburse its value.
Rav Yosef: despair does not cause a thief to acquire the item at all, even by rabbinic law.
Rav Yosef objects to Rabba from a mishna on one who robbed leavened bread that became forbidden when Passover passed.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef objects that after the bread spoils the owner despairs, so the robber should owe full money.
Rava replies that despair transfers ownership only when the other party actually wants to acquire the item.
Abaye raises an objection to Rabba from a baraita.
The verse about the offering being his own is brought as the basis of the baraita.
Asks what the circumstances of the baraita are.
Dilemma: if consecration came before despair it is obvious, so it must come after, proving despair does not transfer ownership.
Rava turns Abaye's reasoning back on him.
A baraita on the zav's bedding is cited as the parallel source.
Asks what the case of the bedding baraita is.
Dilemma: a physical change made by a thief would surely acquire the item, so the case cannot be that.
Resolves it: the robbed bedding belonged to another, as with the consecrated offering.
Abaye raises an objection to Rav Yosef from a mishna.
The Kelim mishna on hides of homeowners versus leatherworkers is quoted.
The mishna continues with the thief and robber cases.
Rabbi Shimon reverses the cases, and the Gemara concludes despair causes acquisition.
Rav Yosef replies that the mishna speaks of hides that were trimmed.
Rabba bar Rav Ḥanan objects that a leather table top needs no trimming.
A prior mishna on finished items and thought is cited to refute that objection.
Rava reports that Rabba's difficulty to Rav Yosef stood unresolved for twenty-two years.
Rav Yosef finally resolved it: a change of name is equivalent to a physical change.
Asks why a physical change through action should acquire the item.
Explains that wood became vessels, and likewise hide was renamed as a table top.
Challenges the principle with the case of a beam renamed as a joist.
A Gittin mishna on a robber's beam built into a house is cited.
Explains the mishna's ruling rests only on the ordinance for penitent robbers.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef replies that a beam built into a house is not a real change of name.
A baraita identifies the obscure terms in Ezekiel as casings and beams, showing a beam keeps its name.
Rabbi Zeira holds that a change which can revert to the original state does not count.
Asks whether a change that does not revert is really considered a change.
A water duct carved from a log changes name and becomes a vessel, a counterexample to Rabbi Zeira.
A baraita on ritual baths shows the order of hollowing and attaching affects validity.
If name change counts, the bath should be invalid even when the log was attached first.
Drawn water is only a rabbinic law, and the detached log already had vessel status, so the cases differ.
A baraita on thieves and robbers who consecrate stolen items is raised as an objection.
The stolen food underwent a name change from untithed produce to terumah or tithe, so it differs.
Rav Ḥisda reports Rabbi Yonatan's view that a change in a stolen item makes the thief acquire it.
The verse about returning the stolen item that he took by robbery is offered as the source.
Asks why the phrase that he took by robbery is needed if it excludes the father's case.
If so, the verse could be written simply, so two lessons are derived from it.
The alternative version derives from the same verse that a changed item must still be returned.
The phrase that he took by robbery seems to show return is needed only if unchanged.
That phrase instead teaches that a son does not add one-fifth on his father's theft.
Ulla states that despair of recovery does not cause the thief to acquire the item.
Malachi's verse is read to compare a stolen animal with a lame one, which has no remedy.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that a stolen animal is disqualified whether or not the owner has despaired, so despair does not transfer ownership.
Rava cites the baraita on the verse about the offering being his own, as the source of this halakha.
Asks when exactly this halakha would be needed, since the disqualification would otherwise be obvious.
Dilemma: if the baraita concerns after despair, the conclusion holds, yet Rava himself said the case can be refuted.
Explains the contradiction by suggesting Rava retracted one view, or that Rav Pappa said one of them.
The Gemara returns to the mishna on fourfold and fivefold payment, limited to ox and sheep.
Asks why the payment should not extend to other animals by verbal analogy with the Shabbat verse.
Rava replies that the repeated ox and sheep in the verse exclude other animals from the payment.
Asks which repeated word of ox or sheep is the superfluous one that Rava relies on.
Shows the proposed readings fail, since a nine-animal payment would require repeating the word for it.
Rejects that objection: the repetition serves a different teaching about payment matching the stolen animal's quality.
Suggests instead that the words ox and sheep at the start of the verse are the superfluous ones.
Objects that the verse would then imply two animals must be stolen and slaughtered together, which the wording excludes.
Asks whether the same problem arises if both animals were stolen and sold.
Raises a further reading where one is slaughtered and the other sold, and the word or excludes it.
Asks why the opening ox and sheep cannot be omitted, leaving them not superfluous after all.
Gives the final reading of Rava's statement: the ox at the end and the sheep at the start are superfluous.
The mishna says a second thief pays only principal; Rav rules the double payment applies if the theft followed despair.
Rav Sheshet says Rav ruled while drowsy, and the ruling conflicts with a baraita.
Rabbi Akiva's baraita explains that slaughtering or selling deepens the thief in sin, so fourfold or fivefold applies.
Asks when that sale took place, and whether it was before the owner's despair of recovery.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If despair made the thief the owner, the fourfold payment for slaughtering or selling would make no sense.
The Sages reply that entrenchment in sin means the thief repeated his sin, even if the sale is invalid.
A baraita compares selling to slaughter, since both are acts that cannot be undone.
Asks when the sale is irreversible, since a sale before despair is easily undone.
If the thief acquired after despair, he would be selling his own animal, so the proof implies no acquisition.
Rav Naḥman explains the baraita as excluding a sale for thirty days, which can answer the proof here too.
Raises an objection from a baraita about the first thief paying double and the second thief paying only principal.
The baraita sets out cases of a stolen animal that was sold or slaughtered and then stolen again.
The baraita's middle clause says the second thief pays double payment to the purchaser after a sale.
Asks when the sale occurred, since if before despair the purchaser should not become owner.
Asks whether anyone holds that a change in possession alone causes acquisition, implying no one does.
Concludes the sale must have occurred after the owner's despair.
If despair acquires, the first thief would own what he sold, and the first clause also seems to conflict.
If the second thief pays only principal, despair cannot cause acquisition, which conflicts with Rav's view.
Rava says the last clause must be corrupted, since a physical change by action does cause acquisition.
Resolves by reversing the middle and last clauses so each case fits the stage before despair.
States the reversed rule: a change without despair gives no acquisition, while a slaughtered animal does.
Rav Pappa keeps the clauses as they are, following Beit Shammai, who hold a stolen item stays with the owner.
Asks whether the first and middle clauses then conflict with Rav's view after despair.
Rav Zevid says the case is before despair, when the owners despaired only while the buyer held the item.
Sets out the dispute: Rav Naḥman holds liability for selling before despair, Rav Sheshet holds exemption.
Rav Naḥman cites the verse and sold, which he reads as covering any sale regardless of timing.
Rav Naḥman holds there is no difference between sales before or after the owner's despair.
Rav Sheshet holds liability only when the sale is effective, since selling must match slaughter.
Asks Rav Sheshet's source for his exemption, and where it is taught.
Rabbi Akiva's baraita says the thief pays fourfold or fivefold because he became entrenched in sin by sale or slaughter.
Asks whether entrenchment is possible for a sale before despair, which is invalid, implying it must be after despair.
Rava says this is no proof, since repeating the sin by an invalid sale also counts as entrenchment.
A further baraita links selling to slaughter as acts that cannot be undone, supporting Rav Sheshet.
Asks when the sale occurred, since before despair it could be undone, so it must be after despair.
Concludes that liability for fourfold or fivefold payment applies only to a sale after despair.
Rav Naḥman interprets that baraita as excluding a temporary transfer for thirty days, rejecting the proof.
Rabbi Elazar holds liability applies after despair, as he stated in his own teaching.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An ordinary theft is presumed to leave the owner despairing of recovering the item.
The Torah's wording that slaughtering or selling brings fourfold or fivefold payment is cited.
Rabbi Elazar concludes that no fourfold payment applies to a sale made before the owner despairs.
Asks whether the Torah could require payment even before despair, as Rav Naḥman held.
Sages reply that slaughter and sale are paired, so the sale must be effective like slaughter.
Asks whether liability might apply only when the sale follows news that the owner despaired.
Sages reply that liability is immediate, just as slaughter is liable immediately.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects from kidnapping, where no despair occurs yet the seller is liable.
Infers that Rabbi Yoḥanan holds liability even when the sale comes before despair.
Asks the halakha if the thief sells after despair; Rabbi Yoḥanan says liable, Reish Lakish exempt.
Explains each view: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds liability at any time, Reish Lakish only before despair.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Reish Lakish from a baraita on a thief who consecrated and then slaughtered.
Asks when the baraita's events occurred, and whether a stolen animal can be consecrated before despair.
Leviticus on a man consecrating his house is read to show one can only consecrate what is his.
Concludes the baraita is after despair, and the thief is exempt only because he consecrated it.
If despair acquired the item, the thief would be slaughtering his own animal, so he should not pay.
Reish Lakish explains the case: the owners consecrated it while it was in the thief's hands.
Asks whether it can be consecrated, since Rabbi Yoḥanan said neither party can consecrate stolen property.
The Sages answer that Reish Lakish follows the view of the pious ones, not Rabbi Yoḥanan.
A mishna on the pious ones redeeming grapes picked by passersby is cited as support.
Asks why the thief still pays double, since the owner's consecration returned the principal to him.
The baraita refers to a thief found guilty before the owner consecrated the item.
Asks what the trial's circumstances were, since consecration should not matter if the court ordered return.
Rava rules that a thief who slaughters or sells after the court orders return is exempt.
Explains that after the definitive ruling he becomes a robber, who does not pay fourfold or fivefold.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava holds that a thief ordered only to return the animal still pays fourfold if he slaughters or sells it.
Replies that this does not challenge Reish Lakish, since the baraita concerns a mere order to return.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that neither party can consecrate a stolen item before the owner despairs.
Asks whether Rabbi Yoḥanan really said this, given his rule that the halakha follows an unattributed mishna.
The mishna on demarcating fourth-year vineyards, orla, and graves is cited, with the Gemara explaining each mark.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel limits the demarcation duty to the Sabbatical year, and the rest is feeding the wicked.
The mishna of the pious ones, who consecrated grapes picked by passersby, is cited against Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Objects that the pious ones' view may be Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's, yet Rabbi Yoḥanan would still have accepted it.
Sages explain Rabbi Yoḥanan's view: the declaration must be phrased as future, so it precedes the picking.
Asks whether Rabbi Yoḥanan could say this, since he held the pious ones and Rabbi Dosa say the same thing.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda is cited: the owner declares in the morning what the poor pick that day is ownerless.
Rabbi Dosa holds the declaration should be made toward evening, in the past tense, after the theft.
Reverses the attributions of the baraita so that Rabbi Dosa and Rabbi Yehuda are swapped.
Asks why reverse the baraita rather than Rabbi Yoḥanan's own statement that the two views agree.
Proposes that Rabbi Yoḥanan actually said the pious ones and Rabbi Yehuda said the same thing.
Rejects that alternative: Rabbi Yehuda would then hold retroactive designation, which he does not accept per a Demai mishna.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna on buying wine from Samaritans, and how to separate teruma and tithes, with a dispute about drinking first.
Asks why the baraita with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa was reversed, since a contradiction remains in Rabbi Yoḥanan's views.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's view on the vineyard declaration implies retroactive designation, which he is established as rejecting.
Rav Asi cites Rabbi Yoḥanan on brothers who divided an inheritance, treating each as a purchaser of the other's land.
Concludes the pious ones actually spoke in the past tense, about grapes already picked by passersby.
Rabbi Yoḥanan followed a different unattributed mishna on the double payment, which a stolen item's second thief owes to the owner.
Concludes a stolen item is under the jurisdiction of neither the owner nor the thief, so neither can consecrate it.
Asks why Rabbi Yoḥanan followed the double-payment mishna rather than the pious ones' unattributed mishna.
Says Rabbi Yoḥanan followed that mishna because a verse supports it.
Leviticus on a man consecrating his house is cited: what is consecrated must be in one's own possession.
Abaye says that were it not for Rabbi Yoḥanan's view, the pious ones would be taken as following Rabbi Dosa.
Explains that the Sages enacted for the poor, not for a thief, so Rabbi Dosa's view is the pious ones' view.
Rava says that without Rabbi Yoḥanan's view, the pious ones would be attributed to Rabbi Meir instead.
Rabbi Meir holds second tithe is God's, yet redemption is established in the owner's possession by a verse.
A verbal analogy with fourth-year fruit uses the word holy in the context of second tithe.
From the analogy, fourth-year fruit can be desacralized by its owner even after theft, as with second tithe.
Gleanings differ, since the owner's ownership of them can be relinquished only while they are in his possession.
Ravina says that without Rabbi Yoḥanan, the pious ones would be attributed to Rabbi Dosa, to avoid a difficulty.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes Rabbi Yoḥanan's principle does not apply to a mishna of one individual, since the ruling is backed by two Sages.
The Sages of Neharde'a hold that no authorization document is written for movable property held by another.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar for the reason behind the Neharde'a halakha.
Ameimar answers that it rests on Rabbi Yoḥanan's principle that neither party can consecrate stolen property.
Another version holds the document is barred only when the debtor denies owing, since the owner's title is doubtful.
Neharde'a also hold an authorization must include an explicit clause transferring actual ownership to the collector.
Abaye holds transfer of a half, third, or quarter suffices, since the litigation concerns the whole item.
Ameimar holds that if the collector seized the item, the court does not take it back from him.
Rav Ashi disagrees: the owner made the collector an agent, so he cannot seize the item for himself.
Another view makes the collector a partner, but the halakha is that he is an agent who may not seize anything.
Mishna: a thief pays fourfold or fivefold when witnesses testify to theft and to the slaughter or sale, with several cases.
Cases of slaughter for medicine, dogs, tereifa, or the Temple courtyard still incur payment, though Rabbi Shimon exempts two.
Asks whether the mishna can be the view that does not follow Rabbi Akiva's two-witness exposition.
If the mishna followed Rabbi Akiva, the thief would be exempt, since the second witnesses prove only part of the act.
A Tosefta story about Rabbi Yosei and the study partners Ḥalafta and Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri is cited.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri and Halafta ask whether three separate years of eating the produce combine into full testimony.
Halafta replies that this establishes presumptive ownership by the one who ate the produce.
Halafta adds that Rabbi Akiva would dispute this, since testimony must concern a whole matter.
Abaye defends the mishna even on Rabbi Akiva's view, citing his acceptance of two-witness betrothal and adultery.
Explains that each pair of witnesses is a complete matter, since theft testimony stands alone as slaughter testimony does not.
Asks what the word matter excludes, according to the Rabbis who reject Rabbi Akiva's exposition.
Suggests it excludes the case of a girl with one hair seen on her back by one pair and on her front by another.
Objects that each testimony is then half a matter and half a testimony, so it is obviously invalid.
Offers instead that each pair says only that the girl is still a minor, so each is half a matter.
The mishna teaches that stealing and selling on Shabbat incurs fourfold or fivefold payment.
Asks why this conflicts with a baraita that says the thief is exempt in such a case.
Rami bar Ḥama explains the exemption: the buyer's act of acquisition itself desecrates Shabbat, so only the capital penalty applies.
The Sages object that a court would not order payment in such a sale, so it cannot be called a sale at all.
Rav Pappa says the case is of the buyer telling the thief to throw the animal into his courtyard, a Shabbat act.
Asks whether this reading follows Rabbi Akiva, who treats an item in the airspace as at rest.
On the Rabbis' view the acquisition and the Shabbat desecration would not coincide, so the thief would owe payment.
Explains the baraita speaks of a buyer who makes acquisition conditional on the animal resting on the ground.
Rava brings the prohibition on a prostitute's fee as proof: the court would not order payment of a fee owed for a capital act.
Rava concludes that payment is owed in court, yet the fig case is still no sale in that the fig acquisition is a Shabbat desecration.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes the thief who transfers title to a buyer this way makes a valid sale, and the mishna on Yom Kippur slaughter is stated.
Asks why the thief pays on Yom Kippur, since the lashes penalty means one cannot be both flogged and charged for one act.
Answers that the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who holds one can be flogged and also liable to pay for one act.
Asks why, on that view, Shabbat slaughter is not also paid, since Rabbi Meir would impose both capital and monetary liability.
A baraita quotes Rabbi Meir that the thief pays for Shabbat or idolatrous slaughter, against the Rabbis who exempt him.
Says the baraita is to be read as a thief who has another slaughter the animal for him, per Rabbi Yoḥanan's disciples.
Asks how the thief can be liable when another person, not he, sins by slaughtering.
Rava says the verse pairs slaughter with sale, which can be done through an agent, so slaughter can too.
Two schools derive from the verse's word or and word for that the agent's act is included.
Mar Zutra objects that an agent cannot have greater power than the principal, so the thief should not be liable.
Rav Ashi replies that the thief is exempt only because he gets the heavier death penalty for Shabbat desecration.
Asks why the Rabbis exempt the thief in the agent case, since he himself committed no capital act.
Explains that the Rabbis are Rabbi Shimon, who holds an unfit slaughter is not slaughter at all.
Objects that Shabbat slaughter is valid, as a mishna in Ḥullin says, so Rabbi Shimon's reasoning fails here.
Explains that Rabbi Shimon follows Rabbi Yoḥanan HaSandlar, who forbids eating Shabbat-slaughtered meat.
A mishna in Terumot on cooking on Shabbat, with the views of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, is cited.
Rabbi Yoḥanan HaSandlar's view is stated: intentionally Shabbat-cooked food is never eaten, so such slaughter is unfit.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yoḥanan HaSandlar's view.
Rabbi Ḥiyya's exposition of Exodus 31:14 equates Shabbat desecration with the prohibition on eating sacred food.
Asks whether the analogy should also forbid deriving benefit from Shabbat-produced items.
The verse says to you, so the product is yours for benefit, though not for eating.
Asks whether the analogy would forbid eating even an unwitting desecration's product, as with sacred items.
The verse says one who profanes it intentionally is put to death, so only intentional acts are included.
Rav Aḥa and Ravina dispute whether Shabbat desecration's product is forbidden by Torah law or rabbinic law.
The rabbinic view derives from the verse calling the day holy but not its products holy.
Asks how the view that the prohibition is Torah law is reconciled with the analogy.

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the Rabbis exempt the thief for an agent's Shabbat slaughter if Shabbat products are forbidden only rabbinically.
The Rabbis exempt only the other cases in the baraita, idolatrous slaughter and the ox sentenced to be stoned.
Asks why Rabbi Meir holds the thief liable when his agent slaughters for idolatry, since the animal is then forbidden.
Rava explains: once slaughter begins the animal is forbidden, and the owner's ownership ends, so payment is due only if the idolatry is at completion.
Asks why Rabbi Meir obligates payment for slaughtering an ox sentenced to be stoned, which is forbidden for benefit.
Rava explains the case: the ox was condemned while in the bailee's house and then stolen from there.
Rabbi Meir follows both Rabbi Ya'akov, that a returned ox counts as returned, and Rabbi Shimon, that a loss-causing item has value.
A mishna is cited where Rabbi Shimon holds the thief pays for sacrificial animals, since their loss causes financial harm.
Rav Kahana asks whether the mishna can follow Rabbi Meir and not Rabbi Shimon, given the last clause.
The last clause implies Rabbi Shimon concedes the thief pays in all other cases, so he agrees with Rabbi Meir here.
Rav Zevid replies that the inference applies only to the immediately preceding cases of medicine and dogs.
The mishna: a thief who slaughters his father's animal pays the other heirs if the father dies later.
Rava poses a dilemma: a thief of partners' ox who admits to one partner, whether he pays the other partner five full or half oxen.
Rav Naḥman says the verse's five oxen means five full oxen, not five halves, deciding the dilemma.
Rava objects from the mishna: if the thief inherits part, it resembles admission to one partner, yet he still pays the others.
Rav Naḥman explains the mishna's case as one where the father stood in trial before dying, so payment was fixed then.
Rava asks what happens if no trial occurred, and why the mishna does not state that distinction directly.
Rava proposes the mishna should distinguish cases by whether the thief stood trial during the father's lifetime.
Rav Naḥman replies the tanna cited the latter clause by a similar case, since he had already cited the first clause.
Next morning Rav Naḥman retracts, holding that the five oxen include five half-oxen as well.

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman explains his earlier remark: he had not eaten ox meat and so was fasting and could not concentrate.
Rava asks what distinguishes the first clause, where the son pays, from the latter clause, where he is exempt.
Rav Naḥman explains that the verse about slaughtering applies wholly to the father's animal in his lifetime, but not after his death.
The mishna on a tereifa found after slaughter, and Rav Ḥavivi infers that slaughter counts only at its end.
If slaughter spans its whole course, a thief slaughtering a sacred-area animal would be unable to own what he slaughters.
Rav Huna and Rav Ashi debate, and Rav Gamda, in Rava's name, explains the mishna's case of severing the simanin partly outside the Temple.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, in the name of Rabbi Levi the Elder, holds slaughter counts only at its end, unlike Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rav Ḥavivi asks whether Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that the prohibition on sacred-area non-sacred animals is not Torah law.

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If slaughter were prohibited by Torah law from its first cut, the mishna's case of a sacred-area slaughter would be difficult.
Rav Aḥa and Rav Ashi debate the mishna's reading, and Rav Gamda, in Rava's name, places the partial slaughter outside the Temple.
Mishna: if one stole an animal on testimony of two witnesses, and those witnesses are found conspiring, they pay the full amount.
Mishna: when only some witnesses are found conspiring, the owed payments are assigned to them, and if the theft testimony fails, the rest falls too.
Abaye holds a conspiring witness is disqualified retroactively from his testimony; Rava holds only from then on.
Abaye relies on the verse against accepting a wicked witness; Rava sees conspiring disqualification as a novelty applied only going forward.
Some say Rava also holds like Abaye, and his limited ruling here was only for this reason.

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's rejection of retroactive disqualification is explained as protecting purchasers from potential loss.
Asks what the practical difference is between the two explanations of Rava's position.
Gives two cases where the explanations diverge, and shows each would lead Rava to reject retroactive disqualification.
Rav Pappa ruled like Rava, but Rav Ashi holds Abaye's view, with a mnemonic listing six Abaye-rule cases.
Asks how the mishna on conspiring witnesses who pay everything fits Abaye's view, given the sequence of testimony.
Explains the question's case: testimony on theft, then slaughter, then each set is found conspiring in turn.
If disqualification is retroactive, the slaughter testimony was already invalid, so why must they pay for it?
Suggests the witnesses were found conspiring about the slaughter first, then about the theft.
Retroactive disqualification from the theft finding would still void the slaughter testimony, so the difficulty remains.
Concludes the halakha follows Abaye: the mishna's witnesses testified to theft and slaughter together, in a single testimony.
Proposes a parallel tannaitic dispute and cites a baraita on partially invalidated testimony for theft and slaughter.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes testimony given by two separate sets from one single testimony on both matters.
Asks what Rabbi Yosei means by two separate testimonies and by one single testimony.
Objects that, on this reading, nothing shows that a later slaughter disqualification voids the earlier theft testimony.
Explains that Rabbi Yosei's two testimonies means one witness set speaking on theft and then slaughter at separate times.
The amoraim assume all agree that a brief pause within one speech counts as continuous testimony.
Asks whether the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei truly disagree here, given Rava's and Abaye's positions on disqualification.
Rabbi Yosei holds like Abaye, that disqualification is retroactive, so a slaughter finding also voids the theft testimony.
Sages reject this: if the pause rule applied, all would agree on retroactivity, but they dispute the pause rule itself.

73b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yosei holds a short pause within speech counts as continuous, so the theft testimony falls with the slaughter testimony.
Asks whether Rabbi Yosei really holds that a pause within a short phrase is like continuous speech.
A Temura mishna on designating an animal as two contradictory substitutes is cited, with Rabbi Meir's view.
Rabbi Yosei rules that if he intended both at the outset his statement stands, but if he changed his mind it is a burnt-offering substitute.
Objects that if he changed his mind before the second phrase, the ruling is obvious, so Rabbi Yosei would not have stated it.
Rav Pappa and the Sages explain the case as a change within the pause of a student greeting a teacher, which is a long pause.
Rava holds witnesses first contradicted, then found conspiring, are put to death, since contradiction starts the process.
Rava cites a baraita on witnesses who blinded a slave's eye, where the contradiction counts as the start of conspiring.
Several problems arise with the baraita as written: why pay the eye's value, and whether the master would welcome emancipation.
Resolves it by positing a competing earlier testimony that the master knocked out the tooth first, so the intermediate witnesses are accepted.
The baraita's final clause: the intermediate witnesses, later found conspiring, pay the eye's value less the tooth's value.
Rava concludes the baraita shows contradiction is the start of conspiring, so the witnesses still owe the full loss.
Abaye replies that the reversed order reading does not prove Rava's view, since there are only two sets of witnesses.
Asks from where Abaye knows his reading of the baraita is correct.

74a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Infers that the latter clause of the baraita is parallel to the first, covering a reversed-order case with conspiring witnesses.
Quotes the baraita's latter clause: a master who knocked out a slave's tooth then blinded his eye, and conspiring witnesses pay the eye's value.
Asks what the circumstances of this clause are.
If the later witnesses do not concede any injury, the conspiring witnesses should pay the slave's full value; the same problem arises on other readings.
Rather, all witnesses concede the injuries and disagree only on order, so the second set reverses the order and renders the first set conspiring.
Asks what the circumstances are if the second set reverses the order by postdating the injuries.
Rejects both postdating and predating: the first set could not have been liable at the time, or the master had not yet stood trial.
Rav Aḥa asks from which case of the baraita Rava draws his inference.
Objects that the first clause's intermediate witnesses lowered the payment, so no rejected testimony was ever conspiring.
Rav Ashi replies that Rava infers from three sets of witnesses, with the intermediate pair contradicted before being found conspiring.
Rava argues that if contradiction did not start conspiring, these witnesses would not owe, so the latter clause proves it.
Abaye replies that the first clause requires three sets, but the latter clause is satisfactory to the slave in any case, so two suffice.
Rabbi Zeira objects to the baraita's premise that a master must indemnify for the second injury.

74b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita rules that the slave goes free for the blinded eye and the knocked-out tooth, with no payment for the tooth
Abaye replies that the Tanna of that ruling is the one who said it, and this is the basis for his response
Exodus 21 supports the ruling: for his eye's sake, not for both eye and tooth
Rav Idi bar Avin brings a further mishnah as support, introducing it as something we also learned
The mishnah on a thief who was convicted by two witnesses and then slaughtered or sold: the false witnesses pay everything
What is the case: witnesses testified on the theft, retracted and testified on the slaughter, and were both times found to be zomemim
If they were already refuted on the theft, then by the mishnah's own wording the slaughter testimony should fail, yet the mishnah says they pay everything
If refutation were not the start of zomemim, why would they pay, so we conclude refutation is the beginning of zomemim
Asks what exactly the case is that the mishnah covers
The case is witnesses who were first found zomemim on the slaughter, and in a dispute they were refuted, and later found zomemim on the theft
Reports the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar about whether false witnesses in a capital case are executed
Concludes that the view of Rabbi Elazar is that they are not executed, and gives his view that witnesses refuted in a capital case are flogged
If Rabbi Elazar held they are executed, why are they flogged? A prohibition warned about by the court's death penalty carries no flogging
States that Rabbi Elazar's view is that they are not executed, and thus they are flogged
Asks what was seen that one authority is relied on here and the other there, since both are two against two
Abaye answers with the case of a Bava Harug who was killed by a blow to the legs
The mishnah: one who steals and slaughters or sells on the testimony of two witnesses, or on one witness or his own confession, pays double but not fourfold or fivefold
The mishnah gives examples: stealing and slaughtering on Shabbat, or for idolatry
Case of stealing from a father, the father dying, and then the son slaughtering and selling
Case of stealing and dedicating the animal, then slaughtering and selling; he pays double but not fourfold or fivefold
Rabbi Shimon says that for consecrated animals one who is liable for their safekeeping pays fourfold or fivefold, and one who is not is exempt
On the testimony of one witness it is obvious, so why does the mishnah say it
It teaches the new point that the case is not obvious
Confession alone is compared to testimony by one witness, as an analogy
Just as one witness joins with others to make him liable, so too confession joins with witnesses; the teaching is meant to exclude the view of Rav Huna
Quotes Rav Huna citing Rav that one who admits to a fine is exempt if witnesses come afterward
Restates the ruling of Rav Huna in Rav's name: admission to a fine, and if witnesses come afterward he is exempt
Rav Chisda raises an objection against Rav Huna from a case
The story of Rabban Gamliel who blinded his slave's eye; the slave rejoiced greatly and found Rabbi Yehoshua
Rabbi Yehoshua asks whether he knows the slave went free
Rabban Gamliel asks why this matters
He answers that he blinded the slave's eye
Rabbi Yehoshua rules his words count for nothing since there are no witnesses; had there been witnesses, he would be liable
We learn that one who admits to a fine, and witnesses come afterward, is liable
Rabban Gamliel replies that he is different, since he admitted not before a court
But Rabbi Yehoshua was the head of the court, so the reply should not apply

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Answers that Rabbi Yehoshua was not sitting in court when he met Rabban Gamliel
A baraita has Rabbi Yehoshua say the admission is worthless because he already admitted, which seems to conflict
Asks whether the two baraitot are simply a dispute between tannaim
The first tanna holds that Rabbi Yehoshua's remark was about having no witnesses, so an admitter who is later proven is liable
The second tanna holds the remark was about the admission already made, so later witnesses do not make him liable
Rejects the suggestion: all agree that a fine-admitter is exempt even if witnesses come later
The real dispute is where Rabbi Yehoshua stood: outside court for the first tanna, inside court for the second
States the disputed case: one who admits a fine and is later proven by witnesses; Rav says exempt
Rav holds the admitter is exempt, while Shmuel holds he is liable
Rava bar Ahilai gives Rav's reason: the doubled verb in Exodus 22:3 excludes self-incrimination from the double payment
Asks why the Torah needs to teach this here at all
The principle comes from another verse, Exodus 22:8, so the second verse must teach the new point that the admitter is exempt
Shmuel reads the doubled wording differently: it teaches that the thief himself pays double, as a tanna in the house of Hizkiyah taught
Rav raises an objection: a thief who admits stealing but not slaughtering pays only the principal
Shmuel replies that the case is where the witnesses returned after the admission
But the later clause of a mishnah teaches that Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon says let the witnesses come, implying the first tanna holds otherwise
Shmuel replies that there is no such thing, and that he follows Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon's view
For Shmuel it is certainly a tannaitic dispute
Asks whether for Rav it is also a tannaitic dispute
Rav replies that even Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon agrees only in the case where the thief is shaken by the witnesses, not when he admits on his own
Rav Hamnuna says Rav's view is reasonable: one who says I stole and is later proven is exempt, because he has already obligated himself for the principal
By contrast, if he first denied stealing, then admitted slaughter and sale, he is liable, since he did not exempt himself from everything
Rava says he was taught this by his elders, since Rabban Gamliel exempts himself from everything
Rav Chisda challenged Rav Huna on this, and Rav Huna gave no answer; the same point was also stated
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: one who says I stole and is later proven is exempt, since he obligated himself for the principal
If he denied stealing and then admitted slaughter and sale, he is liable, since he is not exempt from everything
Rav Ashi says the mishnah and a baraita both support this, and it is precise
The mishnah: one who steals and slaughters or sells on two witnesses, or on one witness or his own confession, pays double but not fourfold or fivefold
Asks why the mishnah lists two witnesses separately: it should have said simply the principal alone for the lesser cases

75b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Answers that the mishnah is indeed teaching a new point
The one who steals and slaughters on two witnesses, or on one witness or his own admission, is liable only for principal: the admission is what matters
Admission by oneself is compared to testimony by a single witness, as an analogy
Just as one witness joins others to create liability, so too self-admission joins witnesses to create liability
But one who steals and slaughters and sells on one witness or his own admission is liable for principal only
Objection: we do not say self-admission is like one witness, since a baraita teaches otherwise
The baraita: if witnesses came upon him and he said I stole but not I slaughtered or sold, he pays only principal
Asks why the baraita does not say simply I stole or I slaughtered and sold
Rather, this is to teach a new point
The reason: one who says I stole is liable for principal and exempt from the rest
But if he denied stealing and witnesses then showed he stole, and he later admitted slaughter and sale, he is liable, since he did not exempt himself from principal
Concludes that admission of slaughter is not an admission in itself; the baraita teaches this point
Since he admitted stealing, even though he denied slaughter and sale and witnesses then proved it, he is exempt from the fourfold or fivefold
Asks why the Torah says fivefold and not fourfold or threefold, and whether this is a tannaitic dispute
Two witnesses testify to theft and two to slaughter, and both sets are refuted; the baraita says the case is then liable to double payment
On Sumchus's authority, the refuted witnesses pay double while the thief pays triple for the ox and double for the sheep
Asks to which clause Sumchus refers, since on the first clause he would not hold that a partly refuted testimony is wholly void
Rather it applies to the later clause, which the Sages hold correctly: he pays double and they pay triple
The dispute differs in another case: when witnesses came, he said I stole and slaughtered and sold, but not in your presence, and they were refuted
The owner brought witnesses who proved the theft and the slaughter and sale; the dispute is over the admission of slaughter
The Sages hold that although the admission of theft came from the witnesses, the admission of slaughter is an admission, and he is exempt
Sumchus holds that since the admission of theft came from witnesses, the admission of slaughter is not an admission, and the first witnesses who were refuted still make him liable
They pay double, while the thief pays triple for the ox and double for the sheep
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika says all agree the admission of slaughter is not an admission; the case is about testimony
The dispute is where witnesses say you stole and he says yes I stole and slaughtered and sold, but not in your presence, only before others
The witnesses came and refuted the claim, and the other witnesses proved theft and slaughter; this is where they disagree
The Sages hold that such testimony is valid testimony, and testimony that cannot be refuted is not testimony
Sumchus holds that testimony which cannot be refuted is valid testimony
But it is established that testimony which cannot be refuted is not valid testimony
That rule applies where no one knows which day or hour, so the witnesses have no testimony at all; here the witnesses support each other
The master said they pay double, since by admitting he stole, he must pay the principal
Rabbi Elazar cites Rav's teaching in his name

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Quotes the case of one who stole and dedicated the animal, then slaughtered and sold it, to be discussed
Objects: for the slaughter he is not liable, since he slaughtered a consecrated animal, but then he should be liable for it; what difference is it whether it was sold to a commoner or to heaven
Identifies this as Rabbi Shimon's view, who holds consecrated animals that are liable for their safekeeping are in the owner's possession
Since the later clause is Rabbi Shimon, the first clause cannot be Rabbi Shimon
Resolves that the case is about light sacrifices, following Rabbi Yose the Galilean, who holds light sacrifices are the owner's property
Asks what the payment is for the most sacred consecrated animals, fourfold and fivefold?
Asks why the mishnah does not separate the cases and teach that light sacrifices differ from the most sacred ones
Rejects that: the difference does not depend on the kind of sacrifice
Objects that the difference between sale to a commoner and sale to heaven is a difficulty, given the case of the ox of Reuven and Shimon
Quotes Rabbi Shimon's view

Granted that Rabbi Shimon holds the sale distinction does not matter, the reverse would have to be taught: the consecrated animal that is liable for safekeeping is exempt, since it has not left the owner's possession
They say Rabbi Shimon's statement concerns a different matter, and so the mishnah teaches it
The mishnah: one who steals from a thief pays fourfold or fivefold; likewise one who steals consecrated property from the owner's house is exempt
The verse in Exodus 22:6 says steals from a man's house, not from a consecrated house, as the source
Rabbi Shimon says consecrated animals that are liable for safekeeping are liable
Asks what the reason is
The verse is read as steals from a man's house and not from a consecrated house, so the one not liable for safekeeping is exempt
Since we heard Rabbi Shimon hold that slaughter that is not fit is not slaughter, consecrated slaughter must also be unfit slaughter
Rav Dimi cites Rabbi Yochanan: if one slaughters unblemished animals inside for the owner's sake, the principal returns to the owner
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avin says the same, when the blood was spilled, and this is what Ravin said when he came
Rabbi Yochanan says the case is one who slaughters unblemished animals inside not for the owner's sake

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resh Lakish says that one who slaughters animals with blemishes outside is still liable
Rabbi Elazar objects to Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish: if slaughter permits, then sprinkling, and redemption as well, should also permit, but they forgot
This is Rabbi Shimon's principle: whatever is about to be sprinkled counts as sprinkled, and whatever is about to be redeemed counts as redeemed
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon: there is a remnant that defiles as food, and a remnant that does not, and here is how
Before sprinkling it does not defile as food; after sprinkling it does, and we maintain the meaning of before sprinkling is before it is seen for sprinkling
We hold that if there was no time in the day to sprinkle it, since it was slaughtered near sunset, it does not defile; but if there was time, it does
Evidently, whatever is about to be sprinkled counts as sprinkled, and whatever is about to be redeemed counts as redeemed, as a baraita of Rabbi Shimon teaches

77a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A carcass or slaughtered animal defiles as food
The reason: since it had a fit time before the sprinkling, it counts as a fit animal

77b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resh Lakish cites Rabbi Shimon's view that a cow is redeemed on the altar, so whatever is about to be redeemed counts as redeemed
Granted Rabbi Yochanan does not hold like Rabbi Shimon, since he wants to read the mishnah as even for unblemished animals; the question is Resh Lakish's view
Asks what the reason is that Rabbi Yochanan does not say like Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Yochanan's reply rests on the verse in Exodus 21:37 about slaughtering and selling
The verse sets the rule: wherever the item is present in the sale, it is present in the slaughter, and where absent in sale, absent in slaughter
Consecrated animals are different, since their sale is not a sale, so they are not counted in slaughter; the authorities follow their own reasoning
The question at issue: one who sells a tereifah, according to Rabbi Shimon
Rabbi Yochanan says he is liable, while Resh Lakish says he is exempt
Rabbi Yochanan holds liability even though the item is absent in slaughter but present in sale; Resh Lakish holds exemption since absent in slaughter means absent in sale
Rabbi Yochanan objects to Resh Lakish: one who steals kilayim and slaughters and sells a tereifah pays fourfold and fivefold
Asks whether this is not Rabbi Shimon's view, and so evidently liability applies even though absent in slaughter but present in sale
Replies that this is the Rabbis' view: a tereifah present in sale is not present in slaughter
Objects: on Rabbi Shimon's view kilayim are present in slaughter but not in sale; so the tanna taught slaughter and the same holds for sale, and the Rabbis should be read the same way
Rabbi Yochanan replies: if Rabbi Shimon, it is because he taught tereifah together with kilayim; but if the Rabbis, we would mix the two cases together
A baraita: one who steals kilayim and a tereifah, slaughters or sells them, pays fourfold and fivefold
This is difficult: the verse says sheh, a lamb, which would seem to exclude kilayim
Rava states a principle: wherever the verse says sheh, it excludes kilayim
Here is different, since the verse says or to include kilayim, and every or includes
A baraita in Leviticus 22:27 says the word ox or lamb excludes kilayim, and goat excludes what is not a hybrid
Rava replies that each verse must be read in its own context: in the theft case the verse excludes kilayim, while in the consecrated case it includes them, or else it excludes

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: in the case of sacrifices too the verse says ox or sheep, and it cannot exclude kilayim from among them
Asks whether the beginning and end of the verse should each include or exclude, reasoning from one clause to the other
If the verse excludes, why two exclusions are needed, and if it includes, why kilayim were not included without the verse
Rava's principle: wherever the verse says sheh, it comes only to exclude kilayim
Asks for what halakhic purpose the verse is needed
Lists the possible purposes: consecrated animals, tithe, or firstborn, and whether one can derive from the rest
A verse says a firstborn ox, which raises the question of whether kilayim are included
Rava's ruling applied to the firstborn donkey: the Mishnah says it is not redeemed if it is a calf, a wild animal, a slaughtered or tereifah animal, kilayim, or a cow
Rabbi Elazar permits kilayim, as the Mishnah teaches
Asks why he permits kilayim, since they are sheh, for what purpose
Rabbi Elazar replies: Rava's ruling on defilement of an animal born of a pure one and conceived from an impure one follows the view not of Rabbi Yehoshua, who derives it from sheep and goats

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava raises a question, in the manner of Rabbi Shimon, about an animal that was mixed up with another
The case: a man vows a burnt offering, sets aside an ox, another person steals it; the thief redeems himself with a lamb according to the Rabbis, and with a bird for Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
The Mishnah: if he said I take on a burnt offering he brings a lamb, but Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says he brings a bull or a pigeon
Asks whether the name burnt offering takes effect on him, or perhaps he can say he wants to offer the best animal, and then the matter is open
Restates the ruling: the thief redeems himself with a lamb according to the Rabbis, and with a bird according to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika teaches it explicitly
Rava states the case: one who vows a burnt offering, sets aside an ox, and another steals it, redeems himself with a lamb per the Rabbis and with a bird per Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya

The Mishnah: one who sells an animal except for one in a hundred that is his or in which he has a partnership, or who slaughters a tereifah animal, or who castrates it, pays double and not fourfold or fivefold
Asks what is the meaning of except for one in a hundred
Rav says except for the animal's limb needed for slaughter; Levi says except for its fleece, and a baraita so teaches
Objects with a baraita: if he sold a limb, a hand, a leg, a horn or a fleece, he does not pay fourfold or fivefold
Rabbi says: a part that is essential to slaughter means he does not pay fourfold or fivefold, but a part not essential to slaughter means he does pay
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: except for the horn he does not pay, but except for the fleece he does pay fourfold and fivefold
Granted for Levi it fits the first tanna, but for Rav, which tanna does he follow?
Rav holds like this tanna, who taught the same view
A baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says that excluding a limb is not a fourfold or fivefold payment, but excluding the horn or fleece is
Asks in what they disagree
The first tanna holds from Exodus 21:37 that one must slaughter and sell the whole animal
Rabbi holds that what applies to slaughter applies to sale, excluding what is not part of slaughter, and the sale is like slaughter
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that a horn is left over that is not for shearing, so it is a remainder and not liable; fleece is for shearing, so it is not a remainder
The other tanna of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's school holds that hands and feet need slaughter so they are a remainder, and horns and fleece do not need slaughter so they are not a remainder
This is difficult: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar appears to contradict himself, or there are two tannaim, and the view is attributed to him
A baraita: one who steals the lame, the crippled, or the blind, or steals an animal belonging to partners, is liable; but partners who steal it are exempt
But a baraita teaches that partners who stole are liable
Rav Nachman replies: there is no difficulty, since one case is a partner who stole from his partner and the other a partner who stole from elsewhere
Rava objects to Rav Nachman: a partner who stole from his partner, and partners who stole, should be liable; Scripture says and slaughter the whole, and that is lacking
Rav Nachman replies: there is no difficulty, since one case is a partner who slaughtered with his partner's knowledge and the other without his knowledge
Rabbi Yirmiya asks: if he sold it within thirty days, outside its work, or while pregnant, what is the status, according to the view that the fetus is part of the mother
No need to ask, since he retained a part in it
But according to the view that the fetus is not part of the mother, what do we say? The options are left open and the matter is unresolved
Rav Pappa asks: if he stole it, cut it up and sold it, what is the status: do we say what he stole he did not sell, or what he sold he did not retain? Unresolved
Our rabbis taught: one who steals and gives to another and slaughters, and one who steals and gives to another and sells it

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists cases: one who steals and dedicates, exchanges, gives as a gift, repays a debt, or sends betrothal gifts from his father-in-law's house, pays fourfold or fivefold
Asks what new point this teaches
It teaches the first clause
The first clause: one who steals, gives to another, and that person slaughters, shows that an agent for a sinful act is effective here, though elsewhere in the Torah no agent exists for a sin
Asks what the reason is
Since sale cannot be done through another, slaughter by another also makes him liable; the later clause is taught as well
The later clause: one who steals and dedicates; what difference is it whether sold to a commoner or to heaven
The Mishnah: one who steals and slaughters or sells outside the owner's domain, or steals outside and slaughters within, pays fourfold or fivefold
But if he stole, slaughtered and sold within the owner's domain, he is exempt

The Mishnah: if he was drawing the animal out and it died within the owner's domain, he is exempt; if he lifted it or took it out of the owner's domain and it died, he is liable; this applies to various kinds of custodians
Amimar asks whether drawing was instituted for custodians or not
Rav Yeimar says: come and hear, from the Mishnah's ruling on handing it to the firstborn son, a lender, or a custodian without pay, that drawing applies to custodians
Asks: is this not about a custodian, so we conclude drawing was instituted for custodians
Yes, the case is a custodian, and so drawing was instituted for custodians
The reply: the thief is taught in the first clause, so the inference fails
The first clause teaches one who steals from the owner's house, and the other clause teaches one who steals from a custodian's house
Rav Ashi tells him not to reject it: what difference is it whether one steals from a custodian's house or from the owner's house
Rather, the case must be about a custodian, and so we conclude drawing was instituted for custodians
Rabbi Elazar says: just as drawing was instituted for buyers, so it was instituted for custodians, and a baraita teaches the same
Just as land is acquired by money, by document, or by possession, so rent is acquired by money, by document, or by possession
Asks: if we say the difference lies in this, what is it

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rent of movables is acquired by document, and Rav Chisda states that rent of land is the same
Rabbi Elazar's case: if they saw him hide the animal in the fields, slaughter and sell it, he pays fourfold or fivefold
Asks why he should pay, since he did not draw the animal
Rav Chisda: this is a case where he struck the animal with a stick
Since they saw him, he is a robber; since he hid from them, he is a thief
But then how is it a case of robbery
Rabbi Abbahu's example of robbery: Benaiah ben Yehoidah took the spear from the Egyptian, per 2 Samuel 23:21
Rabbi Yochanan's example: the men of Shechem who lay in ambush and robbed everyone passing by, per Judges 9:25
Asks why Rabbi Abbahu did not use the same example
He answers that since they hide, they are not robbers
Rabbi Yochanan's reason: they hide so that people will not see them, and they flee from them
Students ask Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai why the Torah is stricter on a thief than on a robber
He replies that one honored the servant's honor over his Master's, while the other did not; it is as if the eye below does not see, and the ear below does not hear
Scripture: Isaiah 29:15 about those who hide plans from the Lord, Psalm 94:7 about saying the Lord does not see
Ezekiel 9:9: they said the Lord has forsaken the land, and the Lord does not see
A baraita: Rabbi Meir cites Rabban Gamliel's parable of two people in a city, one who made a feast
One invited the townspeople but not the king's people; the other invited neither
Asks which of them is punished more
The one who invited the townspeople but not the king's people is punished more
Rabbi Meir says: see how great the power of labor is: an ox that was excused from work pays fivefold, and a sheep that was not excused pays fourfold
Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai says: see how great human dignity is: an ox that walked on its feet pays fivefold, and a sheep carried on the shoulder pays fourfold
The Mishnah: one may not raise small animals in the Land of Israel, but may in Syria and the deserts; no poultry in Jerusalem due to sacrifices, and no priests in the Land of Israel due to purities
One may not raise pigs anywhere, nor keep a dog unless it is tied with a chain
One may not spread nets for doves unless the place is thirty ris from the settlement
A baraita: small animals may not be raised in the Land of Israel, but they may be raised in its forests and in Syria even near settlements, and certainly outside the land
Another baraita: small animals may not be raised in the Land of Israel, but may be raised in the desert of Judea and in the desert of Akko
Even though they said small animals may not be raised, large animals may be raised, because no decree is imposed on the public unless most of the public can bear it
Small animals can be brought from outside the land, but large animals cannot be brought from outside the land
Though they said small animals may not be raised, one may keep one for thirty days before a festival and before one's son's wedding, but may not keep the last one for thirty days
The reason one might think otherwise: if the festival came and he had bought it, thirty days would not yet have passed, so we should not say he may keep it for thirty days
Rather, since the festival came, he has no need to keep it

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The butcher may buy and slaughter, and may keep an animal, provided he does not keep the agunah animal for thirty days
Students ask Rabban Gamliel whether one may raise small animals, citing the Mishnah that one may not
He says one may keep it, provided she does not go out to graze with the flock, and so tie her to the bed's legs

A baraita: a pious man was groaning in pain, the doctors said he would be cured only by drinking hot goat's milk, so a goat was tied to his bed; when his friends saw it they suspected a thief, but he said he was dying for the goat's sin for
Rabbi Ishmael says the houses of Upper Galilee were destroyed because they grazed animals in the woods and judged monetary cases individually, even though they had a small field near their houses

A baraita: a shepherd who repented is not forced to sell immediately but sells gradually, and similarly a convert whose inheritance includes dogs and pigs, and one who vowed to buy a house or take a wife in the Land of Israel

A story: a woman whose son was troubling her swore that whoever came she would not return him; improper men pressed her, and the Sages said she did not intend this, and that just as small animals are forbidden, so small wild animals are for
Rabbi Ishmael says one may raise dogs, cats, monkeys, and weasels, since they are made to dig out the house
Asks what are chulda and senaim, the weasels and squirrels
Rav Yehuda explains the terms, offering several readings of the words for the small animals
Asks what is the meaning of the lower terms
Rav Yehuda says Rav said that we treat Babylonia like the Land of Israel regarding small animals
Rav Ada bar Ahava asks Rav Huna what his view is
Rav Huna replies that ours is a duty to protect them
Rav Ada bar Ahava replies: it is a duty to bury them all, and so he would not sustain the seed of Rav Huna's view
Some say Rav Huna said Rav said that we treat Babylonia like the Land of Israel regarding small animals
When Rav came to Babylonia, Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Asi happened to be staying in the house of Shavua the son, and some say the house of Yeshua the son, and Rav did not enter before Shmuel

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel did not enter before Rav Asi, and Rav Asi did not enter before Rav, as a matter of deference
Asks who was offended, Shmuel or Rav, and who came in response
It was a mere matter Rav did to Shmuel because of an incident in which Rav spoke against him
A story: a cat cut off a child's hand, and Rav came out and taught a ruling
Rav's ruling: a cat may be killed but not kept, with no theft and no obligation to return a lost item to the owner
Explains that the ruling is needed to teach that killing is permitted and no prohibition applies
Asks what the point is of saying there is no theft and no lost-item duty
Ravina says the point is for its hide
Objects with a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says one may raise dogs, cats, monkeys, and weasels since they dig out the house
No difficulty: one case is about a black cat and the other a white cat, and the story of Rav involved a black cat
Ravina asks: what is the status of a black cat versus a white one
The story of Rav's case involving a black cat and a white cat, with a mnemonic in the text
A chain of transmission from several Amoraim, with several versions of the attribution, leading to Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's teaching
We sound an alarm for a blocking caused on Shabbat, and a locked door will not open quickly, and one who buys a house in the Land of Israel is written up with his full name even on Shabbat
Objects with a baraita: other calamities that come on the public, like locusts, flies, wasps, gnats, and snakes and scorpions, do not sound an alarm but cry out
No difficulty: one case is wet and one dry, since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the boil God brought on Egypt was wet outside and dry inside
Exodus 9:10 describes the boil that appeared on man and beast
Asks what is the meaning of a locked door that will not open quickly
Mar Zutra says it is leaning; Rav Ashi says all who cry out will not be quickly helped; Rav Acha of Difti says they are never helped
Rav Acha of Difti's view is his own
Asks whether the case of writing on Shabbat could be right
Rather, as Rava said, one tells a gentile and he does it; the rabbis did not decree on this, since it is a rabbinic prohibition for the settlement of the Land of Israel
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites Rabbi Yonatan: one who buys a town in the Land of Israel is compelled to buy a road from all four sides for the settlement of the Land
A baraita: Joshua stipulated ten conditions

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah: one may graze in the woods and gather wood in one's fields, and gather weeds anywhere except clover, and cut shoots anywhere except the grafts of an olive tree, with rules about springs, boats, and roads
Rav Pappa explains: the rule of grazing in the woods applies to small animals among large ones, but small among small and large among large do not, and large among small is less permitted

The Gemara explains the rule on gathering wood: only deadwood and dried wood from the fields, not other wood, and not uprooted wood; and the weeds may be gathered only while wet, not dry, and not uprooted
One may gather weeds anywhere, except from a clover field
Objects: this would mean clover has a special status, but a baraita says that clover growing among other weeds need not be uprooted
Rav Yirmiya replies: no difficulty; one case is clover for seed and one for fodder, and Rav Pappa adds that the weeds are the animal's food, not a person's food
The Mishnah: one may cut back a planting anywhere except the grafts of an olive tree
Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Berakhya explain, citing an elder, the measure of cutting for olive, reeds, vines, and other trees, from the new or old growth that does or does not bear fruit

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah's rule about not drawing water from a place that sees the sun is supported by Deuteronomy 33:14
Residents of the town may draw from a spring that flows first, and Rabbah bar Rav Huna says they pay for it, though the law is not like him
One may wait by the Tiberias sea, provided one does not spread a sling or station the boat, but one may fish with nets and traps
A baraita: at first the tribes agreed not to spread a sling or station a boat, but one may fish with nets and traps
The Sages teach that the sea of Tiberias fell to Naphtali's portion, and he took the cord and the ban to the south, fulfilling Deuteronomy 33:23
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says: loose property in the mountains belongs to all tribes, but attached property belongs to the one tribe, as shown from Deuteronomy 1:7 about the nations
One may turn behind a fence, even in a field full of crocus
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains: it is needed only to remove a stone from there
Rav Chisda: even on Shabbat; Mar Zutra the pious picked up a stone, returned it, and told his student to throw it
One may walk on the public paths until the second dew falls
Rav Pappa: our rule is that even dew is harsh for it
One must step aside to the sides of the roads because of the stakes of the roads
Shmuel and Rav Yehuda were walking on the road, and Shmuel stepped aside to the side of the road
Rav Yehuda asks whether Joshua's conditions apply even in Babylonia
Shmuel replies: I am saying they apply even outside the Land
Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya were walking on the road; they stepped aside and Rabbi Yehuda ben Kenosa passed by them, taking strides
Rabbi asks Rabbi Chiya who this is who shows greatness before us
Rabbi Chiya replies: perhaps he is a disciple of Rabbi Yehuda ben Kenosa, and all his deeds are for the sake of heaven
When they came to him, he saw him and said that if not for Rabbi Yehuda ben Kenosa, he would have been cut with the iron tool
One who wanders among the vineyards takes strides back and forth
A baraita: one who sees his fellow wandering among vineyards should take strides back and forth until he brings him to the town or to the road, and likewise a wanderer
Asks what the phrase and so means, and whether one might think the rule applies only if the other knows the way
Let him return him: the Gemara teaches that the rule applies to one who does not know the way
A baraita: where does the duty to return a lost body come from; Deuteronomy 22:2 says you shall return it, so it is Torah law
The one in distress is in the way, and it is proper that he takes strides back and forth
A dead person who is found is a matter of mitzvah, and one who acquires the place acquires its place
Objects with a baraita: one who finds a corpse lying in a path turns it to the right or left, and to a field that is fallow, sown, or otherwise, as he likes
Rav Bibi replies: for a corpse lying on a narrow path, one may turn it to any place one wants, because one is permitted to move it
Ten paths of the public domain, as Solomon said
A baraita: if a man's produce is exhausted from his field and he does not let people enter his field, people say what benefit is it to him, and the verse says do not read good as evil
Asks whether it is written that one should not read good as evil
No, but the verse is Proverbs 3:27: do not withhold good from its owners when it is in your power to do it
Is there not a case, and here there is

Rabbi Yehuda says that when removing dung, a man must remove it to the public domain and pile it for thirty days so it can be trodden by people and beasts, as Joshua granted the land on that condition
But there is the view of Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Brokah
A baraita: Rabbi Yishmael says it is a court stipulation that one may enter a neighbor's field and cut his thicket to save one's own hive, paying for the neighbor's thicket
It is a court stipulation that one may pour out a neighbor's wine to save one's honey, and pay the price of the neighbor's wine from the honey
It is a court stipulation that one may dismantle a neighbor's trees to save his flax, and pay the price of the trees from the flax
Joshua granted the land on these conditions, and we do not say it applies to a single individual

82a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: a tree leaning into a neighbor's field and a tree near the boundary bring the owner to court, since Joshua granted the land on that condition
Asks who is the tanna of the ten conditions that Joshua stipulated
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is the one, as Rav Giheta taught explicitly, and Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Berakhya cite an elder who named Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi as author of the ten conditions
Ezra instituted ten enactments, including reading on Mincha of Shabbat, reading on Monday and Thursday, court sessions, laundering, eating garlic on Friday, and women's modesty and mikveh
Reading on Mincha of Shabbat for those who sit at the corners, and reading on Monday and Thursday, were instituted by Ezra
But this was already established from the beginning, as a baraita teaches
