Israel went three days in the desert without water, and the expositors said water means Torah, citing Exodus 15:22 and Isaiah 55:1; when they went three days without Torah, the prophets established readings for them

From the beginning they enacted reading on Shabbat, pausing, reading on Monday, pausing on Tuesday and Wednesday, reading on Thursday, and pausing before Shabbat so as not to go three days without Torah
Explains the variants: one man reads three verses, or three men read three verses each, corresponding to Kohanim, Levites, and Israelites, and the later version corresponds to the ten idlers
Court sessions held on Monday and Thursday, since people commonly come to read in the book
Laundering on Thursday, to honor Shabbat
Eating garlic on Friday for the sake of intimacy, based on Psalm 1:3 about its fruit in its time, attributed to several Amoraim as the one who has relations on Friday night
A baraita: five things were said of garlic: it satisfies, heals, clears the face, increases seed, and kills worms in the intestines; some add it brings love and removes jealousy
A woman should bake, so that bread is plentiful for the poor
A woman should wear an apron for modesty
A woman should cover her hair and immerse herself, which is Torah law, as Leviticus 14:9 says wash his flesh in water, so nothing intervenes between the flesh and the water
Asks what the item is that intervenes
It is hair: they say it is Torah law to examine it, lest something stick or intervene

82b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ezra's ordinances: combing hair and peddlers selling cosmetics so wives stay appealing to husbands.
Ezra instituted immersion for a man who had a seminal emission.
Objection: immersion is already a Torah requirement, so why an ordinance?
Leviticus 15:16 is cited to show that immersion is required by Torah law.
Torah immersion applies only to teruma and sacrifices; Ezra extended it to Torah study.
A baraita lists ten Jerusalem-specific rules, from houses and heifers to balconies, chickens and corpses.
The Gemara restates the rule that a house in Jerusalem is not irredeemable after sale.
Leviticus 25:30 is cited to support the irredeemability rule for Jerusalem houses.
Explanation: Jerusalem was never apportioned to a tribe, so no ancestral ownership applies there.
Jerusalem cannot be the site of the broken-neck heifer ritual.
Deuteronomy 21:1 is cited for the heifer rule, limited to land given to the tribes.
Jerusalem was not apportioned to the tribes, so it falls outside that verse.
Jerusalem cannot become an idolatrous city.
Deuteronomy 13:13 is cited, excluding Jerusalem since it was not apportioned to tribes.
A house in Jerusalem cannot become impure through leprous plagues.
Leviticus 14:34 is cited, again excluding Jerusalem since it was not apportioned to tribes.
Balconies and projections may not be built out from houses in Jerusalem.
Reasons: tent impurity from corpses, and protecting pilgrims from being injured.
Garbage dumps may not be established in Jerusalem.
Reason: repugnant creatures are attracted to refuse heaps and die there impure.
Kilns may not be built in Jerusalem.
Reason: kiln smoke is unsightly, and the Sages sought to preserve Jerusalem's beauty.
Gardens and orchards may not be planted in Jerusalem.
Reason: the odor from discarded weeds or fertilizer.
Chickens may not be raised in Jerusalem.
Reason: chickens peck in refuse and could carry impurity onto sacrificial meat.
A corpse may not be left overnight in Jerusalem.
The Gemara introduces the mishna: pigs may not be raised anywhere.
Baraita background: during the Hasmonean siege, Hyrcanus inside and Aristobulus outside bought sacrifices with money lowered in a box.
A Greek-wisdom elder advised sending up a pig, which struck the Temple wall and shook the land.
At that time the Sages cursed raising pigs and teaching one's son Greek wisdom.
A mishna about that siege is cited: barley and wheat had to come from distant places.
Question: is studying Greek wisdom really prohibited?
A baraita from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is cited against the prohibition, saying in Eretz Yisrael.

83a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why speak Syriac rather than Hebrew or Greek, the only two proper languages
Yosei asks the same about Aramaic in Babylonia, versus Hebrew or Persian
The language is permitted; only Greek wisdom is forbidden, as these are separate matters
Is Greek wisdom really forbidden, given the apparent contrary teaching
Objection: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who seems to permit it
Lamentations verse and Rabban Gamliel's account of children who studied Greek wisdom and were killed
Sages reply that Rabban Gamliel's household was different because of its close ties to the government
Baraita on the komi haircut, which Avtolmos was allowed to wear because of his government ties
The household was likewise permitted Greek wisdom, for the same reason of government ties
Mishnah: one may not raise a dog unless it is tied with chains
Baraita: in a border city one may raise a dog, tying it by day and releasing it at night
Rabbi Eliezer the Great says raising dogs is like raising pigs
What is the practical difference between the two prohibitions
The difference concerns liability to be cursed for raising them
Rav Nachman says Babylonia is like a border city, so dogs may be raised there
The Gemara qualifies that Babylonia here means only Neharde'a, a border city
Rabbi Dostai from Biri expounded a teaching about dogs and the Divine Presence
Numbers verse and its derivation that the Divine Presence leaves Israel if a dog causes a miscarriage
Illustrative case of a woman whose fright from a barking dog caused a miscarriage
Mishnah: one may not set traps for pigeons
Do pigeons really travel that far from their cotes
Objection: a mishnah requires dovecotes to be fifty cubits from the city
Abaye says pigeons fly farther but are satiated within fifty cubits, so they stop eating beyond thirty ris
Baraita: in a settled area one may not set traps even at one hundred mil
Rav Yosef says that baraita refers to a settled area of vineyards, where pigeons rest
Rabba says that baraita refers to a settled area with many dovecotes where pigeons rest
If many dovecotes lie along the way, why not derive the prohibition from the dovecotes themselves
Three resolutions: a gentile's dovecotes, ownerless dovecotes, or dovecotes belonging to the trapper
Chapter-closing formula: the chapter beginning with Merubeh is complete

83b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: one who injures another owes payment under five headings
Damage is assessed by comparing the victim's value as a slave before and after the injury
Pain is assessed by what a person of similar sensitivity would accept to suffer the same burn
Medical costs are owed for injuries caused by the blow, with rules for recurrence and full cure
Loss of livelihood is assessed by the pay of a cucumber watchman, not standard wages
Humiliation is assessed according to the status of both the humiliator and the humiliated
Why assume compensation; the verse eye for eye might mean literally losing an eye
Rejects the literal reading, since a baraita teaches otherwise
Baraita derives human injury payment from the animal case, since both are for money, not corporal punishment
Alternative baraita derivation from the ransom verse: only a murderer's life cannot be ransomed, so limbs can be compensated
To which verse is the baraita referring, since the verse on striking a person concerns killing
Rather, the verses on mortal striking of an animal and on maiming a neighbor teach the same halakha
Objection: the verse that a striker of a person shall die seems to mean literal loss of a limb, not money
Rejects that reading: the verse is juxtaposed to the animal case and says given, meaning money
What difficulty made the baraita need a second derivation rather than deriving from the person verse
Damage halakhot are derived from damage verses, not from death verses
Objection: then human halakhot should derive from human verses, not from animal verses
Deflects the objection by restating the baraita's second derivation from the ransom verse
Objection: the ransom verse must exclude limbs, since it is needed to bar taking money and then killing
The single word evildoing in the flogging verse bars two punishments for one act
Objection: the flogging explanation still leaves the ransom verse needed to teach its primary rule
If so, the verse would omit for the life of a murderer; its presence shows only murderers are excluded from ransom
Once the verse forbids ransom, why is a separate derivation from animal striking needed
Otherwise the injurer could choose between giving his eye or its money value; the animal case settles it
Baraita of Rabbi Dostai ben Yehuda: eye for eye means money, since eyes may differ in size
Objection: if money applied only to unequal eyes, equal eyes would break the principle of one law for all
Objection: perhaps the injurer loses his sight as the victim did, whatever the eyes' sizes

84a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a small man killed a large one, how is the murderer executed
The Torah's one law for all implies taking the injurer's own life and sight, against the monetary reading
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's baraita: eye for eye means money, since cases of unequal limbs show literal reading is impossible
Sages object: if literal punishment is impossible, the injurer is exempt, which conflicts with one law for all
Rather, punish where the Torah's penalty is possible, and exempt where it is not
School of Rabbi Yishmael: the giving in as he has given a blemish refers to money
Objection: if so, the word yitten in that verse should also mean money
Sages reply: the school of Rabbi Yishmael is interpreting a superfluous verse
Since the verse already says so shall it be done, the repeated wording must teach monetary payment
Why is the phrase as he has given a blemish needed at all
It is written only because the verse requires the word given to mean money, so the wording is repeated
School of Rabbi Hiyya: hand for hand means the hand passed from hand, i.e., money
Objection: then foot for foot should likewise mean money, which is an unlikely reading
The school of Rabbi Hiyya is interpreting a superfluous phrase in the verse
If taken literally, the phrase as he purposed would be redundant, so it teaches monetary payment
Why is foot for foot needed, if hand for hand already teaches the point
The Torah wrote foot because hand was written, so the same wording applies to foot
Abaye: the school of Hizkiyya taught that eye and life are separate, so eye for eye is monetary
If literal, sometimes both an eye and a life would be lost for one eye, which is absurd
Objection: the court assesses the guilty party's strength, so Abaye's reasoning could still allow literal blinding
Mishnah on lashes: an officer who kills a flogged man within the assessed limit is exempt, so the assessment principle holds
Rav Zevid, citing Rabba: a wound for a wound teaches that pain is paid even when damage is paid
If literal, why pay for pain at all; the objection is that persons differ in sensitivity, so pain payment is still needed
Rav Pappa, citing Rava: the healing verse teaches medical costs even when damage is paid
If literal, the injurer also needs healing, so why pay medical costs; flesh heals at different rates
Rav Ashi: the word for in eye for eye is linked to the ox case, where the payment is money
What did you see that led you to derive this from an ox rather than from a person
Alternatively, derive from the verse on killing a person: life for life is literal, so eye for eye is literal too
Sages reply: damage halakhot are derived from damage verses, not from death verses
Objection: on the contrary, human halakhot should derive from human verses, not from animal verses
Rav Ashi retracts and derives it from the verse on a man who violates a maiden, which requires money
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer holds that eye for eye means an actual eye
Objection: can Rabbi Eliezer really mean an actual eye, against all the other tanna'im
Rabba: Rabbi Eliezer means the injured party is not appraised as a slave for the injury
Abaye objects: if appraised as a freeman, he has no monetary value, so this cannot be the meaning
Rav Ashi: Rabbi Eliezer means the appraisal is of the injurer, not of the injured party
Case: a donkey severed a child's hand; Rav Pappa bar Shmuel orders four types of indemnity appraised
Rava objects: the mishnah teaches five types of indemnity, not four
Rav Pappa: he meant the indemnities other than damage, i.e. the four beyond it
Abaye objects: a donkey's owner pays only for damage, so only damage is appraised
Rav Pappa rules that the damage must be appraised
Officers object: must the child not be appraised as a slave
Rav Pappa rules that the child be appraised as a slave
The child's father says he does not want his child appraised as a slave, since it would demean him
They object: the father harms the child, who then receives no compensation
The father replies that when the child grows up he will repay him from his own money
Case: an ox chewed a child's hand; Rava orders the child appraised as a slave
Officers object: Rava held that a slave-based penalty cannot be collected in Babylonia
Rava: appraisal is needed to determine value, though payment is not collected by courts in Babylonia
Rava's principle: ox-on-ox and person-on-ox damage is collected in Babylonia, but person-on-person damage is not
What distinguishes person-on-person damage from the other cases, given that ordained judges are needed

84b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuing the question: ordained judges are required and none exist in Babylonia, so what differs for ox damage
Babylonian judges act as agents of Eretz Yisrael judges in ox damage cases, as they do for admissions and loans
If so, why not also act as agents for person-on-person and person-on-ox damage, like admissions and loans
Agency applies only where the ruling is clear to the Babylonian judges, not where an appraisal is needed
Objection: ox and person cases still need appraisal, so market sale values would not settle them; fixed penalties would be enforced
Agency applies only to monetary restitution for loss, not to penalties such as the thief's double or fourfold payment
Person-on-person damage is monetary restitution, so should Babylonian judges act as agents here
Agency applies only to common cases; uncommon person-on-person damage is not covered by it
Humiliation is common, so by that standard Babylonian judges should act as agents for it
Indeed Babylonia collects humiliation compensation, as Rav Pappa awarded four hundred zuz in such a case
Objection: Rav Hisda queried Rav Nachman, who asked whether Babylonia collects penalties at all
Agency applies to common matters involving monetary loss, so humiliation without loss and uncommon damage are excluded
Objection to the halakha: Rava says courts in Babylonia do not collect for ox damage, so ox-on-ox damage conflicts with this
There the ox was innocuous, a penalty, while here it was forewarned, so payment is compensation, not a penalty
Objection: forewarned oxen are uncommon in Babylonia, so agency should not apply to them either
Rabbis from Eretz Yisrael came and forewarned the ox here, in Babylonia, so the matter is not uncommon
Objection: the matter is still uncommon, so agency should not apply, contrary to the resolution
Rava refers to ox damage of the forewarned categories of eating and trampling, which are common and monetary
Mishnah on pain: even when the pain is not in a place causing damage, the injurer pays compensation for it
Who is the tanna who taught that pain is paid even without damage
Rava says this is the view of ben Azzai
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says keviyya is stated first; ben Azzai says habura is stated first, on the verse's terms
Explains the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds keviyya includes burns with no bruise, so habura limits payment to bruised burns
Ben Azzai holds keviyya means a burn with a bruise, so habura extends payment to burns without bruises
Rav Pappa objects: the opposite is more reasonable, since Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and ben Azzai's views are reversed
Rav Pappa's reading: each view is based on the final understanding of the verse, so the mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
Alternatively, all agree keviyya covers burns with or without a bruise, and the dispute concerns the habura wording

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and ben Azzai disagree on applying generalization and detail when the terms are distant
Rabbi Yehuda holds that generalization and detail do not apply here, since the terms are separated
Ben Azzai holds that generalization and detail do apply to the verse despite the separation
If so, why does the Torah need the word habura, given Rabbi Yehuda's reading
Habura teaches an additional payment for the bruise beyond the payment for the burn
Mishnah: pain is assessed by how much a person with similar sensitivity would accept to suffer it
How is pain assessed when the injured party also suffered a bodily injury
Shmuel's father: assess how much a person would accept to have his hand severed
Objection: this would cover all five types of indemnity, and no one would sell his hand for money
Rather, assess the payment for a hand already severed, which is of no further use
Objection: even a severed hand causes humiliation, since flesh thrown to dogs is shameful
Rather, assess what one would accept to change a decreed severing from a drug to a sword
Objection: here too no one would accept money to cause himself pain, so there is no indemnity to assess
Rather, assess what one would pay to have the severing changed from a sword to a drug
Objection: then the mishnah's word take is imprecise and should read give
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: the injured party takes what he would have paid to avoid the sword
Mishnah: for injury causing illness, the injurer must pay for healing
Baraita: if growths arise from the injury and the wound reopens, the injurer pays healing and loss of livelihood
Rabbi Yehuda: even if growths arise from the injury, he pays healing but not loss of livelihood
The Rabbis: the injurer pays for healing and loss of livelihood together, or for neither
With regard to what do the tanna'im disagree
Rabba: the dispute is whether a wound may be bandaged, since bandage side effects are attributed to the injury
Objection to that reading: if Rabbi Yehuda forbids bandaging, the injurer should not pay for healing either
Everyone agrees a wound may be bandaged but not excessively; the dispute is over how the verse's repeated wording applies
Rabbi Yehuda holds the word only excludes loss of livelihood from non-injury growths, so the earlier words restrict it
The later Rabbis: anyone liable for loss of livelihood is liable for healing, and vice versa
Why is the repeated healing wording needed if the later Rabbis accept the pairing
It teaches that a doctor is granted permission to heal, as the school of Rabbi Yishmael derived
Baraita derivation from the verse and heal: the word only excludes non-injury growths from liability
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda: even injury-caused growths are excluded, because of the word only
Two versions of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's view: full exemption, or exemption from loss of livelihood only
Does the verse need to teach the exemption for growths not caused by the injury
The Sages explain: what the baraita means by not due to injury
Baraita: one who ate honey against his doctor's orders and developed garguteni is exempt, as the verse says only
What is garguteni
Abaye: it is necrosis
What is its remedy
Crystalline ice plant, wax, and wine dregs
Halakhot: the injurer may offer to heal the victim himself, but the victim may refuse, and a free doctor is worthless
Halakha: the injurer may bring a distant doctor, but the victim may refuse, since such a doctor may blind the eye
Halakha: the victim may not take the money to heal himself, since he would be negligent and profit from it
Baraita: all these types of indemnity are paid in a case where damage is also paid
From where are these matters derived
Rav Zevid in the name of Rava: the verse wound for wound teaches pain payment alongside damage
The Gemara asks: is this verse not needed to teach an additional halakha

85b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse includes one who injures unintentionally, as if intentionally, and by circumstance, as if willingly
Objection: if that were all, the verse should say the shorter wound for wound, so the longer phrase teaches more
The phrase teaches two things: liability regardless of how the injury occurred, and pain paid alongside damage
Rav Pappa citing Rava: the doubled verb verappo yerappe teaches medical costs paid alongside damage
Objection: that verse is needed for the school of Rabbi Yishmael's derivation that a doctor is permitted to heal
If so, the verse should read verofeh yerappe, and the wording itself shows medical costs are paid alongside damage
Objection: the verse is still needed to repeat the healing wording for the earlier halakhot
If so, the verse could repeat one word twice; the change in wording teaches medical costs paid alongside damage
If pain, medical costs, loss of livelihood, and humiliation are paid even with damage, where are cases without damage
Examples without damage: pain from a burn, medical costs for a drug that whitened flesh, loss of livelihood from confinement, humiliation from spitting
Mishnah and baraita: loss of livelihood is assessed as for a watchman of cucumbers
Objection: the standard of justice seems compromised, since the injured man would earn more as a porter or agent
The baraita replies: justice is not compromised, since the injurer already paid for the hand or leg, which covered lost professional opportunity
Rava's rules: severed hand, broken leg, blinded eye, and deafened ear each have a fixed loss of livelihood assessment
If the court did not assess each injury, does the injurer pay one total value or assess each injury separately
Rava explains the dilemma: pain and humiliation are paid per injury, while the total value covers the rest
Rava's second dilemma: if the court assessed each injury but the injurer had not paid before deafening, is payment separate or total
Rabba's dilemma: if an injury diminishes value only temporarily, must compensation be paid now
Come and hear from the mishnah on Makkot 87a: a striker of a parent or one who injures on Yom Kippur is not liable to capital punishment

86a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah ruling continued: one who injures a parent is liable for all five types of indemnity
In the case of one who injured his parent without bruising him, what are the circumstances
The case is one where he struck the hand, which will recover, so the mishnah's full liability resolves Rabba's dilemma; or the Sages say deafening without bruise
Objection: Rabba himself says deafening a father is capital, since deafening cannot occur without some bruise
Rather, the case is shaving the father's hair without a bruise, since hair regrows and so fits the dilemma
Objection: the case may instead be smearing a depilatory agent, so the hair does not grow back
Smearing causes pain from fissures, medical costs for healing them, loss of livelihood from dancing, and humiliation from losing hair
Abaye and Rava each resolved Rabba's dilemma differently on a hand that is weakened but will recover
Abaye and Rava dispute the compensation owed when one severs a Hebrew slave's hand belonging to another
Explains the slave dispute: the case of injury that does not reduce the master's value, such as a torn ear or nostril tip
Mishnah: humiliation is assessed according to the stature of the humiliator and the humiliated
Whose opinion is expressed in this mishnah
It is the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, not Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yehuda
Baraita: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon each state a different standard for humiliation of Jews
Whose opinion is the mishnah then, if the mishnah is read against this baraita
Rabbi Yehuda may hold a blind person has no humiliation only as regards taking compensation from him, so the mishnah can follow him
Objection: the latter clause about a sleeping person shows no difference by inference, so the mishnah must follow Rabbi Shimon
Who is the tanna of the baraita on intending to humiliate a small person and humiliating a great one
Baraita: one who intends to humiliate a small person but humiliates a great one pays the great person the small person's compensation
Whose opinion is this baraita, if not Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, or Rabbi Shimon
Objection: the baraita cannot be any of these three, since each of them takes a different position on this case
Rabbi Shimon's exemption follows the law of killing, requiring specific intent; Rabbi Yehuda's point is about compensation to slaves
Alternatively, the baraita follows Rabbi Meir: gadol and katan mean actual adult and minor, not wealth
But is a minor subject to humiliation at all
Yes, as Rav Pappa said: a minor who feels humiliation when others shame him is subject to it, and here likewise

86b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Completes Rav Pappa's explanation: the minor in the baraita is one who feels humiliation when others shame him
Mishnah: one who humiliates a naked, blind, or sleeping person is liable, but a sleeper who humiliates another is exempt
Baraita: humiliating a naked person or in a bathhouse is liable, but the humiliation is less than in clothing or the marketplace
Is a naked person subject to humiliation at all
Rav Pappa: a gust of wind lifted his clothes, and the other person then raised them higher to humiliate him
Is one in a bathhouse subject to humiliation
Rav Pappa: the humiliation occurred on the riverbank, where people undress more discreetly
Rabbi Abba bar Memel's dilemma: is humiliation compensation due to the victim's embarrassment or to disgrace, if he died asleep
Baraita of Rabbi Meir: deaf-mutes and minors receive humiliation compensation, imbeciles do not, which bears on the dilemma
Objection: if the compensation is due to disgrace, an imbecile should also receive it
The Sages reply that an imbecile suffers no greater humiliation, so that case does not decide the dilemma; the baraita concerns disgrace
Objection: if due to embarrassment, a minor would not be subject to it, but Rav Pappa holds minors are subject to it
Rav Pappa's version of the dilemma: is compensation due to the victim's own embarrassment or to his family's humiliation
Baraita: deaf-mutes and minors have humiliation compensation, imbeciles do not, which fits family humiliation better
Objection: if family humiliation, an imbecile should also receive compensation
Imbeciles have the greatest humiliation already; Rav Pappa holds minors feel humiliation when others shame them
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: a minor sometimes has humiliation compensation and sometimes does not, depending on his age
Mishnah: one who humiliates a blind person is liable to pay compensation
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda holds a blind person has no humiliation liability, and is exempt from exile, lashes, and court execution
What is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for exempting the blind, from the verbal analogy of your eye not pitying
Baraita on exile for unintentional killing: Rabbi Yehuda holds seeing him not excludes the blind, while Rabbi Meir includes them
Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse on the forest woodcutter includes the blind, so seeing him not is needed to exclude them
Rabbi Meir's reasoning: two restrictions in sequence amplify the law, so the blind are included in the exile rule
How would Rabbi Yehuda respond to this reasoning
Rabbi Yehuda: the verse excludes one who intended to kill another, not one who could not see
Rabbi Yehuda derives exemption from capital punishment, lashes, and exile by verbal analogies to the killer and wicked verses
Another baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says a blind person has no humiliation

87a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda exempts a blind person from all civil laws found in the Torah
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda for exempting the blind from civil laws
The verse on judging between smiter and avenger applies civil laws only to one subject to those two halakhot
Another baraita: Rabbi Yehuda holds a blind person has no humiliation compensation
Rabbi Yehuda exempts a blind person from all commandments stated in the Torah
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi asks the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda on commandments
The verse says this is the commandment, statutes, and laws, so whoever lacks civil liability lacks commandments too
Rav Yosef, who was blind, says he would have celebrated if the halakha exempted the blind, but Rabbi Hanina's ruling changes that
Mishnah: a stringency for humans compared with oxen, and one who strikes a father or mother without bruise pays all five indemnities
Mishnah: one who injures a Hebrew slave or a Canaanite slave of others pays all five; Rabbi Yehuda says Canaanite slaves lack humiliation
Mishnah: encounters with deaf-mutes, imbeciles, minors, slaves, and married women are disadvantageous to the one who injures them
Mishnah: one who strikes a parent with bruise or injures on Shabbat is exempt, since he is judged by his life; a master is exempt for his own slave
Rabbi Elazar asks Rav whom the compensation for injuring another's minor daughter belongs to, and explains the dilemma

87b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav's ruling: the Torah granted the father only the profits of his minor daughter's youth, and nothing more
Objection from the mishna on injuring a Hebrew slave, where the owner's loss of labor is excluded
Abaye: Rav concedes that loss of livelihood for a minor daughter is paid to the father, since her earnings are his
Objection from a baraita: a daughter's injurer is exempt from paying her father, unlike others who injure her
So too here, the baraita speaks only of loss of livelihood, which goes to the father; the other indemnities go to the daughter
Contradiction from another baraita: the father pays adult children at once and invests for minors, yet is exempt for his own
No contradiction: the father is exempt when children depend on his table, liable when they do not
Challenge: the daughter's sustenance requirement implies she should get the compensation, even if the father feeds her
As Rava son of Rav Ulla said, the rule covers only the surplus beyond what the daughter needs for sustenance
Why does the baraita say the father invests for minor sons, and not that their compensation goes to the father
The father cares only about money that comes to his children from his own loss, not money from others
Objection: a found item comes to children from elsewhere, and the father still cares about it
Profit that involves no physical pain the father cares about; injury involving pain, from elsewhere, he does not care about
Objection: the first baraita itself says others who injure the daughter pay her father, so the father cares about injury money
That father is captious and not dependent on the table; the latter baraita's father is not captious, so the distinction holds
What is meant by a safe investment for the minor
Rav Hisda: buy a Torah scroll for the child; Rabba bar Rav Huna: buy a date palm that yields dates
Reish Lakish: the Torah granted the father only the profits of youth, and nothing else
Rabbi Yochanan: the father receives even compensation for his daughter's wound
Objection: an injury does not reduce a daughter's value in the way a wound does, so even Rabbi Elazar's dilemma concerned only injury

88a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar raised no dilemma on a wound that does not lower value; Rabbi Yochanan's case is a face wound that lowers it
Mishnah: one who injures a Canaanite slave of others is liable for all five types; Rabbi Yehuda excludes humiliation
What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda that Canaanite slaves have no humiliation compensation
The verse 'when men strive together, a man and his brother' limits humiliation to those with brotherhood, excluding slaves
Objection: by that logic, conspiring witnesses against a slave should not be executed, since a slave is not a brother
Rava cites Rav Sheshet: the verse 'remove the evil from your midst' applies in any case, including to slaves
Objection: according to the Sages, a Canaanite slave should be eligible for kingship as one of your brothers
The Sages reply that the convert case shows the verse's wording means the choicest of your brothers, excluding both converts and slaves
Objection: according to the Sages, a slave should be eligible to testify, since the verse speaks of a false witness against his brother
Ulla: a slave is disqualified by an a fortiori inference from a woman, who is disqualified despite her fitness to enter the congregation
Objection: a woman is disqualified for a reason absent in a slave, since she is unfit for circumcision, which a slave is fit for
A minor proves that fitness for circumcision is irrelevant to testimony, since a minor is circumcised but disqualified
Objection: a minor is not obligated in mitzvot, a difference a slave lacks, so the minor comparison fails
A woman proves the point: she is obligated in mitzvot yet disqualified from testimony
The derivation returns to a common denominator: women, minors, and slaves all lack full mitzvah obligation and are disqualified
Objection: what is notable about the common denominator is that a woman or minor is not a man, so it cannot extend to slaves
Derivation from a robber, who is disqualified because his own actions caused it
Objection: a robber is disqualified because of his own actions, which a slave's actions did not cause
Derive from a robber together with a woman or minor, whose shared feature of partial mitzvah observance excludes slaves
Mar son of Ravina: fathers shall not be put to death for children refers to slaves, who lack lineage with their children
Objection: the second half of the verse would then also disqualify converts, who lack lineage with their parents
A convert has lineage with his descendants, so the exclusion applies only to a slave, who lacks lineage in both directions
Converts are fit to testify, since the verse's two clauses teach two halakhot, and a slave is a fortiori disqualified
Why is the phrase nor shall children be put to death for fathers needed, if the first clause already covers the case
Since the verse states fathers for children, it states the reverse as well, so the two clauses are written in parallel
Mishnah: an encounter with a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor is disadvantageous, since one who injures them is liable
Case: the mother of Rav Shmuel bar Abba had signed over her property to her son before her death

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Shmuel bar Abba's dispute over his mother's property; Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's rule that a husband repossesses a wife's usufruct sales
Rabbi Yirmeya cites the mishna: a father who transfers property to his son retains use, so a sale by the son does not pass beyond the father's life
Rabbi Yirmeya's inference, its attribution to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, and the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the purchaser's rights
Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: the mishna's case is one where the son survived the father, so the property passed to the son first
Gemara: Rabbi Yochanan holds ownership of usufruct equals ownership of the property, so the son sold what was not his
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's reasoning: the purchaser acquires in either case, since the son's sale is of property he owned
Gemara: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds usufruct ownership is not like ownership of the property, so the son sold his own property
Rabbi Yirmeya argues that the mishna shows usufruct ownership is not equivalent to property ownership, so Shmuel's ruling stands
Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel: the husband's rights are not similar to the mishna on a father's transferred property
Rav Yosef asks what the reason is for distinguishing the two cases
Rav Yosef: the son sells because he is an heir with an existing right, which the wife's husband, not her son, holds
Abaye objects: a son inherits from a father and a father from a son equally, so the mishna supports no such inference
Abaye: the husband's rights rest on the rabbinic ordinance of Usha, which applies to husbands only
Rav Idi bar Avin cites a baraita on divorce witnesses, confirming the Usha ordinance is a known rule

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Conspiring witnesses who made a wife's marriage contract appear paid owe only its financial advantage, not its full value
The financial advantage is the price a person would pay for the contract, given that husband inherits if she dies during the marriage
Rav Idi bar Avin: without the Usha ordinance, why would the husband inherit, instead of her selling the whole contract
Abaye: this is no proof for Usha, since some property is non-sellable by the wife regardless of the ordinance
Abaye: the money from selling the financial advantage goes only to the wife, since otherwise the witnesses could object that she loses nothing
Rav Shalman: the wife still loses nothing, since the household gains, and that benefit returns to her
Rava: the money from the financial advantage is the wife's alone, and the husband takes no profits from it or from property bought with it
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna cite a mishna on slaves and married women as a source for the Usha ordinance
Even with Usha, the wife could sell the financial advantage, so the mishna must concern a wife without usufruct property
Why does the mishna say she lacks money, when she could sell the financial advantage of her contract
Rabbi Meir: a man may not keep a wife for an hour without a marriage contract, so she cannot sell its advantage
What is Rabbi Meir's reason, and why would selling the contract not make a husband divorce her more easily
The financial advantage is mere words, a legal possibility rather than a possession, so it is not mortgaged for debts
Objection: why not, since the financial advantage has a market value and is sold for dinars
Shmuel's rule on sold promissory notes: she need not sell, since she could later forgive the debt, and the Sages will not cause loss
Suggestion: she should sell her contract to the one she injured, which the Gemara must refute

89b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: She may forgive the debt toward her husband, but in any case the court need not force a sale of the financial advantage
If she would forgive the debt anyway, why does a baraita say she does not lose her contract when she injures her husband
That baraita follows Rabbi Meir, who forbids a husband to keep a wife for an hour without a marriage contract
What is Rabbi Meir's reason, since a husband could divorce her and collect compensation either way
The baraita concerns a large contract sum, which deters the husband from divorce since he would lose the excess
Suggestion: let the Torah-minimum part stay and sell only the excess to the husband as compensation
The baraita concerns a contract equal to the Torah minimum, where a four-dinar gain would not outweigh losing twenty-five
The latter clause of the baraita says she can lose contract value; when does that happen
Rava: the clause concerns the stipulation that sons inherit the mother's contract, which a sale under duress does not abrogate
Is the Usha dispute a tannaitic dispute, as two baraitot on slaves emancipated by a wife's injury suggest
The baraitot may reflect whether a wife may sell usufruct property before or after the Usha ordinance, following Rava's view

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava: consecration, leavened bread, and emancipation abrogate any lien, so emancipation frees a slave from the husband's lien
Shall we say that Rava's statement is a dispute between tanna'im
No: all agree with Rava that liens are abrogated; alternatively, the tanna'im disagree on whether usufruct equals ownership
Baraita: a seller of a Canaanite slave conditions the sale on thirty days of service to the seller before transfer
Rabbi Meir: only the first owner is included in the day-or-two exemption, since usufruct equals ownership
Rabbi Yehuda: only the second owner, whose money the slave is, is included in the exemption
Rabbi Yosei: both owners are included, and since the matter is uncertain in capital law, neither is punished
Rabbi Eliezer: neither owner is included, since one must both own and use the slave to be exempt
Rava's reason for Rabbi Eliezer: the verse for he is his money refers to a slave unique to the owner
In accordance with whose opinion is Ameimar's ruling on a sale of usufruct property by husband and wife
Ameimar follows Rabbi Eliezer, who requires both ownership and usage, so the sale accomplishes nothing
Who is the tanna who taught the baraita on half-slaves and slaves of partners
Baraita: a half-slave half-freeman, or a slave of two partners, is not emancipated by loss of a non-regenerating limb
Rav Mordechai, citing Rava, says this is Rabbi Eliezer's view, since his money refers to a slave unique to one owner
Mishnah: compensation for striking, slapping, pulling hair, spitting, or uncovering a woman's head, in sela, dinar, and zuz amounts

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Principle: humiliation is assessed by the victim's honor; Rabbi Akiva says even poor Jews are treated as freemen who lost property
Story: Rabbi Akiva fines a man who uncovered a woman's head four hundred dinars, and the man breaks a jug of oil to pay her
The man sets up witnesses and argues the woman's own uncovering shows no humiliation, so he owes nothing
Rabbi Akiva rejects the claim: self-injury is exempt but others who injure are liable, so the man still owes
Mishnah: one who injures himself or cuts his own saplings is exempt, but others who do so are liable
Does the one-hundred-dinar amount of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili refer to Tyrian or state coinage
Story of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who ruled one hundred dinars of Tyrian coinage, cited as a proof
What did Rabbi Yehuda Nesia mean by saying this is I and this is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
Objection: if he witnessed and ruled, a witness would become a judge, which Rabbi Tarfon's and Rabbi Akiva's baraita disputes
Rabbi Tarfon's case concerns night, when judgment is not held, or Rabbi Yehuda Nesia did not witness and merely relied on witnesses
Does Rabbi Akiva really hold that a witness cannot become a judge
Baraita of Shimon HaTimni: the fist is unique because witnesses attest to it, so any item submitted to the court can ground liability
Rabbi Akiva objects: courts do not see how hard a blow landed, and a roof or building cannot be inspected, so witnesses must suffice
Rabbi Akiva's reading: the verse's fist means items submitted to witnesses, excluding a stone that has left the striker's possession
Objection: if Rabbi Akiva agrees a witness can judge when the blow was seen in court, he contradicts his own baraita
Shimon HaTimni's view is not Rabbi Akiva's own; Rabbi Akiva may hold that a court that saw the act cannot judge it
Baraita: an innocuous ox that kills is judged capitally and not monetarily, while a forewarned ox is judged monetarily and then capitally
If the court first judged the forewarned ox capitally, why not also judge it monetarily afterward
Rava: the Sages of Rav's school explained it follows Shimon HaTimni, whose fist analogy extends to any submitted item

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava's conclusion that a court evaluation is needed before liability for an ox's damage, and that a capital verdict is not delayed for it.
Rava's reconciling reply that even on Rabbi Akiva's view the baraita concerns a case where the owner fled.
How can a court try a monetary claim against an absent owner when the case was not tried as capital?
The owner had been present when the witnesses were accepted, and only afterward fled.
Ultimately, from where is the damage paid when the owner has fled?
Payment comes from the plowing fees earned by the ox.
If so, the court should try the monetary case first and the capital case afterward, so why does the baraita say otherwise?
Rav Mari answers that plowing money counts as the owner's other property, not as the ox's own value.
Does the court evaluate whether an act could cause damage, as it does for killing, or not at all?
The mishna on pits is cited as a source: an animal injured but not killed in a shallow pit still incurs liability.
Objection: the mishna counts depths from below upward, so damage liability applies even at one handbreadth, meaning no evaluation for damage.
Rejection: the mishna counts from above downward, and damage is in fact evaluated, requiring conditions that could really cause injury.
A baraita on blinding or deafening a slave is brought as proof that damage requires evaluation for emancipation.
Objection: the slave may have been frightened into injury, and a baraita about frightening someone shows injury can come from fright.
A baraita on the five kinds of indemnity is cited; the evaluated sum is fixed, showing that damage is evaluated.
The dilemma is whether one evaluates if an object is capable of causing this damage. What is the halakha?
Shimon HaTimni's baraita comparing a fist with any item submitted to judges to assess its harm is cited as proof of evaluation.
Rava's ruling on an injured man healed early is cited as support for his view.
The mishna on spitting and removing a cloak is quoted, and Rav Pappa limits the ruling to spittle that reached the body.
Why not? Should spittle landing on clothing be treated like humiliation by words?
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin says humiliation by words alone is exempt from payment, though it remains a sin before Heaven.
The mishna rule that payment for humiliation is set according to the victim's honor.
Does the first tanna state his view leniently, for a poor person, or stringently, for a rich person?
Rabbi Akiva's remark that poor Jews are treated as freemen is cited to show the first tanna speaks leniently.
The mishna relates an incident of uncovering a woman's head in the marketplace and Rabbi Akiva's assessment.
Is time to pay granted to an assailant for compensation?
Objection from Rabbi Hanina: time to pay is not granted for injuries.
Reply: time is refused for bodily harm that causes money loss, but granted for humiliation, which causes no monetary loss.
A mishna example of a woman standing at her courtyard entrance is cited as a case.
Objection from a baraita: Rabbi Akiva says one may injure oneself, which seems to conflict with the mishna.
Rava resolves it: the baraita concerns bodily injury and the mishna concerns humiliation, so there is no contradiction.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna teaching that one who injures himself is exempt, though he is not permitted to do so.
Rabbi Akiva's reply: humiliation is permitted, but others who injure a man are liable for actual injury.
Is a person really not permitted to injure himself, as the answer implied?
Objection from a baraita on an oath to do evil to oneself, which seems to imply self-injury is permitted.
Shmuel says the baraita concerns an oath to sit in a fast, which is permitted.
If so, can one compel others to fast, when doing evil to others is prohibited?
Yes, by confining others so that they cannot get food.
Objection: a baraita defines doing evil to others as striking a man and injuring his brain, so the parallel must include injury.
Resolution: this is a dispute between tanna'im, one holding that a person may not injure himself and another that he may.
Which tanna holds that one may not injure himself, and is the Rabbi Elazar source a correct inference?
Perhaps killing differs from injury, so the Rabbi Elazar source does not settle the matter for injury.
A baraita on rending garments for the dead, with Rabbi Elazar's flogging, is offered as a source extending the prohibition to self-injury.
Objection: garments are different, since tearing them is an irreversible loss, and that does not apply to bodily injury.
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's baraita on the nazirite who afflicted himself is cited to show self-harm is forbidden in any manner.
Mishna: one who cuts down his own saplings is exempt, though others who cut them down are liable.
Rabba bar bar Hana's baraita before Rav: if the other party told him to cut or kill, he is exempt from paying.
Rav objects that this reading would leave the baraita nothing, since the mishna's cases are an ox standing to be killed and a tree standing to be cut.
If so, what is the claimant asserting when he says he intended to do the act?
The answer: such an act is a mitzva, as a baraita teaches.
The verse on spilled blood being covered is cited: whoever spilled it must cover it.
An incident in which Rabban Gamliel obligated one party to pay ten zehuvim after a dispute over slaughter and covering the blood.
Rav rules that a palm tree bearing a kav of dates may not be cut down.
Objection from a baraita giving a yield threshold for olive trees, which seems to conflict with Rav's ruling on palms.
Olives are different because they are valued; Rabbi Hanina explains the baraita as speaking of a fig tree cut before its time.
Ravina rules that if the tree is worth more as timber, cutting it is permitted.
A baraita also teaches this, citing the verse that distinguishes a fruit tree from a barren tree as the source.
Since the verse's end includes everything, why does it need to specify that the tree is not a fruit tree?
The verse teaches that a barren tree takes priority over a fruit-bearing tree for cutting.

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse with the word only is cited to limit the rule, excluding a case where the item is worth more than its price.
Shmuel's tenant brings dates that taste of wine, and Shmuel asks where they came from, which is the vines.
Rav Hisda's story: he tells his tenant to uproot the vines, illustrating the distinction between palms and vines.
Mishna: even after paying, the injurer is not forgiven until he asks the injured party for forgiveness.
The story of Abraham and Abimelech is cited to show that refusing to forgive is cruel.
Mishna on injuries done on condition of exemption, distinguishing harm to the body from harm to property.
A baraita: the payment pattern applies to humiliation, and the injurer is not forgiven for pain until he asks.
The verse on the prophet's wife in Abimelech's story is cited to show the need to ask for forgiveness.
Explanation: a prophet's wife must be returned, whereas another man's wife need not be returned in the same way.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani citing Rabbi Yonatan: a man's wife must be returned in any event.
Objection: Abimelech was misled by Abraham and Sarah's claim of siblinghood, so the claim that he sinned conflicts with this.
Explanation: a stranger's inquiry about his wife teaches that Abimelech, a Noahide, should have learned and did not.
The verse that God closed all the wombs of Abimelech's house is cited as the basis for causes of barrenness.
Rabbi Elazar: the two barrenness causes are of two kinds, from the man's seed and from the woman's seed and birth.
A baraita lists the causes of barrenness: two from the man and three from the woman.
Ravina gives a longer list, adding the ring-shaped orifice as a further cause of barrenness.
The verse on closed wombs: in the school of Rabbi Yannai they said even Abimelech's hen did not lay an egg.
Rava asks Rabba for the source of the principle that one who prays for another with the same need is answered first.
Rabba cites the verse on God restoring Job's fortunes when Job prayed for his friends.
Rejoinder: that is the source for you, but I derive the principle from the Abraham verse instead.
The verses on Abraham praying for Abimelech and God remembering Sarah are cited as the source of the principle.
Rava asks Rabba for the source of a common saying, tied to the earlier principle.
Rabba answers from Jeremiah: God asks why they contend against Him, all of them having transgressed.
Rejoinder: that is your source, but I derive the matter from the verse about keeping God's commandments.
The Exodus verse asking how long they will refuse to keep God's commandments and teachings is cited.
Rava asks who the five men were that Joseph took from among his brothers.
Rabba answers in Rabbi Yochanan's name: the five are the names repeated, Judah among them.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani cites Rabbi Yonatan on the verse about Reuben and Judah, with the tradition about Judah's bones and Moses' prayer.
Immediately God heard Judah's voice, and his bones stopped being carried to the heavenly academy.
The verse about bringing Judah to his people is cited within this story.
Judah could not follow the Sages' words or finish a halakha, and the verse on his hands sufficing for him is cited.
The verse that he will be a help against his adversaries is cited.
Rava asks Rabba for the source of a common saying that poverty follows the poor.
The mishna: the wealthy bring first-fruits in gold and silver vessels, while the poor bring them in willow baskets.
Rejoinder: that is your source, but I derive the matter from the verse on a different case.

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse on the impure becoming impure is cited as the basis for the preceding point.
Rava asks Rabba for the source of the saying that one should rise early and eat in summer and winter, as the proverb goes.
Rabba answers from Isaiah: they will not hunger or thirst, nor will the heat or sun strike them.
Rejoinder: that is the source for you, but I derive the matter from a different verse.
The verse in Exodus on serving God, blessing bread and water, and removing sickness is cited, with the meaning of its parts.
A baraita: the sickness that the verse removes is identified, and bread with salt and a jug of water cancel its many forms.
Rava asks Rabba for the source of the saying that a friend who calls you a donkey should be given a pack-animal's load.
Rabba answers from Genesis: Hagar explains that she is fleeing from her mistress Sarai.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that a shameful thing that is in you appears first in the east.
Rabba answers from Genesis: Abraham's servant says that he is the one who came.
Rava asks for the source of the saying about one who walks bent over, with his eyes looking about like a duck's.
Rabba answers from Samuel: God will do good to my lord and remember your handmaid.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that a tenth cup reaches the one who was passed over, and the other did not eat.
Rabba answers from Kings: Adonijah's guests were not called, including Solomon, Zadok, and Benaiah.
Rejoinder: that is the source for you, but I derive the matter from a different verse.
The Genesis verses on Isaac bringing Rebecca into Sarah's tent and Abraham taking Keturah are cited.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that wine gives benefit to its master but is a cure to its drinker.
Rabba cites the verses on laying hands on Joshua and Moses's laying of his hands on him.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that a dog in its hunger eats the dung of the donkey.
Rabba cites Proverbs: a satisfied soul treads on honey, while a hungry soul finds all bitter things sweet.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that a bad palm tree walks near a fruitless one, as it is dried.
Rava says the matter is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and in the Writings, as taught in the Mishna and a baraita.
Verses from the Torah, Prophets, and Writings are cited for the Esau-Ishmael, Jephthah, and Ben Sira examples.
A Mishna rules that whatever attaches to impurity is impure, and a baraita says a wagtail sought out a raven only for its kind.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that one who reads a friend's book should not ignore the bank of the river.
Rabba cites Ezekiel: you were cleansed, yet you were not cleansed from your impurity, so you will not be cleansed again.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that one should not throw a stone into a well from which one drank.
Rabba cites Deuteronomy: do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother, nor an Egyptian, for you were a stranger in his land.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that if there is no generation to delay, then one should not delay.
Rabba cites Judges: Barak tells Deborah that if she goes with him he will go, but if not, he will not go.
Rava asks for the source of the saying that when we were younger we were men, but now that we are old we are children.
Rava cites Exodus: God went before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire, and it is written later as well.

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse about God sending an angel before the people to guard them on the way is cited.
Rava asks Rabba for the source of the saying that after the master, his property is pulled away.
Rabba answers from Genesis: Lot, who went with Abram, had flocks, herds, and tents.
Rav Hanan: one who accuses his fellow of a matter is punished first, as the verse states.
Genesis verse: Sarai says to Abram that her wrong is upon him, cited as support.
Genesis verse: Abraham came to mourn Sarah and weep for her, cited for the case where one has a claim in the land.
Rabbi Yitzchak: woe to the one who cries out more than the one who is wronged, and a baraita agrees in substance.
Rabbi Yitzchak: never regard a common person's curse as light, since Abimelech cursed Sarah and it was fulfilled.
Genesis verse: the covering of the eyes given to Sarah is cited as the fulfillment of Abimelech's curse.
The Gemara's account: Sarah speaks to Abraham and the curse is fulfilled in her seed, with eyes covered in the house.
Genesis verse: when Isaac was old and his eyes dimmed, cited as the fulfillment of the curse.
Rabbi Avahu: a person should be among the pursued, not the pursuers, since the verse makes turtledoves and doves fit for the altar.
Mishna: one who blinds another's eyes, and so on, is liable as the mishna sets out.
Rav Asi asks Rava why the first clause of the mishna differs from the latter clause.
Rava answers: the first clause applies because a person cannot forgive harm to the head of his limbs.
Objection: can a person forgive his own pain, when a baraita says one who asks to be struck on condition of exemption is exempt?
Rav Asi asks whether Rava has heard anything about this matter.
Teachings in the names of Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Oshaya: the matter concerns family disgrace.
Rava: the matter is that a person cannot forgive harm to the head of his own limbs.
Rabbi Yochanan: some cases are a non-explicit prohibition, and some a negative precept that is a priestly matter.
A baraita is cited supporting Rabbi Yochanan's distinction between a case that is a stated matter and a case that is not.
Mishna: one who breaks a jug or tears a garment on condition of exemption is liable.
Objection from a verse: guard and do not lose, guard and do not tear, guard and do not distribute to the poor.
Rav Huna: there is no contradiction, since one case is where the item came into his hand and one where it did not.
Rabbah objects that guarding applies only to what came into his hand, so the reading is wrong.
Rabbah: both cases are consistent, since one comes into his hand as a guardian and the other as a tearer.
The story of a purse of charity deposited with Rav Yosef, who was negligent and was held liable after it was stolen.
Objection from Abaye: a baraita teaches guard and do not distribute to the poor, which conflicts with the ruling.
The poor of Pumbedita should be ordered to wait for summer; the guardian's duty is to guard, not to distribute.
The chapter-closing formula marking the end of the chapter that begins with the one who injures.

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a robber who turns wood into vessels or wool into garments, or who pays for a ewe or ram, must pay at the time of the robbery.
The Gemara restates the mishna's cases: wood made into vessels cannot be planed back, and wool made into garments cannot be unwoven.
Objection from a baraita: a robber who stole wood and planed it, or wool and combed it, pays at the time of the robbery, which conflicts.
Abaye: our mishna teaches a rabbinic change, and the rule is stronger for a Torah-level change.
Abaye continues: wood made into vessels is planed boards that can be returned to their original state, a rabbinic change.
Wool spun into cloth can be unraveled, so it is a rabbinic change; the mishna teaches only Torah-level change.
Rav Ashi: our mishna too teaches a Torah-level change, since bleaching is not a change that can be reversed.
Objection: a baraita says one who did not give the cloth to him until it was dyed is exempt, and one who did not dye it is liable.
Abaye: no contradiction, as one follows Rabbi Shimon and the other the Sages, who differ on whether carding and weaving combine.
Rava: both are Rabbi Shimon, with no contradiction, since one case is where the wool was combed and the other where it was carded.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abin: one case is where it was whitened and another where it was cleaned.
Now one may say that dyeing is not a change for Rabbi Shimon, while bleaching is a change.
A baraita on carding, dyeing, weaving and their combination is cited for the view of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda.
Abaye: no contradiction, as one is the view of the Sages according to Rabbi Shimon and the other is Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda's view.
Rava: the Sages do not dispute Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, but dyeing differs because it can be reversed with a dye-removal process.
Abaye: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda, Beit Shammai, and others hold that a change stays in its place.
What is the case of Beit Shammai, as we said?
A baraita: one who gave someone wheat for a sum and made it fine flour, olives and made oil, grapes and made wine.
One teaching forbids it, while another teaches that it is permitted, which conflicts with the rule.
Rav Yosef: teach the baraita Gurion, as it is the correct reading.

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel permit the mixed item, as the mishna states at the start of this section.
What is the reasoning of Beit Shammai?
Beit Shammai cite a verse read to include the changed forms of the item in the prohibition.
Beit Hillel cite the same verse, read to limit the prohibition to the item itself and not its changed forms.
Beit Shammai reply: the verse's word for them is needed to include their offspring, so the reading is different.
Beit Hillel: from the two readings we learn that the item is excluded and not its changed forms or offspring.
Objection: Beit Hillel also have the verse saying both, which conflicts with their reading.
What is the case of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov?
A baraita: a robber who baked stolen flour and separated challah cannot make the blessing, and the verse on blessing and cursing God applies.
What is the case of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?
A baraita: a robber who increased the value may take the increase, or tell the owner that his property is before him.
What is he saying?
Rav Sheshet: the baraita means that if the robber increased the value, the owner takes the increase, and the item stays in its place.
Objection: if so, even an increase should be explained by the ruling for those who return stolen goods.
What is the case of Rabbi Yishmael?
A baraita: the obligation of the corner of the field and separating from the sheaves, and tithing, is taught for the sake of Rabbi Yishmael.
On Rabbi Yishmael's behalf they said that one also separates from the dough and gives it to the owner.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether all these tanna'im repeat their views only to teach the view of Beit Shammai.
Abaye: no, Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not dispute this matter.
Rava resolves the disputes: each tanna's view applies only to the specific case of dyeing, a high-status item, or a blessing, with Rabbi Yishmael's view applying to the corner of the field.
The verse about leaving the remainder for the poor is cited to support Rabbi Yishmael's reading of the corner of the field.
Objection: if one says the verse teaches the gifts to the poor, that is different, since it is not the same case.
Rabbi Yonatan asks: what is the reason of Rabbi Yishmael, that a change does not acquire, or perhaps elsewhere he holds that a change acquires?
The Gemara answers: the reason is the verse about leaving the remainder, and if it is said the reason is that a change does not acquire, the verse teaches the corner.
Objection: why did the Torah write leave the remainder, and the Sages also need it, so the verse must be needed for something else.
A baraita: one who declares his vineyard ownerless and picks early is liable for the gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and corner, but exempt from tithes.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Objection: did Shmuel really say that, given his ruling that one does not assess for a thief or robber but only for damages?
For Rava, who says that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view concerns the case of contradiction that is reversed, there is no difficulty.
The halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, since a change stays in its place, in the case of a contradiction that is reversed.
Shmuel's ruling is about damages only, in the case of a contradiction that is not reversed.
For Abaye, who says that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view concerns a contradiction that is not reversed, what can be said?
Abaye teaches it this way: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said the matter as recorded.

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara states the ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
But Rav Yehuda does not hold that way, so the ruling cannot be attributed to him.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: a stolen item that was changed still returns to its owner, as a matter of Torah law.
The verse in Leviticus about returning the stolen item is cited as the source for the Torah-level rule.
But if you say our mishna is due to a rabbinic enactment for penitents, the Torah-level rule would not follow.
Objection: Rabbi Yochanan himself says the halakha follows the anonymous mishna, which denies a person who dyed the item liability.
Reply: the case is a robber who made stolen wood into vessels, a change that returns to its original state.
A baraita: the Sages do not accept returned money from robbers or from those who take interest, and the Sages do not favor the receiver.
Rabbi Yochanan: this mishna was taught in the days of Rabbi, as a baraita teaches.
A baraita story: a man who wished to repent was told by his wife that he would not be given even a belt, so he refrained and did not repent.
Objection from a baraita: the father left money from interest, and the sons, knowing it was interest, are not liable to return it.
Reply: the sons are not liable, but the father would be; the baraita's first clause concerns them, and the second clause is the proper teaching.
The second clause: the father left a cow, a cloak, and any specific item, and the sons are liable to return them out of respect for their father.
Explanation: the verse forbidding cursing a ruler of your people applies to one who repents, and here too the case is one who repented.
If he repented, what does the creditor need from him? He should have returned it, but he died before he could.
Objection from a baraita: even if they collected the money, robbers and those who lend at interest must return it, which is conflicting.
Objection from another baraita: the shepherds, tax collectors, and collectors have difficult repentance, and they return to those they know.
Objection: if so, why is their repentance difficult? And the second clause says that for those unknown, the money is used for public needs.
Rav Chisda: pits, cisterns, and caves are where the matter applies.
Reply: no contradiction, as one case is before the enactment and the other after it, and as Rav Nachman says, where the stolen item remains, both cases are after the enactment.

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reconciliation: here the stolen item stands where it is stolen, and there it stands where it is not stolen.
Objection: but a belt that was stolen still stands, which conflicts with the reconciliation.
What is the value of a belt? The Sages did not make an enactment where the stolen item still stands.
Objection from a mishna: one who built a stolen beam into a house must take its value, because of the enactment for penitents.
Reply: that case differs, since the house would be harmed, so the Sages established that the item is not considered stolen.
Mishna: one who steals a pregnant cow that then gives birth, and so on.
A baraita with three views: Rabbi Meir has the thief return the animal, its wool, and its offspring; Rabbi Yehuda says the stolen item returns; Rabbi Shimon says the item is valued in money.
The Gemara asks the basis of Rabbi Meir's view: does he hold that a change stays in its place, or that a change acquires, and here it is a penalty?
A baraita on stealing an animal that aged, or slaves that aged, is cited to show Rabbi Meir holds that a change acquires.
If Rabbi Meir holds that a change does not acquire, the baraita would not distinguish; so he holds that a change acquires, and here it is a penalty.
Reply: Rabbi Meir speaks according to the Rabbis' view; for the Gemara's own view a change does not acquire even for an animal, and a slave is treated as land.
A baraita: one who had a garment dyed red and the dyer dyed it black, or the reverse, Rabbi Meir says the dyer pays for the wool but not for the increase.
Reply: if Rabbi Meir held that a change does not acquire, he would pay the value of the wool and the increase, so he holds that a change acquires.
A baraita: if one stole a cow that aged, or slaves that aged, Rabbi Meir says the thief pays in the case of slaves, and the owner takes his property as it is.
Here it is a penalty; when does the penalty apply, only when done intentionally, or even when done unintentionally?
A baraita: five may be collected from those under a lien, including fruits, the increase of fruits, and a document of debt without guarantee.
Whose view is it that a guarantee is not a scribal error? It is Rabbi Meir, and the baraita teaches fruits and the increase of fruits.
The case is: one who stole a field from another, sold it to a third party, who improved it, and the owner can collect the increase as it leaves his hand.

95b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Creditor collects principal from sold property and enhancement from unsold property, since the owner takes both.
Is the purchaser perhaps an ignoramus who acted unintentionally, and if so does the baraita penalize even unintentional acquisition?
No, the case concerns a Torah scholar who knew the seller had no right to sell, so he is penalized.
A mishna on a dyer who ignored instructions shows the dyer pays only the wool's value, not its enhancement.
If unintentional acquisition were penalized, the dyer would owe enhancement too, so the mishna implies penalty only for intentional acts.
Rabbi Yehuda says the stolen item is returned as is, while Rabbi Shimon says it is appraised as of the robbery.
What is the practical difference between their positions, since both seem to agree the robber keeps no enhancement?
Rav Zevid says they disagree about enhancement still on the item: Yehuda gives it to the victim, Shimon to the robber.
Rav Pappa says both agree the robber keeps the enhancement, and they differ on whether he keeps a share like a shepherd.
A mishna on a pregnant cow or sheared ewe, read by inference, supports the view that the animal is returned as is.
By Rav Zevid, this mishna follows Yehuda, but by Rav Pappa it fits neither Yehuda nor Shimon, so the reading fails.
Rav Pappa replies that the robber pays the value at robbery in any case, and the mention of birth is just a matter of wording.
A baraita matches Rav Pappa's view, with Shimon appraising the item to fix the robber's share of enhancement.
Rav Ashi asks whether a robber's share of enhancement is paid in money or taken as a portion of the meat itself.
Rav Ashi says the question can be resolved from a ruling already given by Shmuel.
Shmuel's list of three cases where the court appraises enhancement and pays in money is brought as the source.
Ravina objects that Shmuel also says a creditor collects all enhancement, which contradicts the paying-in-money ruling.
Rav Ashi reconciles the two: one ruling concerns enhancement reaching shoulders, the other enhancement that does not.
Ravina objects that Shmuel collected even enhancement reaching shoulders in daily practice, so the reconciliation fails.
Rav Ashi again replies that this is not a difficulty, upholding his reconciliation.

96a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara restates the distinction: enhancement is collected when the debt covers both land and enhancement, not when it covers land alone.
Ravina objects that the distinction works only on one view of whether a purchaser with money can remove the creditor.
Rav Ashi replies that the debtor designated this field alone as repayment, so the creditor has a lien only on it.
Rava rules that a robber who enhances and sells or bequeaths stolen property passes on the enhancement, and the victim must pay for it.
Rava asks whether a purchaser who enhanced the stolen item must be paid for the enhancement by the victim.
Rava resolves his own question: a seller transfers every right that will come to him, including rights to the enhancement.
Rava asks whether enhancement made by a gentile robber is compensated.
Rav Aha objects that this would institute an ordinance for the benefit of a gentile.
Ravina replies the case is where a gentile sold to a Jew, so the Jew is like the gentile and gets no rights.
The case is clarified: a Jew robbed, a gentile enhanced and sold, and then a Jew bought it.
Should the ordinance apply when a Jew robbed the item and a Jew later bought it, with a gentile between them? The question is left unresolved.
Rav Pappa rules that a robber who cut down a stolen palm tree and moved it does not acquire it.
What is the reason for that ruling?
The tree is still called a palm tree after being cut, so the change is not significant enough to acquire it.
Rav Pappa lists further changes: fashioning logs into beams or boards acquires them, but shrinking large beams to small ones does not.
Rava rules on palm fronds, leaves and brooms: a change that makes the item a new kind acquires it, but a broom made into rope does not.
What is the reason a broom made into rope is not acquired?
The robber could unravel the rope back into a broom, so the change is not permanent and he does not acquire it.
Rav Pappa asks whether splitting the central twin-leaf of a lulav counts as a change that lets the robber acquire it.
A baraita says that if the central twin-leaf was removed, the lulav is unfit, which is brought to settle the question.

96b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the split twin-leaf case should be like the previous one, so the robber acquires the lulav by the change.
Replies that a removed leaf makes the lulav lacking and unfit, unlike a split leaf that leaves it complete and unchanged.
Brings a baraita saying a split twin-leaf makes the lulav like one with the leaf removed, implying the robber acquires it.
Rav Pappa rules that a robber who turns earth into a brick does not acquire it, but one who turns a brick into earth does.
Objects that the robber might return the brick to its original form and so should not acquire it either.
Replies that the brick made from earth is a different brick, so a new entity has come into existence.
Rav Pappa rules that a robber who turns a silver bar into coins does not acquire it, but one who turns coins into a bar does.
Objects that the robber might melt the coins back into a bar, so he should not acquire them either.
Replies that the coins made from the bar are new coins, so a new entity has come into existence.
Rav Pappa rules that cleaning old black coins to make them new does not acquire them, but blackening new coins does.
Objects that the robber might clean the blackened coins back to new, so he should not acquire them.
Replies that the blackness of the coins was already known, so the change is irreversible and the robber acquires them.
The mishna states the principle that all robbers pay the value the item had at the time of the robbery.
Asks what the words stating the principle add to the mishna.
Rabbi Ela says a stolen lamb that became a ram, or calf that became an ox, is acquired by the change, so no fourfold penalty applies.
Tells of a robber who used stolen oxen to plow and sow, and Rav Nachman rules he pays half the land's enhancement.
Rava objects that the oxen did not alone cause the enhancement, and a stolen item should be returned as it was.
Rav Nachman rebukes Rava for questioning his rulings and says he compels this experienced robber to pay the enhancement.
The mishna says a robber pays the value at the time of robbery if the animal or slaves aged; Rabbi Meir says for slaves, the item is returned.
The mishna says a robber pays the value at robbery if a coin cracked, produce rotted, or wine fermented.
The mishna lists cases where the robber returns the item as is, such as invalidated coins, impure teruma, and a goring ox.
Rav Pappa explains that aging in the mishna includes a weakening so severe the animal will never regain its former health.
Objects that the mishna itself says aged, so a lesser weakening should not count as a change.
Rav Pappa replies that he meant a weakening that is like aging, from which the animal will not return to health.
Mar Kashisha transmits Rav Yochanan's ruling that a stolen lamb or calf that changed is acquired by the robber.
Rav Ashi objects that this teaching was stated in the name of Rabbi Ela, not Rabbi Yochanan, so the attribution is wrong.
The mishna states Rabbi Meir's view that for Canaanite slaves the robber says that which is yours is before you.
Rav Ḥanina bar Avdimi transmits Rav's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir.
Asks how Rav could set aside the majority of Sages and rule in accordance with Rabbi Meir.
