Explains that a baraita is taught with the opinions reversed, and Rav also taught the mishna in the opposite way.
Asks what Rav's reason was for reversing the mishna's opinions.
Objects that Rav should rather reverse the baraita to match the mishna, rather than reverse the mishna.
Replies that Rav also learned the mishna in the reversed order, so the text he used matched the baraita.
Offers another explanation: Rav reversed one mishna based on two baraitot, a principle that applies in this case.
Brings a Tosefta on disputes over offspring of exchanged animals or sold slaves, where Rabbis say no oath applies to slaves or land.
Rav's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir is stated, though the Rabbis are the ones who hold this position.
Asks why Rav did not simply say the halakha follows the Rabbis, since that is what he means.
Explains that Rav is speaking according to the reversed version, where Rabbi Meir is the one saying the robber says that which is yours is before you.

97a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that if a slave is like land for Rav, the one who used him should be exempt, which seems to contradict the view of the slave being like land.
Explains the case is one where the slave was used outside working hours, so the owner lost nothing, as with the courtyard rent ruling.
Rejects the comparison: a courtyard is satisfactory to its owner in either reasoning, but a slave's weakening is not satisfactory to his owner.
Asks whether it is satisfactory to the owner that his slave be weakened by labor for another.
Replies that it is satisfactory to the owner that the slave's work habits are not undone.
Tells how Rav Yosef bar Ḥama's household seized debtors' slaves with his approval and made them work against the owners' will.
Rabba asks his father why he does this.
Rav Yosef cites Rav Naḥman that a slave is not worth his bread, and his son answers that this applies only to a slave who does no labor.
Rav Yosef bar Ḥama says he follows Rav Daniel, who exempts one who seizes a slave and works him from paying the master.
Rabba objects that this applies only when the seizer is not owed money, since otherwise it looks like interest.
Cites Rav Naḥman's ruling that one who lends money and then lives in the creditor's courtyard must pay rent to avoid the appearance of interest.
Rav Yosef bar Ḥama concedes and says he will stop seizing his debtors' slaves.
Rav says the ship's owner may take the larger of rent or diminished value, while Shmuel says only the diminished value.
Rav Pappa reconciles them: one case is a ship available for rent, and the difference lies in whether the seizer intended to rent or rob.
The mishna says a robber who cracked a coin pays its value at robbery, while an invalidated coin is returned as is.
Rav Huna explains that cracked means actually cracked, and invalidated means invalidated by the government.
Rav Yehuda says a coin invalidated by the government is like a cracked coin, and the mishna refers to a coin valid in another province.
Rav Ḥisda objects that if invalidation counts as a change, then the mishna's rotting produce and fermented wine should also be treated the same.
Rav Huna replies that produce and wine changed in taste and smell, while the coin itself did not change.
Rava objects to Rav Yehuda that the mishna's impure teruma, which is like an invalidated coin, is returned as is.
Rav Yehuda replies that teruma's damage is not visible, while the invalidated coin's loss of value is evident on sight.
Introduces a dispute over a loan repayable in a coin that later becomes invalidated, where Rav gives his ruling.

97b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel rules the debtor may repay with an invalidated coin, telling the creditor to spend it in a place where it is still valid.
Rav Naḥman explains Shmuel: this applies only when the creditor plans to travel to that place.
Rava objects from a baraita that second-tithe sanctity cannot transfer to coins not in circulation, without distinguishing travel plans.
Rav Naḥman replies that the baraita's kingdoms let such coins leave their borders, so they count as valid where spent.
Asks how Shmuel's coins could be brought into another kingdom if the kingdoms are particular and confiscate invalid coins.
Replies that the coins can be brought with difficulty, since authorities search only sometimes, though they are particular when they do.
Brings a baraita that sanctity cannot transfer to Eretz Yisrael coins in Babylonia or Babylonian coins in Eretz Yisrael, to challenge Shmuel.
Explains the case is one where the kingdoms are especially particular and the coins cannot be transported.
Asks what use Babylonian coins would have in Babylonia if they could never reach Jerusalem.
Replies that such coins are used in Babylonia to buy an animal to bring up to Jerusalem.
Cites a baraita that all money circulates in Jerusalem, seeming to conflict with the restriction on Babylonian coins.
Rabbi Zeira says the two baraitot refer to different times, depending on whether Israel or the nations hold power.
Describes the coins of ancient Jerusalem and of Abraham, with their inscriptions, as taught in a baraita.
Rava asks Rav Ḥisda whether a debtor repays a loan with a coin the government has enlarged, or the original weight.
Rav Ḥisda says the debtor gives the coin in circulation at payment, even if it is very large, as Rava presses.
Rava objects that a heavier coin lowers produce prices, so repaying with it gives the creditor interest.
Rav Ashi replies that if the price fell due to the coin's change, the debt is reduced accordingly for the debtor.

98a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If produce lost value because of market prices, the debt is not reduced for the debtor.
Challenges the rule: a coin's metal content rises in value when melted, so repaying with it would be interest.
Gives a precedent of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua exchanging old dinars at a set ratio.
Rabba rules that one who throws another's coin into the Great Sea is exempt, since it lies before the owner who can take it.
Rava objects from a baraita that money lost in the Great Sea is considered lost, which conflicts with Rabba's view.
Rabba rules that one who effaces a coin's image is exempt, but one who files it down must pay for the loss.
Rava objects from a baraita that a slave struck near his eye or ear and not blinded or deafened is not freed.
Explains Rabba follows his own view that deafening a father causes unseen injury, so a coin's flattening is different.
Rabba rules that one who slits the ear of another's cow is exempt, since the cow keeps its other uses.
Rava objects from a baraita that acts involving red heifer water are exempt by human law, implying visible harm is liable.
The Sages respond that even slitting an ear is exempt by human law, and the baraita is teaching about invisible damage.
Rabba rules that one who burns another's promissory note is exempt, since the lender still owns the debt in principle.
Rami bar Ḥama objects and asks what the circumstances of Rabba's ruling are.

98b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If no witnesses know what the promissory note said, how can liability be assessed at all?
Rava says it refers to a case where the debtor trusts the creditor's account of what the note said.
Rav Dimi bar Ḥanina says Rabba's ruling that burning a promissory note is exempt follows the Rabbis against Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objects that Rabba's ruling on burning leavened bread shows Rabbi Shimon's view applies to items of monetary value.
Explains that for Rabbi Shimon the damage counts as liability, while the Rabbis exempt it when the item lacks intrinsic monetary value.
Asks whether, on Rabbi Shimon's view, a promissory note with no intrinsic value is still considered to have monetary value.
Ameimar rules that the burner of a note pays the debt amount or only the paper's value, depending on the view; an incident follows.
The mishna says that for leavened bread that Passover elapsed over, the robber says that which is yours is before you.
Asks which tanna holds that for items whose benefit is forbidden one says that which is yours is before you.
Rav Ḥisda says it is Rabbi Yaakov, as a baraita teaches.
Cites a baraita on an ox sentenced to be stoned, where Rabbi Yaakov allows return even after sentencing.
Asks whether the disagreement is really about returning items whose benefit is forbidden, as Rav Ḥisda concludes.
Rabba replies that everyone agrees such items may be returned, so the dispute must concern something else.
Rabba points out that the Passover case would then be disputed too, and so the dispute must be about a different point.
Rabba explains the dispute: the Rabbis say an ox cannot be sentenced in its absence, while Rabbi Yaakov says it can.
Rav Ḥisda meets Rabba bar Shmuel and their conversation about returning forbidden items begins.
Rav Ḥisda asks whether Rabba bar Shmuel has learned any teaching on returning items whose benefit is forbidden.
Rabba bar Shmuel says yes, a baraita learned from a verse.
Cites the verse on restoring what was robbed as the basis that the robber must return the same item.
A baraita lists cases where the robber says that which is yours is before you, including invalidated coins and rotted produce.
Argues that the Rabbis do agree the forbidden-benefit item is returned as is, so Rav Ḥisda's analysis fails.
Rav Ḥisda tells Rabba bar Shmuel not to tell the Sages he erred.
A baraita says that if produce rotted, the robber says that which is yours is before you.
Objects that a mishna says a robber pays the value at robbery when produce rotted, so the baraita conflicts with it.
Rav Pappa reconciles: the mishna covers all the produce rotting, while the baraita covers only part of it.
The mishna says craftsmen who damage items given to them to fix are liable, and a builder who breaks stones or damages them too.
Rav Asi explains the rule applies only when the carpenter was given finished vessels to fix and then broke them.
Asks the reason a carpenter who builds from given wood is exempt.
A craftsman acquires a vessel through the enhancement of his work, so damage to it is damage to his own property.
Challenges Rav Asi by asking whether the mishna's first clause refers to giving wood, which would contradict him.

Asks how the analogy works if one Tanna holds that the first case concerns a thief and the second a claimant, and the other does not.
Explains that the phrase refers to the thief himself.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba objects to Rabbi Yochanan with a baraita on a claimant who admits eating, noting that the baraita requires double payment.
Asks what case the baraita concerns, since the baraita says double payment.
Explains the case: he ate a carcass, or a tereifah, or a son of an improperly slaughtered animal, or he stood in court and was told to pay.
Cites Rava's ruling that one who slaughters and sells is liable only once, as support for the point.
Asks why the thief remains a thief as long as the matter is undecided, and whether one could explain it as a partner.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who claims theft about a lost item pays double.
Cites Exodus 22:8, on every lost item about which one says, as the reason for the ruling.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects with Exodus 22:6 and 22:8, arguing that giving and claiming must both be adult.
Answers that the case is one where he ate while a minor, and as an adult he pays by the same reasoning.
Asks why the baraita does not say eating and claiming must both be equal, if that is the point.
Rav Ashi replies that a lost item comes from a person of intent, while the other case does not.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: a claimant of theft about a deposit is not liable unless he denies in part and admits in part.
Cites Exodus 22:8, which says this is that, as the source for that ruling.
Introduces the dispute of Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef, who holds a differing view.

107a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the passages are mixed up, since the verse about the loan is written here.
Cites Exodus 22:8, which says this is that, as the verse the passage relies on.
Asks whether the case is a loan, and what the difference is between a loan and other cases.
Introduces Rabba's ruling on a claim that is partly admitted.
Asks why the Torah says that one who admits part of a claim must swear about the rest.
Explains that a person does not brazenly deny a debt to the creditor's face, so the claimant must swear on the whole, and a loan differs from a deposit.
Rami bar Chama taught about the four types of bailees.

107b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists the cases that require denial in part and admission in part: the unpaid bailee, the borrower, and the paid bailee and hirer.
Rava asks the reason Rami bar Chama holds that the unpaid bailee is explicitly written in the verse.
Derives the paid bailee from the unpaid bailee by a verbal analogy, and reads the vav as adding to the first matter.
Explains which bailee the hirer resembles, under each of the two opinions.
Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef states that a claimant of theft about a deposit is not liable until he has laid his hand on it.
Gives the reason from Exodus 22:7 and infers that the Mishnah speaks of one who did lay his hand on the item.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba states that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling applies to an animal standing at the manger.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether the ruling applies only to the animal at the manger, or even when the hand was laid on it.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba cites Rav Asi's report of Rabbi Yochanan: a claimant of loss who then claims theft is exempt.
Explains the exemption: the owner was already discharged by the first oath.
Restates the same teaching about a claimant of loss in a deposit who later claims theft.
Rav Sheshet's ruling: a claimant of theft about a deposit is exempt once he has laid his hand on it.
Derives the ruling from the verse of Exodus 22:7: he is exempt only if he did not lay his hand on it.
Rav Nachman objects that three oaths are imposed on the bailee, including one that the item is not in his control.
Replies by analogy: the oath that he did not lay his hand on the item is exempt from double payment when it is proven he did.
Rami bar Chama asks whether an oath that obligates double payment exempts from the fifth, or the reverse, and what the case is.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether money that obligates double payment exempts from the fifth, or whether the oath does, when witnesses and admission both occur.
Rava cites a baraita: a person who denies theft and swears, then witnesses come, pays double; if he admits on his own, he pays principal and fifth.
Objects that witnesses, not the oath, are what make him liable for double, and concludes that money which obligates double also exempts from the fifth.
Ravina asks whether two people sharing an ox who each swear, and witnesses come for one, yield one or two fifths in one case.
Rav Pappa asks whether two fifths or two double payments arise from one person, and whether the verse rules differently for two kinds of money.
Rava's proof from Leviticus 5:24: the Torah multiplied fifths over one principal, so the fifth is money.
Asks to whom the double payment is due when the owner sued the bailee, who swore and paid, and then the thief was found.
Abaye holds that the double payment goes to the owner of the deposit, since the bailee's oath burdened him.
Rava holds that the double payment goes to the bailee, since he paid; the two disagree on the Mishnah's wording.
Cites the Mishnah on one who deposits animals or utensils that are stolen or lost, and whether the bailee pays or swears.
Abaye infers from the first clause, and Rava from the last clause, explaining the reason the bailee did not wish to swear.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava infers from the Mishnah's latter clause that the bailee pays the owner only when he did not wish to pay before swearing.
Asks how the Mishnah's latter clause fits with Abaye's view that the payment goes to the owner of the deposit.
Abaye replies that the Mishnah teaches he swore and refused to pay before the oath, so he pays after it to the owner.
Asks how the Mishnah's first clause fits with Rava's view.
Rava replies that the Mishnah teaches he paid and did not wish to stand by his oath, so he pays the one who holds the deposit.
Presents a case where the owner sued the bailee, who swore and the thief was found, and asks whether the thief is exempt by the bailee's admission.
Rava resolves that if the bailee swore truthfully the thief is exempt by his admission, but if falsely he is not exempt.
Rava asks whether a bailee who wished to swear falsely but was not allowed to do so is treated as having sworn; the answer is left undecided.
Rav Kahana teaches the ruling in the form of this question, and Rav teaches it differently.
Rava asks what the law is if the bailee swore falsely; the answer is again left undecided.
Asks whether the thief is exempt when the owner admitted, and whether the bailee can say to the owner that he has the item instead.
Abaye rules: if the bailee was unpaid and wished to swear, he may do so; if he was paid, he makes the case with the owner and does not swear.
Rava rules that in both cases the bailee makes the case with the owner and does not swear.
Objects that this would contradict Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling, which allowed the unpaid bailee to swear.
Rava explains the case: the bailee swore first, and the ruling applies only where he has already sworn.
Rabah Zuti asks whether a deposit that was stolen under duress and returned, then lost through negligence, still counts as protected; the answer is left undecided.
Mishnah: cases of a claimant who swears, a thief who is found, one who robs his father and swears, and one who pledges property to his son.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: a robber's heirs may not keep the stolen item, but return it to his sons or brothers, and creditors collect when there are no heirs.
Rav Yosef rules that this applies even to the purse of charity.
Rav Pappa rules that the robber must say that this was his father's robbery.
Asks why the robber would waive the claim for himself.
Cites the Mishnah that a victim may waive the principal but not the fifth, showing that a waiver is effective.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that there is no difficulty: one is Rabbi Yossi the Galilean and the other Rabbi Akiva.
Cites a baraita on Numbers 5:8: a robber's heirs and the court, with Rabbi Yossi the Galilean and Rabbi Akiva disagreeing about the remedy.
Explains the positions: Rabbi Yossi permits waiver for others but not for oneself, while Rabbi Akiva bars it in both cases.
Rav Sheshet objects that the case would then have to be taught in two stages, which makes the teaching redundant.
Rav Sheshet resolves the baraita: Rabbi Yossi allows waiver for others but not for oneself, and the other party gains by the lien.
Rava resolves the difficulty by saying Rabbi Akiva's ruling bars a robber from waiving for himself but allows waiver for others.

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Infers from the view of Rabbi Yossi the Galilean that he holds even the robber himself may waive the claim.
Asks how the Torah's rule of giving the robbery to the priests can apply to a convert's robbery.
Rava explains the case: he robbed a convert who swore, the convert died, and he admitted after death, so God assigns it to the priests.
Ravina asks whether a robbery by a female convert is covered, since the verse says a man.
Rav Aharon cites a baraita on Numbers 5:8 about a robber's heirs and the priests, and reasons from the verse about a robbery that is returned to the priests.
Objects that Numbers 5:10 says each man's holy things belong to him, which seems to conflict with the rule.
Resolves the objection: the verse refers to a priest who is impure, who has no share in the item.
Cites a baraita on Leviticus 27:21 and Numbers 5:10, and on the priest who brings offerings at any time and gets the skins.
Explains the case: if the animal had a blemish, it is given to the priest of that watch, and the skin and service belong to him.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the priest who is to receive the robbery is old or sick, it is given to any priest of his choice, while the service and skin go to the watch.
Asks how an old or sick priest can be the one who receives the payment, if he cannot perform the service himself.
Rav Pappa explains that he can perform the service with difficulty, and eating with difficulty is coarse and counts for nothing.
Rav Sheshet holds that a priest who is impure, bringing a communal offering, gives it to any priest and the skin goes to the watch.
Asks how that case works, if there are pure priests or if there are none, and who may eat.
Rava suggests the case is one of pure priests with blemishes, of that watch.
Rav Ashi states the case of a High Priest who is a mourner: he gives to any priest, and the service and skin go to the watch.
Asks what this teaches us, since it is already taught in the Mishnah.
Explains that the Mishnah's point is that a mourner High Priest cannot appoint a deputy, though he may give to relatives.
Mishnah: a robber of a convert who swears and dies pays principal and fifth to the priests and the guilt-offering to the altar; the fifth is not essential.
Cites several baraitot on the words asham and hashav, showing which part is principal and which the fifth, and what the case covers.
Rava rules that a robbery of a convert returned at night is not a valid return, nor is one returned in halves, and that it must reach each priest.
Cites the verse on the guilt-offering, requiring a return to each priest, as support for Rava's ruling.
Rava asks whether a deposit of the convert's robbery belongs to the watch of Yehoyariv, or to the watch it belongs to.

110b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a priest's share can be given to a priest of the watch of Yedaiah, or whether the watch of Yehoyariv is the one it belongs to.
Rava asks whether priests may divide a robbery of a convert against another such robbery, by analogy to the guilt-offering.
Rav Acha son of Rava teaches it explicitly, and Rava rules that priests may not divide a robbery of a convert against another.
Rava asks whether priests inherit or receive gifts from a convert's robbery, and what practical difference this makes.
Rav Zeira asks whether, even if priests receive gifts, the gift of ten animals from a robbery is subject to tithe, citing a Mishnah.
Cites a baraita listing the twenty-four priestly gifts, including the robbery of a convert, as support for the point that they are gifts.
Concludes that the word gift shows the priests receive gifts, not inheritance.
States a fragment of the Mishnah: the priest gives the money to the watch.
Abaye infers that money atones for half, and argues by analogy from a sin-offering and a guilt-offering whose owner died.

111a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara cites Resh Lakish's saying that it is better to give a little than to leave a widow, as a remark on the case.
Mishnah fragment: the priest gives the money to the watch of Yehoyariv.
Baraita: if the guilt-offering was given to Yehoyariv and the money to Yedaiah, the money is returned against the guilt-offering, says Rabbi Yehuda; the Sages say the reverse.
Asks how the case works if the guilt-offering was given to Yehoyariv's watch and the money to Yedaiah's watch, with each claiming its own.
Rava explains the case, and the Gemara gives the reasons for Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that the owners are penalized, and the Sages' view that the priests acted improperly.
Baraita on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling: if the priests of Yehoyariv offered the guilt-offering first, the offering is invalid and its hide goes to the owner.
Objects that the baraita has Rabbi Yehuda returning the money against the guilt-offering, which conflicts with his stated view.
Explains the case: the watches left and no one claimed, so the waiver was made between them.
Second baraita: if the guilt-offering remains, the money is returned against it, which is obvious in Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Explains the second baraita: the case is one where both watches left and did not claim the money.
Asks what if one would say the priests waived claims against each other.
Teaches that since they did not claim, the return is made first in the usual way.
Mishnah fragment: one who brings back the stolen item before bringing his guilt-offering has not fulfilled the obligation.
Asks where the rule that the money comes first is derived from.
Rava derives the rule from Numbers 5:8, where the words the guilt-offering comes first, implying the money comes first.
Objects that by the same logic the regular offering would come first, and a baraita says nothing precedes the morning offering.
Rava replies that the burnt offering is the first offering, while the other party derives the point from which he atones, which has not been completed.
Mishnah fragment: the owner gives him the principal.
Baraita: one who brings the money but not the guilt-offering has not fulfilled, and a guilt-offering that is consecrated and the one not consecrated are compared; the fifth does not hinder.
Chapter closing formula: the end of the chapter that begins with the robber who gathered wood.

111b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: heirs of a robber who fed stolen goods to children are exempt, but liable for guaranteed property.
Rav Hisda holds the owner may collect from either robber while he has not despaired of recovery.
Asks the reason the owner may choose whichever robber to collect from.
Stolen property stays the owner's, so the second robber took from the owner and the first remains liable.
Cites the mishna on the robber's children as a refutation of Rav Hisda's view.
Rav Hisda replies that the mishna applies only after the owners have despaired of recovery.
Rami bar Hama holds an heir's domain is equivalent to a buyer's, so the item fully changes hands.
Rava disagrees: an heir's domain is not equivalent to a buyer's, so the item does not fully change hands.
Asks how Rava explains the mishna in light of his own position.
Explains the mishna as dealing with a case where the stolen goods were already eaten.
The second clause implies the first clause concerns extant stolen property, supporting the inference.
Rava replies that the mishna means only guaranteed family property, even if the stolen item is gone.
Objects that Rabbi taught his son the mishna covers even a plowing cow or donkey, implying extant property.
Rava replies that he follows Rabbi Oshaya's interpretation, which he presents as the correct reading.
Brings Rabbi Oshaya's baraita to support Rava's reading of the mishna.
Claims the baraita refutes Rav Hisda, since it exempts heirs for consumed goods.
Rav Hisda replies that the baraita addresses cases after the owners despaired.
Claims the baraita refutes Rami bar Hama, since it obligates heirs for extant stolen goods.
Rami bar Hama replies that the baraita addresses a case after despair, mirroring Rav Hisda's reply.

112a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Adda bar Ahava teaches Rami bar Hama's principle on a case of heirs holding interest money they know is interest.
Rami bar Hama says an heir's domain equals a buyer's, so inherited property is acquired and the heirs are exempt.
Rava rejects that equivalence: an heir's domain is not like a buyer's.
Rava says the interest case is different, given the reasoning that follows.
Brings the verse forbidding taking interest from one's brother, so the father, not the sons, is cautioned to repay it.
Explains how the two teachers read Rami bar Hama's statement, on the baraita or on the mishna.
Cites a baraita: heirs must repay stolen goods if adult, while minors are exempt; adults who say they lack the accounts are exempt.
Asks why heirs who say they do not know the accounts should be exempt, since they hold stolen property.
Rava clarifies that the heirs claim to know the accounts and that nothing is owed, so they are exempt.
Cites a second baraita: heirs who consumed stolen goods are obligated, whether adult or minor.
Objects that minors should not be liable, since a minor causing damage is exempt; the rule must be restated.
Rav Pappa restates the baraita: the obligation applies when the stolen goods are still extant and not yet eaten.
Rava rules on a borrowed cow that died under heirs, then on heirs who ate it, adding that guaranteed land means payment.
Explains that the final ruling of Rava is read in two ways, with different implications for the two clauses.
Rav Pappa holds that a stolen cow slaughtered on Shabbat creates liability, while a borrowed one does not.
Brings a baraita expounding the verse about restoring the item robbed, to argue the robber must return the same item.
Derives from that exposition the baraita rule: heirs who received stolen goods must return them, adult or minor.
Attributes to Sumakhos the view that adult heirs are obligated but minors are exempt.
Narrates a dispute: a minor brother-in-law shut the house door against Rabbi Yirmeya, who brought the matter to Rabbi Avin.
Rabbi Avin rules that the brother-in-law is the claimant, since he holds the presumptive ownership of his father's house.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that he can produce witnesses who saw him take possession during the father's lifetime.
Rabbi Avin asks whether the court accepts such witnesses at all.

112b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that a teaching obligates adult and minor heirs alike, and notes that Sumakhos's dispute is on the other side.
Replies that everyone agrees, and the position stands like Sumakhos, to exclude the view being attacked.
Narrates that the matter reached Rabbi Abbahu, who then responds to the dispute.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Rav Yosef bar Hama's teaching in the name of Rabbi Oshaya as a source.
States the rule: a minor who seizes a field is removed from it and must bring witnesses once grown.
Asks whether that case is comparable, since the minor lacks his father's possession here.
Rav Ashi reports Rabbi Shabtai's view that witnesses are accepted even when the litigant is absent.
Rabbi Yohanan objects: how can witnesses be accepted in the absence of the litigant?
Explains Rabbi Yose bar Hanina's accepting such witnesses when the litigant or witnesses were ill or traveling.
Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's view that witnesses are accepted when the litigant is absent.
Mar Ukva says Shmuel's view was clarified to him: it applies when the court summoned the litigant who did not come.
Rules that the absent party may claim he will go to the great court, whether or not the case was opened for him.
Ravina explains that the case concerns a party who took a writ from the great court.
Rav holds that a document is ratified in the absence of the litigant.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that a document is not ratified in the absence of the litigant.
Rav Sheshet offers to explain the reasoning behind Rabbi Yohanan's position.
Brings the verse about the ox's owner standing by his ox to support the view that the litigant must be present.
Rava rules that the court ratifies a document in the litigant's absence, even if he stands and protests.
Rules that a litigant who asks for time to bring witnesses against a document is granted three additional court days.
Rules that the court issues a ninety-day ostracism notice and does not seize property during the first thirty days.
Gives the reason for not seizing property during the middle thirty days: the debtor may be selling property to pay.
Rules that after ninety days a document of authorization is written, and it is issued at once if the debtor refuses to come.
Rules that the ninety-day waiting period applies to loans but not to deposits, where the document is written immediately.
Rules that the document of authorization covers only land, not movable property, to protect the debtor's chance to recover.
Rules that if the creditor owns land, a document may be drawn up to collect from any property of the debtor.
Objects that this is not so: no document covers movables even with the creditor's land, since land may depreciate.
Rules that the debtor is notified before the document is written only when he lives nearby, not when distant.
Rules that for a distant debtor with relatives nearby or passing caravans, the court waits up to a year.
Cites Ravina's earlier delay of twelve months for Mar Aha, until a caravan went and returned, as a precedent.
Objects that Ravina's case differs, because that creditor was violent and the document could not be retrieved from him.
Rules that in ordinary cases the court waits only until a messenger goes and returns within the week.
Ravina holds the court's messenger is credible like two witnesses for excommunication, but not for issuing a document.
Ravina rules that a defendant may be given a time to appear by word of mouth from a trusted woman or neighbors.
Qualifies that this applies only when the defendant is not in the city.

113a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rule: a defendant in town who was told by the court's agent cannot claim he did not hear of the summons.
Qualifies the rule: it applies only if he did not pass the court's door, and only if he came on the same day.
Rava rules that the writ is torn for one who does not appear, and only once he agrees to obey.
Objects that this is not so: the writ is torn as soon as the defendant says he will obey.
Rav Hisda rules that courts fix sessions on Monday and Thursday, with later sessions set in turn, written for the next day.
Narrates that Rav Asi visited Rav Kahana and saw a woman summoned morning and evening, with a writ written against her.
Rav Asi asks whether the master holds Rav Hisda's ruling about fixed Monday and Thursday sessions.
Rav Kahana replies that the ruling covers a man who was prevented and absent, while a woman in town who does not come is rebellious.
Rav Yehuda rules that no session is set on Nisan or Tishrei holidays or the eve of festivals, nor on Friday eve of Shabbat.
Asks the reason for not setting sessions on the eve of Shabbat.
Explains that the litigant is occupied with preparing for Shabbat.
Rav Nahman rules that a session is not given to a wedding party for a wedding, nor to a group for a group, in general.
Gives the reason: he fears that, nowadays, there are deceivers who would exploit this arrangement.
Cites the earlier mishna and Rabbi's teaching to his son that even a plow cow or donkey must be returned, to support the claim.
Rav Kahana asks Rav what the law is for one who lives on another's table and eats at his table.
Rav replies with the verse from Proverbs, giving to the wise and he will become wiser still.
Mishna: one does not take from the tax collector's purse or charity box, but may take from his own home or the market; a baraita adds the rest.
Objects: but Shmuel held that the law of the kingdom is law, so tax collectors' dealings are binding.
Qualifies Shmuel's ruling: it applies only to a tax collector with no fixed rate, and the house of Rabbi Yannai says to the one who acts on his own.
States the teaching that one may not wear mixed fibers, even on ten garments, to smuggle goods past the tax.
Cites a baraita showing the mishna does not follow Rabbi Akiva's position that smuggling past the tax is permitted.
Explains that the two views dispute whether an unintended act is permitted, and that the prohibition on smuggling stands.
Asks who then permits smuggling to avoid the tax.
Objects again with Shmuel's principle that the law of the kingdom is law.
Repeats the qualification: Shmuel's ruling concerns a tax collector without a fixed rate, as the house of Rabbi Yannai says.
States the teaching that vows may be made to tax collectors, whether or not the item is an offering or royal property.
Objects once more with Shmuel's principle that the law of the kingdom is law.
Repeats the qualification that the ruling concerns a tax collector without a fixed rate, per the house of Rabbi Yannai.
Rav Ashi says the case is a tax collector who is a Canaanite, as taught in a baraita about an Israelite and a Canaanite forced to court.
Brings the baraita: if one can win under Israelite law, do so; if not, tell the Canaanite the rule and circumvent.
Gives Rabbi Yishmael's view that one may come against the Canaanite by circumvention.
Gives Rabbi Akiva's view that one may not circumvent, because of sanctifying God's name.
Asks whether robbing a Canaanite is permitted.
Objects that a baraita taught Rabbi Akiva derived from the verse that robbing a Canaanite is forbidden.

113b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives from the verse about reckoning with the buyer that a creditor may not hold a pledge to lock in the debtor.
Rav Yosef resolves the apparent conflict: one verse concerns a Canaanite slave, the other a resident stranger.
Abaye objects that both verses are written side by side, so the resolution does not hold.
Cites the verses about strangers and resident aliens, showing the law applies to the idolater who is a resident.
Rava answers there is no conflict: one case concerns a robbed item, the other a forfeited loan.
Abaye objects that a Hebrew slave's forfeited loan cannot be the same as his case.
Explains Rava's position is consistent with his view that a Hebrew slave's body is owned by his master.
Reports R' Shimon Hasida's view: robbing a Canaanite is forbidden, but finding his lost item is permitted.
Rav Huna derives from the verse about eating the nations' possessions that robbery of a Canaanite is forbidden only when they are in your hand.
Rav Hama reports Rav's rule that the lost item of a Canaanite is permitted to keep.
Asks from where the permission to keep a Canaanite's lost item is derived.
Derives the rule from the verse on returning a brother's lost item to a brother, not to a Canaanite.
Objects that the rule may apply only where the item cannot reach its owner, not where it can be returned.
Ravina derives from the verse about finding it that the rule holds when the item reaches the finder's hand.
Reports R' Pinchas ben Yair: where there is a desecration of God's name, even a lost item is forbidden.
Shmuel rules that a mistaken payment, a loss through error, is permitted to keep.
Cites examples of Shmuel, Rav Kahana and Ravina trading with Cutheans, where the mistake was returned or kept.
Rav Ashi's example: a Cuthean's vine tendrils hanging in an orchard, and whether one must return them.
Relates that a Cuthean sitting in an orchard said the Cuthean's property may be taken.
The Cuthean replies: take the price of an Israelite's item, but do not take the price of the body.
Shmuel rules that the law of the kingdom is law.
Rava supports this with the observation that they cut down palm trees and build bridges, which we cross.
Abaye objects: perhaps the owners despaired of them, so that the king's law does not apply.
Rava replies that if the king's law were not law, how could they have despaired at all.
Objects that the king's men do not act as the king commanded.
Explains that the king's agent acts as the king himself, taking the lawful amount rather than destroying the whole.
Rava rules that whoever is found in the house pays the king's tax, and this applies to a partner.
Rava rules that a tenant pays from his own tenancy, and a town tax is owed only for land and the current year.
Rava rules that one may not buy from residents within the boundary of a town, but may buy from those outside it.
Ravina rules that if owners pursue them, buying is forbidden even outside the boundary.
Rava, or Rav Huna, describes the case of a Jew who was proclaimed and went up and down the town.
Rules that an Israelite who knows testimony for a Cuthean, and testifies against his Jewish friend in Cuthean court, is excommunicated.
Asks the reason for excommunicating such a person.
Answers that the Cutheans extract money, so the testimony causes monetary harm to the Jew.

114a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the rule that a single witness suffices only in certain courts, and not in others, such as the post station case.
Rav Ashi recalls the occasion when he was at the house of Rav Huna.
Raises the dilemma whether a respected man trusted like two witnesses may take money without testifying, and leaves it unresolved.
Asks why an Israelite who sold land to an idolater next to a fellow Israelite is excommunicated.
Proposes that the reason is the neighbor's right of first refusal, as in a case of the land of a neighbor.
Objects: the master said one may buy from and sell to idolaters, so no neighbor's right applies.
Explains the penalty as a condition: the seller is excommunicated until he accepts liability for all harm arising from the land.
Mishna: if tax collectors take a donkey and give another, or robbers take a cloak and return another, these are his, since owners despaired.
Mishna: an item rescued from a river, from a troop, or from bandits belongs to the rescuer if the owners despaired; likewise a swarm of bees.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka holds a woman or minor is believed to say a swarm came from a certain place, and one may enter to save it.
Rules that one may not cut down his neighbor's sukkah on condition of paying the price.
Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka, permits cutting it down while paying the price.
Baraita: one who takes the item returns it to the earlier owners, since despair does not acquire, with other versions and the mishna's conclusion.
Rav Ashi holds the rule applies only to robbers who are idolaters, not to Israelite bandits, and states his reasoning.
Rav Yosef objects: the opposite is more reasonable, since an idolater's court judging by his own law does not show despair for Israelites.
Qualifies the reading: the restriction concerns idolaters judging in their courts, but for Israelite bandits the owners do not despair.
Cites the mishna on hides: the owner's hides are impure if he intended them, but a robber's and a thief's are not, per Rabbi Shimon's reversal.
Ulla holds the dispute concerns the unspecified case, and in a known case all agree that despair acquires.
Rabbah holds that even in the known case there is a dispute.
Abaye objects to Rabbah: do not dispute Ulla's view, since the mishna follows it, because the owners did not despair.
Rabbah replies: we teach the mishna because there is no despair in the owner's view, as the mishna's tax collector case shows.
Asks whether the mishna follows the Sages or Rabbi Shimon, and which case is the robber and which the thief.
Explains that Ulla's view works for all parties, while Rabbah needs the mishna to follow Rabbi Shimon for an armed bandit.
Concludes that if so, the robber is of two kinds, which matches the distinction being drawn.
Objects with a baraita listing thief, robber, and forcer with their consecrated and tithed goods, which may conflict with the reading.
Repeats the explanation for Ulla and Rabbah, concluding that the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon on an armed bandit.
Concludes that the mishna's distinction is consistent with a robber being of two kinds.
Suggests the mishna is Rabbi's own, citing Rabbi's teaching that a thief is like a robber.

114b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that the rule stands: a thief is treated like a robber, following Rabbi Shimon, as Rabbi says.
Raises a dilemma whether Rabbi means the thief is like a robber under the Sages, without acquisition, or under Rabbi Shimon, with acquisition.
Cites a baraita on tax collectors taking a donkey as a source to test the dilemma.
Asks whose view the tax collector baraita follows: the Sages or Rabbi Shimon, and which party is the thief.
Argues that if Rabbi follows Rabbi Shimon, acquisition holds, but if he follows the Sages, the baraita fits no known authority.
Resolves the baraita: it concerns an armed bandit, following Rabbi Shimon, which yields two kinds of robber.
Cites another baraita on a thief, robber, and forcer, with consecrated and tithed goods, as a further test.
Asks whose view that baraita follows, the Sages or Rabbi Shimon, and whether a thief is treated like a robber.
Explains that if Rabbi follows Rabbi Shimon, acquisition holds, and the armed bandit case again yields two kinds of robber.
Rav Ashi objects to Rabbah with a baraita: Rabbi taught Rabbi Shimon that even a plow cow must be returned for the father's honor.
Concludes that since the reason is the father's honor, Rabbi must be speaking of a robber in Rabbi Shimon's view.
Mishna clause: a swarm of bees likewise belongs to the rescuer.
Asks what the word likewise means here, and what it teaches.
Explains that even a swarm of bees, a rabbinic acquisition, could be thought to be acquired anyway; the teaching is that owners' despair makes it his.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka holds that a woman or minor is believed to say a swarm came from a particular place.
Objects that a woman and a minor are competent witnesses, so the view is not conclusive on its own.
Rav Yehuda, in Shmuel's name, explains the case: owners pursue the swarm and a woman or minor innocently speaks of its origin.
Rav Ashi holds an innocent speaker is valid only for a woman's testimony, not a minor's.
Ravina objects that a swarm of bees differs, since its acquisition is rabbinic and not Torah law.
Objects with Shmuel's account of a man who spoke innocently about his childhood and was given priestly food.
Relates the anecdote of the man who was raised to the priesthood by Rabbi's decision on the basis of his innocent speech.
Objects with the report of a similar case that came before Rav Dimi.
Relates the case of a boy who spoke innocently about his captive mother and was given priesthood, showing leniency.
Baraita fragment: one may not cut down a neighbor's sukkah.
Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka: it is a court condition to enter and cut or save, with payment from the other's swarm.
Mishna: if a man recognizes his utensils and books in another's hand and a theft was reported in town, the buyer swears how much he paid.
Asks what should be feared: perhaps the holder sold the items and is now producing them himself.
Rav clarifies the case: people came into the house, one stood and shouted that his utensils were stolen at night.
Rav Kahana relates the case of a breach through which household members carried utensils out on their shoulders, with all calling them stolen.
Objects: perhaps the items were not utensils but books, or the carried goods were small items in place of larger ones.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba explains Rabbi Yohanan: the case is where they also name books, and the loss was assumed for the larger goods.
Rabbi Yose bar Hanina qualifies: the case is where they name a book, but perhaps the old ones were carried and the new ones were claimed.
Rav gives an example: they say these items belong to a certain man and these books to another.
Objects that Rav said otherwise: one who entered through a breach, took utensils and left is exempt.
Explains Rav's ruling: exemption applies only to one who came through the breach from the start, risking his life, and not to others.
Rava states that the restriction applies only to a householder who is accustomed to selling his utensils, not one who is not.

115a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that no return is needed at all, since the seller perhaps needed money and sold the item himself.
Rav Ashi states the case: a thief's reputation has gone out in town.
Reports two traditions on a thief who sold and was later identified: Rabbi Hiyya's view and Rabbi Yohanan's, in Rabbi Yanai's name.
Rav Yosef reconciles them: before despair the second buyer prevails, after despair the first; both accept Rav Hisda's view.
Abaye objects that the two do not really disagree, since priestly gifts before despair are taken as stated.
Cites a mishna on a cow's innards, with priestly gifts that the butcher or buyer must give to the priest and deduct.
Rav explains the mishna: only where the buyer weighed for himself; if the butcher weighed, the butcher is responsible.
Explains Abaye's position through Rav Zevid: the dispute concerns owners despairing in the buyer's hand, not the thief's.
Holds that despair followed by change of ownership acquires, while change followed by despair does not, and the rule is uniform.
Rav Pappa holds all agree a cloak returns to its owner; the dispute concerns items sold in the market-custom case.
Rav, in Rabbi Hiyya's name, holds the first owner prevails, since the buyer may collect from the thief, and no market custom applies.
Rabbi Yohanan, in Rabbi Yanai's name, holds the second owner prevails, the buyer collecting from the householder under market custom.
Objects with a case where Rav Huna's student Hanan the Wicked stole a cloak and sold it.
Rav Huna rules that Hanan the Wicked's sale stands because the owner cannot recover from him, so the cloak is treated as identified.
Rava rules that a known thief gets no market custom protection.
Objects that Hanan the Wicked was well known, yet market custom was applied to him, so the rule cannot be that simple.
States the rule: where a thief paid his debt from his own assets, market custom does not apply to the buyer.
Gives the reasoning and example: money lent against a pledge, valued at market price, falls under market custom.
Ameimar holds market custom does not apply; Mar Zutra holds it does, and the halakha follows the latter.
Offers Zavina's case of an item sold at equal value, showing market custom applies to a fair sale.
Rav Sheshet holds market custom does not apply; Rava holds it does, and the halakha follows him in all cases.
Excepts a thief who paid his debt from his own assets, or from his surroundings, from the general rule.
Relates Avimi bar Nazi's case, where a cloak was taken as security for a loan and the thief was later identified.
Ravina rules that a thief who paid his debt takes back the first money, and the second creditor's money is returned first.
Rav Kahana objects: perhaps the cloak was given along with the first money, so the ruling does not follow.
Ravina replies that the creditor is trusted just as he was trusted at first.
The case reached Rabbi Abbahu, who rules that the halakha follows Rav Kahana.
Relates the case of a stolen book sold to a Pefunah dealer and then to a buyer, with Abaye's proposed resolution.
Rava objects: a buyer from a thief has market custom protection, so a buyer from a buyer raises a different question.
Rava's resolution: the book owner pays the second buyer and collects from the Pefunah dealer and the first buyer.
Mishna: one man's jar of wine and another's jug of honey; if the honey jar cracks and one saves the honey by pouring wine into it.

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rules that a rescuer who saves his friend's donkey during a flood is entitled only to his wages, not to a claim on the friend's goods.
Asks why the rescuer should not claim the goods as ownerless, and whether a teaching says otherwise.
Cites a baraita about one carrying wine and oil who sees the jars breaking and must not declare them tithed produce.
R' Yirmiyah explains that the declaration works only when the press is being pressed and the cloth tied, as in the case described.
Continues the baraita: if he said nothing, he said nothing at all, and the rule is cited accordingly.
Objects with a baraita about a traveler carrying money who is threatened by a bandit and must not declare his produce bound to the money.
Asks what case is meant, and why one able to save the goods at the outset should not declare it.
Explains that one able to save by effort should not declare it, and where loss occurs at the outset he should not declare at all.
Objects with a baraita: a man with ten jars of untithed produce who sees one broken or exposed may not declare it, due to priestly loss.
R' Yirmiyah answers: a broken jar can still be used, so the declaration applies to a broken jar but not an exposed one.
Objects that an exposed jar would be fit only for sprinkling, yet a baraita forbids pouring exposed water in a public domain.
Cites a baraita forbidding various uses of exposed water, including straining through a strainer, following R' Nehemiah.
R' Nehemiah holds that a strainer is a problem only if the lower part is exposed, since a snake's venom floats and stays in place.
Resolves that the ruling applies only if the jar is not sealed, since a sealed jar can be opened by someone placing an item on its mouth.
Asks whether one may separate impure produce from impure produce, citing R' Nehemiah's view.
Objects with a baraita permitting separation from impure to impure, and from pure to impure, but not from impure to pure.
Cites R' Nehemiah's position that even impure over impure is permitted only for doubtful produce, and the same applies here.
Asks why oil is treated differently from wine, given that oil is fit for lighting.
Explains that wine too is fit for sprinkling, and sprinkling is not nothing; so wine should be treated the same.
Objects with Shmuel's statement in Rabbi Hiyya's name: one may drink a measure of wine for a sela and sprinkle a measure for two.
Explains the case is one of a new wine, not the old.
Objects that oil and wine are both fit for others, and the risk to the priest is the same in each case.
Concludes with a tanna's dispute over a jar of wine of terumah that became impure, following the Houses of Shammai.

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Hillel and R' Yishmael son of R' Yosei: pour out all if in a house, but use it for sprinkling in a field; no third ruling settles it.
Sets a case: one tells another that he will save his goods for him, with the rest of the case to follow.
Asks why the rescuer cannot claim he was only joking, and whether a teaching is not clear on this.
Cites a baraita: a prisoner who fled and was carried across by a ferryman for a dinar, who owes only the fare.
Explains that the joking claim does not apply here, since the case resembles only the latter clause of the baraita.
Continues the baraita: if he said the dinar is for the fare and to carry him across, he pays the fare and the rest.
Asks why the first clause and the latter clause of the baraita differ.
Rami bar Hama's case: a fisherman who spoiled a fisherman's net and was told he damaged the nets for a small coin.
Recites the mishna about a flood carrying away a donkey and a friend's donkey, as a source for the rule.
Explains the need for both clauses: where the rescuer acted by hand, he must pay full value; where by itself, only the fare.
Rav Kahana asks Rav whether one who went down to save and the item came up on its own is owed anything.
Rav replies that Heaven loves him, meaning his good deed brings reward.
Relates Rav Sapra's case on the caravan: a lion killed one man each night, and he left a donkey's wine for the lion to drink.
Rav Aha objects to Ravina: why should Rav Sapra acquire it, when the owner abandoned it only expecting the lion, not all?
Rav Sapra replies that his act was for the benefit of the matter, to remove the danger.
Rav asks Rabbi whether one who went down to save and did not save is owed anything.
Rabbi replies that this is a borrowing, so the borrower owes only the fare.
Objects with a baraita on an employer who hires a laborer and the rule that follows.

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A case: one hires a man to bring cabbage and doves to a sick person; he finds him dead or recovered and must pay the wages.
Objects that the cases are not comparable, since the agent there did his mission and here he did not.
Cites a baraita on a caravan in the desert attacked by an army: losses are reckoned by money, not by lives, as the custom of the donkey drivers.
Rules that drivers may stipulate that whoever loses his donkey is replaced by another donkey at the inn, but not if he asks them to watch it.
Explains that the rule is needed where the owner has another donkey, since one guard is different from two.
Cites a baraita on a ship in a storm: losses are reckoned by cargo weight, and the sailors may stipulate replacement at a station.
Sets out the case where a ship goes to a place that ships do not sail to, so no replacement is owed.
Explains the case: in Nisan the distance is one anchor, in Tishrei two; so one may not claim an extra loss from a sea route.
Cites a baraita on a caravan attacked by an army: a member who saves the goods saves them for the middle, or for himself if he said so.
Asks what case is meant by the baraita's terms.
Explains: if he could save everything, even the latter clause means saving for the middle; if not, even the first clause means saving for himself.
Rami bar Hama explains that this concerns partners, where one partner divides without the other's knowledge and the other disagrees.
Rava holds the case concerns laborers, following Rav: a laborer may return even in the middle of the day, and it is as if in the owner's possession.
Cites the verse that the children of Israel are my servants, not servants to servants, as the reason a laborer may leave.
Rav Ashi explains: if he could save by effort, he reveals his intention for himself; if not, he did not reveal intention for the middle.
Mishna: one who takes a field from his fellow and the rain or waterlogging ruins it: if it was from the robber, he must restore another field.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reads the mishna's wording through several verses, to decide whether the loss is from the robber or from the wind.
Concludes the mishna: if the loss is from the robber, he is liable to restore another field.
Asks what the case is: did they seize his land, or only part of it?
Objects that the mishna's first statement already shows the loss is from the robber, so the case must be otherwise.
Explains that the case is needed where the robber showed the field, with a different phrasing of the mishna.
Relates a case where non-Jews took a field, and a man who showed them the field was brought before Rav Nachman, who held him liable.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya asks Rav Nachman whether the ruling is a judgment or a penalty.
Rav Nachman replies that it is our mishna, and the matter of showing applies after the robber has departed.
Rav Yosef asks Rav Huna bar Hiyya what difference the ruling makes to him.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a rule is a judgment or a penalty, since the derivation depends on which it is.
Asks what proof shows that one does not derive rules from a penalty.
Cites a baraita: earlier they said the one who defiles and the one who pours a libation, then the one who separates terumah, a rule applied to the penalty case.
Explains that the Sages at first feared a larger loss and not a smaller one, and later feared even the smaller loss.
Objects with a teaching of Abba, father of Rabbi Abin: earlier they said the defiler and terumah, and later the libation.
Asks the reason for the change in the Sages' view.
Explains that the reason is they do not derive from a penalty; at first they followed Rabbi Abin, and later Rabbi Yirmiyah.
Rabbi Abin rules that one who throws an arrow and tears a shirt is exempt in his walking, since lifting and placing is one act; Rabbi Yirmiyah holds the acquisition at lifting.
Narrates that Rav Huna bar Yehuda came to Rava's house, bringing a case where a Jew was forced by idolaters.
Rava asks whether a case came into Rav Huna's hands of a Jew forced by idolaters who showed another's property.
Rav Huna replies that he held the Jew liable, since the property came into his hands.
Rava objects: return the case to its owner, for it is taught that a Jew forced by idolaters who showed another's property is exempt.
Rabbah rules that if the Jew showed it on his own, it is like taking and giving it into the hand, so he is liable.
Relates a case where forced idolaters seized a Jew and he showed a jar of another, and Rav Ashi exempted him.
The Sages object to Rav Ashi: but it is taught that if he took and gave it into the hand, he is liable.
Rav Ashi explains: that holds where he did not first place the item on him; where it was placed on him from the start, the lighter ruling applies.
Rabbi Abbahu objects to Rav Ashi with a baraita: if a forced man handed over a bundle of straw or grapes, he is liable.
Narrates a case where two claimed a found item, and one brought it to the king's officer.
Abaye holds that the one who gave it up may say it was his, since he handed over his own.
Rava objects: everything depends on the one who holds the item, so this is not the right conclusion.
Rava rules that one is held in ban until he produces the item and stands before the court.
Relates a case where a man wanted to show, and his fellow came before Rav, who insisted that he show it.
Relates Rav Kahana sitting before Rav, and a stick slipping from Rav's hand as he read a verse.
Rav reads the verse about children lying at the head of every street like an antelope in a net, to argue that the property of Israel is not pitied once it falls into idolaters' hands.
Restates the rule: once Israel's property falls into the hands of idolaters, no pity is owed to it.
Rav Kahana replies: until now the Persians did not mind bloodshed, but now the Greeks do; go up to the land of Israel and do not contradict Rabbi Yohanan.
Narrates that for seven years one went to find Resh Lakish seated and reciting the day's lesson to the Sages.
Resh Lakish raised difficulties and resolutions; the Sages asked him and he went on.
Relates that Rabbi Yohanan said to Resh Lakish, a lion came from Babylon to study with him, and he rejected his teaching for seven generations.
Rabbi Yohanan says to Resh Lakish: you said you would become a fox; Resh Lakish replies he hopes these seven generations will be reversed.
Resh Lakish restates his teaching, raising and resolving objections, and is answered in the first generation.
Relates that Rabbi Yohanan sat with a shackle, a large old man was sitting, and was pulled and tested by Resh Lakish.
Relates Rabbi Yohanan's death: Resh Lakish's mockery upset him, and he died.
Rabbi Yohanan asks the Sages to see how the Babylonian Resh Lakish behaves.
The Sages reply that his ways are like this: he sits by the cave, and was seen doing so.

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates Akha's exchange with his teacher: the master enters first to the student, and the teacher opens the door, with the anecdote on how doubts were resolved.
Narrates a case where Rav Ila sat with Rabbi Abbahu and others, and wanted to hold a man liable on the basis of a mishna.
Cites the mishna: a judge who acquits the guilty and convicts the innocent, and must pay from his own pocket.
Rav Ila replies: Rav's rule covers one who took and gave an item into the hand; the case goes to the court of Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim.
Narrates a case where a man's silver cup was stolen by robbers, he gave it to them, and Rabbah exempted him.
Abaye objects: this man saves himself with another's money.
Rav Ashi explains: one must consider whether a wealthy man acted with his own money, or whether they came for the silver.
Narrates a case where a man's bag for ransom of captives was stolen and he surrendered it, and Rava exempted him.
Abaye objects again: but this man saves himself with another's money.
Rava replies: there is no greater ransom of captives than this.
Narrates a case where a man's donkey was loaded onto a ferry, and another drowned it; Rabbah exempted the drowner.
Abaye objects again that the man saves himself with another's money.
Explains Rabbah's consistency: the pursuer's pursued property, and one may not save oneself by another's money.
Rules that one who breaks the pursuer's vessels to save the pursued is exempt, and a stranger's property is liable, by the reason of saving another from a pursuer.
Mishna: if a river washed away his field, the owner says to him: here is yours before you.
Baraita: if one stole a field and a river washed it away, he must restore another field, per R' Elazar; the Sages say the owner says here is yours.
Asks in what the two sides dispute.
R' Elazar derives from the verses the general and particular inclusions and exclusions, while the Sages derive from general and particular categories.
Objects with a baraita on a cow: one who stole a cow and a river washed it away must restore a cow per R' Elazar, yet the Sages say here is yours.
Asks in what case they dispute.
Rav Pappa resolves: the case is one where he stole a field from his fellow and it was washed away.

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Summarizes the dispute on a cow lying in a field that a river washed away: R' Elazar follows his view and the Sages follow theirs.
Mishna: one who robbed or borrowed from his fellow, or deposited with him in a settled area, need not return it in the desert, but if he went out to the desert he must return it there.
Objects with a contrary teaching: a loan can be collected anywhere, but lost items and deposits only where they were left.
Abaye explains the teaching: a loan may be claimed anywhere, but deposits only at their place, unless the depositor was going into the desert too.
Mishna: one who says you robbed me, lent me, or left a deposit, and he does not know whether he returned it, is liable; if he says he does not know, he is exempt.
Reports disputes over a claim of a mina that the other party says he does not know: some hold liable, others exempt, reasoning from the presumption of ownership.
Restates the mishna's clause: if he says he does not know whether I lent it, he is exempt from paying.
Asks how the two clauses can be read, if the claimant never sued.
Explains that the claimant did sue, and the first clause concerns one who must leave with a clear conscience before heaven.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that one who says he does not know whether a mina is his is liable before heaven.
Mishna: one who takes a lamb from the flock, returns it, and it dies or is stolen is liable, but if owners do not know, and counted the flock, he is exempt.
Rav holds the exemption requires knowledge that counts, and the mishna's wording that it is whole implies that counting alone exempts.
Shmuel holds the exemption applies whether or not the owners know, and counting in whole is what exempts.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that knowing the count exempts, and where unknowing no counting is needed, as the first clause shows.
Rav Hisda holds that knowing counts, while the unknowing needs knowledge, and the first clause shows this.
Rava's position begins, and the daf breaks off here.

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks the reason for Rav Hisda's ruling, since the teaching was taken up and Rava said so.
Objects with Rava's ruling: one who sees a fellow take a lamb from the flock and throws it, and it is lost, is liable though he did not count.
Asks whether the case of not counting is the same as the case of not knowing.
Objects that Rav said so, yet Rav also said that one who returned it to the flock in the desert is exempt.
Rabbi Hanan bar Abba says Rav concedes in the case of Rekuta, and asks whether it is a dispute between Tannaim.
Baraita: one who stole a lamb from the flock or a sela from the purse must return it to the place of the theft, per R' Yishmael; R' Akiva requires the owner's knowledge.
Explains the disputes: whether the sela is known or unknown, and whether a guard who stole from his master's premises must return it to the place of theft.
Cites a baraita in which one teacher says a robber who hid the item in the count is exempt, and another says he is not exempt.
Resolves that the two teachings dispute only Rabbi Yitzhak's view that a man checks his purse constantly, depending on whether one holds it.
Explains the cases: one had the item placed in his purse, another in his hand, and another had other coins in his purse.
Mishna: one may not buy wool, milk or kids from shepherds, or from keepers of fruit, wood, and produce, but may buy from women wool, linen vessels and eggs.
Baraita: one may not buy goats, kids or shearings from shepherds, but may buy sewn items, milk and cheese in the desert, not in town.
Baraita: one may buy four or five sheep and four or five shearings, but not two sheep or two shearings.
Rabbi Yehudah holds that one may buy from domesticated flocks, not wild ones; the general rule is that anything the shepherd sells and the owner notices may be bought.
Asks whether, if one may buy four or five sheep, the case of buying five needs a separate ruling.
Rav Hisda explains: four out of five, or four from a small flock and five from a large one, and resolves the apparent conflict.
Resolves the contradiction: one teaching is about domesticated flocks and the other about the case of a lamb of the shearer.
Rabbi Yehudah repeats: from domesticated flocks one may buy, from wild ones not.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yehudah's words refer to the first clause, which is stricter, or to the latter clause, which is more lenient.
Objects with a baraita: Rabbi Yehudah says one may buy from domesticated flocks and not from wild ones, and everywhere one may buy four or five sheep.

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that since the rule is stated everywhere, it follows the latter clause and is the lenient reading, not the mishna on fruit keepers.
Reports that Rav bought a tenant's produce, which is the case under discussion.
Abaye objects: but we learned that one may not buy from fruit keepers of wood and fruit.
Rav's reply: the rule concerns a keeper who has no share in the land, whereas a tenant with an interest sells on his own account.
Cites a baraita on buying from fruit keepers while they sit selling, and the rule against buying from the back of the garden.
Sets up the question of when one may buy from a robber: Rav says once most of the goods are his, Shmuel says even a minority.
Reports Rav's and Shmuel's positions and Rav Yehudah's ruling for Ada the broker, that money entrusted to others can be claimed.
Rav Hisda and Rav Huna dispute whether one may destroy his property to deny a robber, citing the verse about the righteous inheriting the spoils.
Narrates that Rav Hisda had a tenant who withheld and gave less, and who took the grain for himself.
Cites the verse that the wealth of the sinner is stored for the righteous, to ground the case.
Cites the verse about the godless man's hope, and that God takes a man's soul when he takes unjust gain.
Rav Huna and Rav Hisda dispute whose soul is at stake: the robbed man's or the robber's.
Cites the verse that such are the ways of everyone greedy for gain, who takes the life of its owner.
Argues from the verse not to rob the poor and the verse that God will plead their cause and take the soul of those who take it.
Objects: the other verse also says he will take the soul of its owner, so the reading must be fixed.
Explains that the verse means the one who takes the soul is the one who takes, because they take a soul.
Rabbi Yohanan says whoever robs his fellow of a perutah is as if he takes his soul, citing the verse about the ways of the greedy.
Cites verses that a man's harvest and his children are eaten, and that blood spilled by Judah and Saul's house is counted against them.
Objects: the soul spoken of is his own, not the soul of his sons and daughters.
Objects with a verse on the flesh of sons and daughters; perhaps this holds only where the robber did not pay.
Objects with the verse on innocent blood: perhaps this applies only where done by hand, not where merely causing harm.
Explains Saul's killing of the Gibeonites: the verse counts him as having killed them, since he killed the city of priests that supplied them.
Concludes that one may buy from women.
Baraita: one may buy from women wool vessels in Judah and linen vessels in the Galilee, but not wine, oil or flour, nor from slaves or children.
Rules that alms collectors may be bought from for small amounts only, and that dealers may buy olives by measure.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says one may buy olives from women during the festival in the upper Galilee, since a man is ashamed to sell at his door.
Narrates that Ravina visited Mahoza, where women came before him with bracelets and remnants, and he accepted them.
Rabbah says to Ravina: but it is taught that alms collectors may take a small amount but not a large one.
Ravina replies that these are small things for the people of Mahoza.
Mishna: the launderer's lint is his; the carder's lint belongs to the owner; the launderer takes three threads; the tailor's remnant of three by three belongs to the owner.
Baraita: one may buy lint from the launderer, since it is his, and the launderer takes the two top threads, which are his.

119b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah rules on how far a carder may card, stretch, and even out cloth.
Objection: the baraita says two threads but the mishnah says three.
Reconciles the two rulings by thick versus thin threads.
Baraita: carding is done along the weft, not the warp.
Another baraita seems to state the opposite rule.
Reconciles them: ordinary garment versus elegant cape.
Baraita: no more than three stitches per loop in the cloth.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether drawing the needle in and out counts as one stitch or two; unresolved.
Baraita: evening out cloth is done lengthwise, not widthwise.
Another baraita seems to state the opposite.
Reconciles them: a garment versus a belt.
Tosefta: what may be bought from a carder, and cushions or mattresses stuffed with strands.
Asks why the cushion or mattress purchase is permitted.
The strands were transformed by a change of form, so the buyer acquires them.
Tosefta: what may and may not be bought from a weaver.
Asks why woven wool is mentioned if spun wool is already permitted.
Tosefta: what may and may not be bought from a dyer.
Asks why clothes are mentioned if spun threads are already permitted.
Tosefta: the tanner's trimmings belong to the customer, the washing residue to the tanner.
Mishnah case: the threads were black on a white garment.
Rav Yehuda: a launderer is called katzra and takes the short shreds.
Rav Yehuda: all threads count toward the measure; Yitzhak is particular about them.
Mishnah: a tailor's leftover thread belongs to the customer.
Asks how much thread is needed in order to sew.
Rav Asi: enough thread equal to a needle's length beyond the needle.
Dilemma: is it a needle's length, or a needle's length plus any amount?
Brings a baraita on a tailor's thread shorter than needed to sew, tied to customer's inclination.
If the needle-length rule holds, why state less than that measure?
Alternatively, if the rule is a needle plus any amount, the phrasing is odd.
Concludes the baraita supports the view of a needle's length beyond the needle.
Quotes the mishnah phrase on the sawed or cut-off piece of wood.
A baraita seems to contradict the mishnah on which tools belong to whom.
Rava reconciles by noting the two tool names refer to different regional usage.
Mishnah case: a craftsman working at the owner's place.
Baraita: stone cutting and pruning and weeding do not count as theft unless the owner is particular.
Rav Yehuda: twigs and branches are not theft, but in a place where owners care they are.
Ravina: the particular locale is what matters for the theft rule.
Closing formula ending the chapter and the tractate Bava Kamma.
